title: Frictions in Shadow Banking: Evidence from the Lending Behavior of Money Market Funds

new_fields.research_question: Do frictions in short-term, market-based lending by money market mutual funds create a channel through which risk taking by these intermediaries generates negative spillovers, disrupting the ability of unrelated, creditworthy non-European firms to raise short-term financing when the funds' investors withdraw capital? The paper further asks whether lender-borrower relationships matter in supposedly arm's-length short-term credit markets.
new_fields.data_description: The authors construct a novel dataset of security-level holdings of U.S. prime money market mutual funds (MMMFs), observing which funds hold which issuers' short-term debt (commercial paper and similar instruments). The data allow construction of fund-issuer pairs and measurement of each fund's exposure to Eurozone banks. Aggregate weekly MMMF assets come from the Investment Company Institute. The analysis centers on two symmetric three-month windows in 2011: a pre-period (March–May 2011) before large investor redemptions and a post-period (June–August 2011) during the redemption episode. Key variables include fund-level Eurozone bank exposure, fund flows/redemptions, fund yields, issuer-fund lending amounts, issuer characteristics (size, credit rating, nationality), and measures of relationship strength between funds and issuers. Primary observations are at the fund-issuer-period level for cross-sectional change regressions, supplemented by fund-level flow regressions.
new_fields.institutional_context: During 2010–2011, mounting fears over peripheral Eurozone sovereign debt (Greece, Ireland, Portugal) raised concerns about Eurozone banks holding that debt. On June 15, 2011, Moody's placed three major French banks (BNP Paribas, Credit Agricole, Societe Generale) on review for downgrade due to Greek exposures. This announcement triggered a 'slow-motion run' on U.S. prime MMMFs: aggregate assets fell roughly $180 billion (11%) between June 8 and August 31, 2011—the largest three-month decline outside the 2008 crisis. Crucially, MMMFs differed substantially in their pre-existing exposure to Eurozone bank debt (over a quarter of prime MMMF assets in May 2011), generating plausibly exogenous cross-sectional variation in the funding shock hitting otherwise similar funds. Because MMMFs lend to many non-European issuers as well, the same issuer often borrowed from both high- and low-Eurozone-exposure funds, allowing comparisons of lending changes to the same borrower across differently shocked lenders.

title: Do Private Firms Invest Differently than Public Firms? Taking Cues from the Natural Gas Industry

new_fields.research_question: Does a firm's listing status (public versus private) causally affect its investment responsiveness to changes in investment opportunities? Specifically, do private firms respond differently than public firms when output prices rise or when new growth opportunities emerge, and does this differ by the capital intensity of the project?
new_fields.data_description: The authors assemble a project-level panel of 74,670 individual drilling projects in the U.S. onshore natural gas exploration and production industry, covering both publicly listed and privately held firms. For each project, they observe detailed characteristics including location (county), capital requirements, ownership, well-level output/production, and transfers of asset ownership over time. They complement this with natural gas prices (across regions), hand-collected capital expenditure and well-count data from 10-K filings of SIC 1311 public firms (2006–2009), shale discovery dates and locations for 102 counties, IPO activity of sample firms, and stock market reactions to asset acquisitions. The unit of observation is the project (well/tract), aggregated to firm-county-year for several tests. The sample spans the period surrounding major U.S. shale discoveries.
new_fields.institutional_context: The U.S. natural gas industry provides an unusually clean setting because output is a fungible commodity sold at prices set in a competitive market, so public and private producers face essentially identical output prices, similar per-well costs (no meaningful scale economies in drilling costs), and comparable technology. Two sources of plausibly exogenous variation in investment opportunities are exploited: (1) fluctuations in natural gas prices, which shift the profitability of drilling for all firms symmetrically, and (2) the discovery of economically viable shale formations in specific counties, which represent large, localized, capital-intensive growth opportunities arriving at discrete points in time. Shale discoveries in 102 counties create a before/after contrast for firms operating in affected versus unaffected areas, while detailed tracking of tract ownership permits observation of asset sales between private and public firms following these discoveries.

title: The Price of Sin: The Effects of Social Norms on Markets

new_fields.research_question: Do societal norms against vice-related businesses affect financial markets by shaping who owns these stocks, how they are priced, and the returns they earn? Specifically, does norm-based avoidance by certain investor classes depress prices and generate higher expected returns for companies producing alcohol, tobacco, and gaming, and do affected firms alter their financing decisions in response?
new_fields.data_description: The authors assemble firm-level data on publicly traded U.S. 'sin' stocks—companies producing alcohol, tobacco, and gaming—and compare them to industry comparables using Fama-French (1997) industry groupings. Stock return data span 1926-2004 (from CRSP); cross-sectional return analyses with firm characteristics cover 1965-2004; institutional ownership data cover 1980-2003 (broken down by banks, insurance companies, mutual funds, independent investment advisors including hedge funds, and others such as pension plans and universities); analyst coverage data cover 1976-2003 (from I/B/E/S); and capital structure (leverage) data cover 1962-2003 (from Compustat). Key variables include institutional ownership shares, analyst coverage counts, monthly returns, market-to-book ratios, market capitalization, past returns, and leverage ratios. The unit of observation is the firm (or firm-month/firm-year).
new_fields.institutional_context: Identification leverages the fact that alcohol, tobacco, and gaming firms are subject to a widespread societal norm against vice, which constrains investors whose holdings are visible or scrutinized (pension funds, universities, religious organizations, banks, insurance companies) but not less-constrained arbitrageurs (mutual funds, hedge funds) or individual investors. Comparisons against carefully chosen industry-comparable non-sin firms isolate the effect of sin status from industry- and characteristic-based heterogeneity. The paper additionally exploits time variation in norms: smoking was not broadly viewed as a vice until the 1960s, generating a shift in the social acceptability of tobacco that can be used to compare tobacco-stock outcomes before and after this change. Heightened litigation risk (e.g., tobacco litigation prior to the 1997 state settlement) reinforces the norm-based channel affecting valuations.

title: Hedge Fund Activism, Corporate Governance, and Firm Performance

new_fields.research_question: Does intervention by activist hedge funds in publicly traded firms create value for target-firm shareholders, and does it lead to real changes in corporate policies, operating performance, executive turnover, and compensation? Specifically, how do stock prices respond around the announcement of activist intervention, and do post-intervention changes in payout, leverage, profitability, and CEO outcomes persist?
new_fields.data_description: The authors hand-collect a comprehensive dataset of hedge fund activism episodes in U.S. public firms from 2001 through 2006, identified primarily through Schedule 13D filings with the SEC (which must be filed when an investor acquires more than 5% of a firm's shares with an intent to influence). The sample includes both hostile and non-hostile interventions, stated activist objectives (strategic, operational, financial, governance), ownership stakes, holding periods, and exit information. They merge these events with stock returns (for abnormal return analysis in a (-20,+20) window and 1-year post-announcement drift), accounting data on payout, leverage, EBITDA/Assets, EBITDA/Sales, return on assets, CEO compensation and turnover, institutional ownership, analyst coverage and ratings, and takeover defenses. Observations are at the target-firm/activism-event level, with matched control firms by industry, size, and valuation.
new_fields.institutional_context: The setting exploits the U.S. disclosure regime under Section 13(d) of the Securities Exchange Act, which requires any investor acquiring beneficial ownership exceeding 5% of a public firm's equity with an intent to influence control or policy to file a Schedule 13D within 10 days. This filing is a discrete, publicly observable event that reveals the activist's identity, stake, and stated objectives, providing a clean announcement date for measuring market reactions. Passive holders instead file Schedule 13G, and larger institutions file quarterly Form 13F holdings reports. Hedge funds differ from mutual funds and pension funds because they are largely unregulated, use high-powered incentive contracts, can take concentrated and leveraged positions, and face fewer conflicts of interest with target management. The 2001–2006 period witnessed a marked rise in such activism, following the decline of 1980s-style control-oriented blockholder activism after the proliferation of takeover defenses.

title: Markup Pricing in Mergers and Acquisitions

new_fields.research_question: Do pre-announcement stock price runups in target firms substitute for, or add to, the post-announcement premium paid by bidders in successful takeovers? In other words, when a target's stock price rises before a formal bid (potentially reflecting leaked information or anticipated bids), does the eventual bidder pay a lower offer premium dollar-for-dollar, or does the runup get added to the final deal price, making it a net cost to the acquirer?
new_fields.data_description: The study uses a sample of 1,398 successful tender offers and mergers involving NYSE- and Amex-listed target firms over the period 1975-1991. Key variables include daily target stock returns used to construct the pre-bid runup (abnormal target returns during the period before the initial formal bid announcement) and the post-bid markup (abnormal target returns from the first bid announcement date through the final resolution of the deal). These combine to form the total control premium. The analysis also incorporates deal- and information-related covariates such as the form of payment (cash vs. stock), whether the deal is a tender offer or merger, the presence of multiple competing bidders, prior 13D filings indicating toehold purchases above 5%, and other pre-bid public news. The unit of observation is a successful M&A transaction.
new_fields.institutional_context: U.S. takeover regulation and disclosure rules create a well-defined timeline that enables the decomposition of the total premium into a pre-bid runup and a post-bid markup. Before a formal bid, the bidder's intentions are private information, but leakage, toehold accumulation, or illegal insider trading can cause the target's stock price to rise. SEC rules requiring 13D filings when an investor crosses the 5% ownership threshold, together with public announcements and press reports, generate observable events that can legitimately move prices before a bid. Once the first bid is announced, the target is publicly 'in play,' potentially triggering competing bids and auction-like dynamics until a final outcome is reached. Contemporary SEC insider-trading prosecutions (e.g., Boesky, Levine) and shareholder lawsuits alleging that leaks inflated acquisition prices motivate testing whether runups substitute for, or add to, final deal prices.

title: Testing Asymmetric-Information Asset Pricing Models

new_fields.research_question: Does the degree of information asymmetry among investors causally affect equilibrium asset prices and investor demands, and if so, through what channel? Specifically, do increases in asymmetric information lower stock prices and reduce uninformed (retail) investors' demand, and does liquidity risk mediate this relationship?
new_fields.data_description: The study combines several U.S. equity market datasets covering Q1 2000 through Q1 2008. Sell-side analyst coverage data are used to identify 4,429 stock-level coverage terminations arising from 43 brokerage research department closures, plus terminations triggered by the September 11, 2001 attacks, and exogenous coverage initiations. Stock prices and returns come from standard market data sources, used to compute daily cumulative abnormal returns against market-model and alternate benchmarks. Institutional holdings data (13F-type) and retail trading measures capture demand responses. Additional variables include bid-ask spreads and other information-asymmetry proxies, turnover, payoff-uncertainty measures, and liquidity-risk betas constructed following Acharya and Pedersen (2005). The unit of observation is the stock-event, with daily frequency around termination/initiation announcements.
new_fields.institutional_context: Between 2000 and 2008, 43 U.S. brokerage firms shut down their equity research departments, abruptly ending analyst coverage for thousands of stocks. These closures were driven by the brokerages' own economics (e.g., post-Global Settlement pressures), not by analysts' private information about covered firms' prospects, and were publicly announced via termination notices and financial media. Because retail investors disproportionately rely on analyst-produced public signals while institutions have in-house research, losing an analyst plausibly widens the information gap between these groups without conveying news about firm fundamentals. A second shock exploits the September 11, 2001 destruction of analyst workplaces, which exogenously reduced coverage for a subset of stocks. A third setting uses exogenous increases in coverage. Together these shocks provide variation in information asymmetry that is arguably orthogonal to firms' expected future payoffs, enabling identification of price and demand effects.

title: The Value of Bank Durability: Borrowers as Bank Stakeholders

new_fields.research_question: Do borrowing firms bear significant costs when their lending bank unexpectedly faces insolvency, and do they benefit when the bank's durability is restored through government intervention? In other words, are borrowers stakeholders in their banks because of relationship-specific quasi rents generated by private information and monitoring, rather than merely recipients of fungible public-information-based credit?
new_fields.data_description: The sample consists of publicly traded U.S. firms with publicly documented lending relationships with Continental Illinois Bank (including direct loans, syndicated loans where Continental Illinois served as lead manager or participant, and other credit facilities) during 1984. Lending relationships were identified from public disclosures. The authors compute daily excess stock returns around specific announcement dates associated with the bank's de facto failure and its subsequent FDIC rescue. Cross-sectional regressions relate client firm abnormal returns to characteristics including client leverage, size of the credit facility, whether the firm has contemporaneous lending relations with other banks, whether Continental Illinois served as direct lender versus syndicate participant, and whether the firm has publicly traded debt. At year-end 1983, Continental Illinois was the seventh largest U.S. bank holding company.
new_fields.institutional_context: In 1984, Continental Illinois Bank—then the seventh largest U.S. bank holding company and a major corporate lender and syndicated-loan manager—experienced an unexpected de facto failure followed by an unprecedented FDIC rescue in which regulators took direct control while keeping the bank operating as a publicly traded, government-supported institution. This episode generated two plausibly exogenous, sharply dated shocks to bank durability: a sequence of announcements revealing impending insolvency (reducing expected bank continuation) and the subsequent rescue announcement (restoring durability). Because the shocks originated in the bank and were unrelated to borrowers' own fundamentals, and because this was the last major bank crisis before the 'too big to fail' doctrine was formally articulated, the setting provides cleanly identified variation in the continuation value of bank-borrower relationships for firms with documented ties to Continental Illinois.

title: Bank Governance, Regulation, and Risk Taking

new_fields.research_question: How does a bank's ownership structure influence its risk-taking behavior, and how does the effect of national bank regulations (capital requirements, deposit insurance, activity restrictions) on bank risk depend on the comparative power of shareholders within the bank's corporate governance structure? Additionally, how do shareholder protection laws mediate the influence of large owners on bank risk?
new_fields.data_description: The authors compile a new cross-country bank-level database covering up to 296 publicly listed banks across 48 countries, focusing on the 10 largest banks by total assets (as of end-2001) in countries for which La Porta et al. (1998) provide shareholder rights data; New Zealand is excluded. Ownership variables include whether the bank is widely-held (no owner with ≥10% voting rights), voting and cash-flow rights of the largest owner, voting and cash-flow rights of senior managers, board representation of large owners, and family ownership. Three bank-level risk measures are used: the z-score (inverse probability of insolvency), equity return volatility, and earnings volatility. Country-level controls include bank regulations (capital stringency, deposit insurance, activity restrictions) and shareholder protection laws.
new_fields.institutional_context: Identification leverages cross-country variation in bank regulations and shareholder protection laws combined with bank-level variation in ownership concentration. Countries differ substantially in capital adequacy requirements, the generosity and design of deposit insurance schemes, and restrictions on banks engaging in non-lending activities such as securities and insurance underwriting. They also differ in the strength of legal protections for minority shareholders, as measured by La Porta et al. (1998). Within each country, banks vary in whether they are widely-held or have a controlling shareholder with substantial cash-flow and voting rights, and in whether managers hold equity stakes. This two-level variation—national regulatory and legal environments interacted with bank-specific governance structures—allows the authors to test whether the marginal effect of regulation on risk differs systematically across banks with different ownership concentrations, and whether powerful shareholders matter less where legal protections for small owners are strong.

title: When Does the Market Matter? Stock Prices and the Investment of Equity-Dependent Firms

new_fields.research_question: Does nonfundamental variation in a firm's stock price causally affect its real investment decisions, and is this effect concentrated among firms that must rely on external equity to finance marginal investments? More broadly, when does stock market mispricing matter for the real economy through the corporate investment channel?
new_fields.data_description: The authors use firm-level Compustat data on U.S. public corporations to construct measures of investment (capital expenditures scaled by capital), Tobin's Q, cash flow, and financing variables (including new equity issuance). They also use CRSP stock return data to compute future realized three-year stock returns as a proxy for the nonfundamental component of prices expected by managers. Equity dependence is measured using the Kaplan-Zingales (KZ) index, following the implementation of Lamont, Polk, and Saa-Requejo (2001), built from leverage, cash holdings, cash flow, dividends, and Q. Firms are sorted into quintiles by the KZ index, and investment-Q and investment-future-return sensitivities are compared across quintiles. The unit of observation is the firm-year.
new_fields.institutional_context: Identification leverages cross-sectional heterogeneity in firms' reliance on external equity financing. A simple model based on Stein (1996) shows that only firms with insufficient internal wealth and debt capacity to fund first-best investment ('equity-dependent' firms) should have investment that responds to nonfundamental stock-price movements; firms with ample cash or unused debt capacity can insulate investment from mispricing. The KZ index serves as an ex ante proxy that sorts firms by the degree of this financing friction, predicting who should and should not exhibit price-sensitive investment. To separate mispricing from fundamentals embedded in Q, the authors exploit future realized stock returns as a proxy for managers' perceived over- or undervaluation: equity-dependent firms should show a more negative investment-future-return relationship, a prediction not implied by fundamentals-based explanations.

title: Does Governance Travel Around the World? Evidence from Institutional Investors

new_fields.research_question: Does ownership by institutional investors — particularly foreign institutions and those domiciled in countries with strong shareholder protection — causally improve firm-level corporate governance practices and outcomes (CEO turnover sensitivity to performance, firm valuation) in firms around the world? The paper also asks whether the direction of influence runs from institutional ownership to governance rather than the reverse, and whether effects differ by the legal environment of both the investor and the firm.
new_fields.data_description: The authors assemble an annual firm-level panel covering 23 countries over 2003–2008. The sample comprises roughly 2,000 non-U.S. firms per year (plus about 5,000 U.S. firms), accounting for approximately 71% of non-U.S. world market capitalization and 96% of U.S. market capitalization by 2008. Firm-level corporate governance data come from RiskMetrics (formerly ISS), from which they build a composite governance index (GOV41) based on 41 attributes covering board structure, audit, anti-takeover provisions, and compensation/ownership. Institutional ownership data identify holdings by domestic vs. foreign institutions and by independent vs. non-independent types (mutual funds/advisors vs. bank trusts/insurance companies). Additional firm-specific variables include Tobin's Q, stock returns, CEO turnover, and insider ownership, drawn from standard firm-level databases such as Worldscope.
new_fields.institutional_context: Identification exploits the substantial cross-country and cross-firm variation in institutional ownership that emerged during the 2000s wave of financial globalization, combined with heterogeneity in shareholder protection across countries (e.g., La Porta-style legal origin distinctions). Foreign institutional investors — especially those from countries with strong minority shareholder protection — face different incentives than domestic institutions, which often have business ties with local corporations and may be loyal to management. This creates variation in monitoring intensity across firms. The authors exploit within-firm changes in institutional holdings over time, lead-lag ordering between ownership changes and governance changes, and the interaction between the legal environment of the investor's home country and of the portfolio firm's country. High-profile activism episodes (e.g., TCI at Deutsche Börse and ABN AMRO) motivate the channel. Instrumental-variables strategies and firm fixed effects address endogenous matching between investors and well-governed firms.

title: How Does Financing Impact Investment? The Role of Debt Covenants

new_fields.research_question: Does a financing friction materialized through the transfer of control rights from borrowers to creditors causally reduce corporate capital investment? The paper further asks whether the investment response is stronger when agency and information problems between borrowers and lenders are more severe, thereby clarifying the mechanism linking financing and investment.
new_fields.data_description: Loan-level data come from a July 2005 extract of Loan Pricing Corporation's Dealscan database, covering dollar-denominated private loans made by bank and nonbank lenders to U.S. corporations from 1981 to 2005. The basic observation unit is a loan (facility/tranche), typically senior secured, with information on amount, promised yield, maturity, and—critically—restrictive financial covenants (e.g., minimum net worth, current ratio). Loan data are matched to borrower financial statements to compute accounting variables underlying covenants, the distance between these variables and covenant thresholds, violation indicators, and quarterly corporate capital expenditures scaled by capital. Controls include measures of investment opportunities, financial health, debt overhang, other contractual features, and abnormal accruals. The analysis is conducted at the firm-quarter level with firm and year-quarter fixed effects.
new_fields.institutional_context: Private debt contracts routinely include financial covenants (e.g., minimum net worth, minimum current ratio) whose breach—known as a 'technical default'—does not require missed interest or principal payments. The instant an accounting variable crosses the contractually specified threshold, control rights shift discretely from the borrower to the creditor, who can then threaten to accelerate the loan and thereby intervene in management, renegotiate terms (interest rate, maturity, available funds), or directly influence investment decisions. This sharp, contractually determined change in control rights at a known accounting cutoff is plausibly unrelated to small differences in the underlying accounting variable near the threshold, generating exogenous variation in violation status for borrowers just above versus just below the covenant boundary.

title: Control Rights and Capital Structure: An Empirical Investigation

new_fields.research_question: To what extent and through what mechanism do incentive conflicts between firms and their creditors shape corporate debt policy? Specifically, when creditors acquire control rights following breaches of financial covenants, how does this reallocation of rights affect borrowers' net debt issuance, leverage, and choice of lender?
new_fields.data_description: The authors construct a novel data set by combining Compustat quarterly financials for nonfinancial U.S. firms from 1996 to 2005 with hand-collected financial covenant violation indicators extracted from firms' 10-K and 10-Q SEC filings using a Perl-based text search of 20 covenant-related terms. The unit of observation is the firm-quarter, with the final sample comprising 135,736 firm-quarter observations after requiring at least four consecutive quarters of data and nonmissing values for key variables (total assets, sales, tangible assets, debt, net worth, cash, working capital, EBITDA, cash flow, net income, interest expense, market-to-book, and book/market equity). Key outcomes include net debt issuance scaled by lagged assets and leverage ratios. Variables are Winsorized at the 5th and 95th percentiles. A random subsample of violators' SEC filings is also hand-read to classify creditor responses (spread increases, facility reductions, collateral demands, lender switching).
new_fields.institutional_context: Private debt contracts in the U.S. typically contain financial covenants (e.g., thresholds on leverage, interest coverage, net worth) whose breach constitutes a technical default. Upon violation, creditors are contractually granted acceleration and termination rights, allowing them to demand immediate repayment, withdraw unused credit, raise interest spreads, or require additional collateral—even though violations rarely lead to payment default or bankruptcy. SEC Regulation S-X requires public firms to disclose uncured covenant breaches in their 10-K and 10-Q filings, making violations observable in the population of listed firms beginning in 1996 when electronic SEC filing became mandatory. Because covenants are written on continuous accounting variables crossing discrete thresholds, a violation is a sharp, quasi-random event at the covenant boundary for firms near the cutoff, enabling comparisons of otherwise similar violators and non-violators to isolate the causal effect of the transfer of control rights on financing policy.

title: Investment and Financing Constraints: Evidence from the Funding of Corporate Pension Plans

new_fields.research_question: Does a firm's capital expenditure (and to a lesser extent R&D and acquisition spending) depend on the availability of internal financial resources, above and beyond what is captured by investment opportunities and cash flow? In particular, when financially constrained firms experience exogenous drains on internal cash, do they cut real investment, and is this response stronger for firms with observable markers of financing constraints?
new_fields.data_description: The analysis combines Compustat financial data with plan-level pension data from IRS Form 5500 filings collected by the U.S. Department of Labor, matched to corporate sponsors. The main estimation sample covers fiscal years 1990-1998 (the period for which complete 5500 research files are available), with SEC 10-K pension disclosures used for a longer descriptive overview through 2004. The unit of observation is firm-year. Key variables include capital expenditures, R&D, acquisitions, cash flow, Tobin's Q, pension assets and projected benefit obligations, pension funding status, mandatory pension contributions (decomposed into predictable and unexpected components driven by asset returns and interest rates), credit ratings, firm age, dividend payout, and cash holdings. Roughly a quarter of sample firms had at least one year in which required pension contributions equaled 10% or more of capital expenditures.
new_fields.institutional_context: U.S. firms sponsoring defined benefit pension plans are legally required to fund promised retiree benefits through dedicated pension assets. When the market value of those assets falls below the present value of pension liabilities (discounted at the 30-year Treasury rate during the sample), ERISA and the Pension Protection Act of 1987 impose mandatory cash contributions determined by a sharply nonlinear, kinked formula of the plan's funding ratio: overfunded plans owe nothing (and face deductibility ceilings on voluntary contributions), while underfunded plans owe normal cost plus amortization and a 'deficit reduction contribution' equal to 13.75%-30% of the shortfall, with the percentage itself a kinked function of the funding ratio. The Retirement Protection Act of 1994 further altered these thresholds. Year-to-year funding status moves largely with pension asset returns and interest-rate-driven liability revaluations, generating plausibly exogenous, firm-specific shocks to required cash outflows that are unrelated to the firm's investment opportunities once funding status itself is controlled for.

title: Does Employment Protection Reduce Productivity? Evidence from US States

new_fields.research_question: Do mandated employment protections that raise firms' costs of dismissing workers reduce establishment-level productivity and distort production choices? Specifically, how do increased dismissal costs affect employment flows, firm entry, capital-labor substitution, labor productivity, and total factor productivity at US establishments?
new_fields.data_description: The analysis uses two establishment-level US Census Bureau datasets covering 1970-1999. The Longitudinal Business Database (LBD), sourced from US tax records and Census surveys, provides annual employment and payroll data for essentially all US private establishments across most industries, enabling analysis of employment flows and firm entry/exit. This is complemented by the Annual Survey of Manufacturers (ASM), used as a balanced panel of continuously-surveyed ongoing manufacturing plants, which contains detailed operating data including output, capital investment, and employment needed to compute labor productivity and total factor productivity. The unit of observation is the establishment-year. Key variables include employment levels and volatility, entry rates, capital intensity, labor productivity, and TFP. State-level timing of legal changes is merged in to identify treatment.
new_fields.institutional_context: Between the early 1970s and early 1990s, US state courts gradually eroded the longstanding common-law doctrine of employment-at-will by adopting three wrongful-discharge exceptions: the implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing, the public-policy exception, and the implied-contract exception. These judicially-created doctrines generated substantial litigation and raised the uncertainty and expected cost of firing workers in adopting states. Adoption timing was driven by the idiosyncratic flow of cases reaching state high courts and the dispositions of sitting judges, producing staggered, plausibly surprise changes across states, with many states never adopting particular exceptions. This state-by-state, time-varying rollout of dismissal-cost regimes, combined with non-adopting states serving as contemporaneous comparisons, provides exogenous variation in employment protection that can be linked to changes in establishment outcomes.

title: People, Places, and Public Policy: Some Simple Welfare Economics of Local Economic Development Programs

new_fields.research_question: Who bears the incidence of spatially targeted economic development subsidies and public investments, and under what conditions do the national benefits of such programs exceed their costs? Specifically, how do worker and firm mobility, housing supply elasticity, and localized market failures (agglomeration spillovers, public goods, labor market rigidities) determine whether subsidies to disadvantaged areas improve the welfare of intended beneficiaries versus being capitalized into land rents or diverting activity from other regions?
new_fields.data_description: The paper is a theoretical and review piece rather than an original empirical analysis. It draws on descriptive statistics and prior empirical studies concerning place-based programs in the U.S., Europe, and Asia. Reported figures include U.S. federal spending of roughly $15 billion per year on spatially targeted development (GAO 2012), approximately $80 billion per year in state and local location incentives (Story, Fehr, and Watkins 2012), and €49 billion per year from the European Regional Development Fund (2007–2013). State-level subsidy accounting values are tabulated by state (e.g., Texas $19.1B, Michigan $6.65B, Pennsylvania $4.84B). The paper also cites wage and unemployment disparities across U.S. metros (e.g., Stamford vs. Jacksonville; Flint vs. Iowa City in 2009) and reviews empirical estimates from the existing literature on Enterprise Zones, Empowerment Zones, the TVA, UK Regional Selective Assistance, and Chinese Special Economic Zones.
new_fields.institutional_context: Place-based policies target specific geographic areas—neighborhoods, cities, or regions—with tax abatements, wage and investment subsidies, infrastructure, and regulatory relief, rather than targeting individuals based on personal characteristics. Prominent examples include the U.S. Tennessee Valley Authority's New Deal infrastructure investments in the underdeveloped South; state Enterprise Zones (e.g., 42 in California) modeled on the UK's Thatcher-era zones; federal Empowerment Zones and Renewal Communities for distressed urban neighborhoods; large discretionary firm-specific deals (e.g., Panasonic in Newark, Ford in Kentucky, Samsung in Austin); the European Union Regional Development Fund favoring low-income/high-unemployment regions; the UK Regional Selective Assistance; Italian transfers to the South; and China's Special Economic Zones granting strengthened property rights and FDI incentives. EU state-aid rules generally prohibit subsidies but explicitly exempt aid to deprived regions (Article 87, Treaty of Amsterdam), reinforcing the spatial targeting framework.

title: How General Is Human Capital? A Task-Based Approach

new_fields.research_question: How transferable are skills accumulated on the job across occupations, and to what extent do skills tied to the bundle of tasks performed in an occupation (rather than to a firm, occupation, or general experience) contribute to individual wage growth and shape occupational mobility patterns over the life cycle?
new_fields.data_description: The analysis combines two German data sources. The first is a 2% sample of social security administrative records covering complete job histories and wages for over 100,000 workers in Germany from 1975 to 2001, providing low-measurement-error panel data on employment, occupation codes, tenure, and earnings. The second is the Qualification and Career Survey, a large repeated cross-section of roughly 30,000 employees conducted at four separate points in time, which records the specific tasks (e.g., analytical, manual, interactive activities such as negotiating, teaching, managing) performed in each occupation. By merging occupation-level task intensities from the survey with the individual panel, the authors construct a continuous measure of skill distance between occupations and worker-level measures of task-specific human capital. The unit of observation is a worker-year.
new_fields.institutional_context: The setting exploits detailed occupational classifications in German social security data together with survey-based information on the task content of occupations. Because occupations combine multiple general tasks (analytical, manual, interactive) in different proportions, workers moving across occupations carry partially transferable skills whose portability depends on the similarity of task bundles. The continuous task-distance measure across occupation pairs—and its variation across workers' realized occupational transitions—provides the empirical leverage to separate task-specific human capital from firm tenure, occupational tenure, and general experience. The long 1975–2001 panel of German careers, combined with four waves of task surveys that capture changes in occupational task content over time, allows the authors to track how the distance of occupational moves evolves with labor market experience and to quantify wage returns to accumulated task-relevant skills relative to other human capital components.

title: The War on Poverty's Experiment in Public Medicine: Community Health Centers and the Mortality of Older Americans

new_fields.research_question: Did the establishment of Community Health Centers, which delivered subsidized primary care directly to poor and underserved communities starting in the mid-1960s, reduce mortality among older Americans over the subsequent decade? How do the estimated mortality effects compare to the poor/non-poor mortality gap and to the cost-effectiveness of contemporaneous insurance expansions?
new_fields.data_description: The analysis combines county-level age-adjusted mortality rates from US Vital Statistics covering roughly 1959 through the late 1980s with the staggered timing of CHC establishment across US counties from 1965 to 1974 (and later expansion through 1980). Mortality data are disaggregated by age group (infants, children, adults 50+, adults 65+) and by cause of death (including cardiovascular causes and accidents for placebo tests). County-level controls include federal per capita medical spending and other War on Poverty program variables. The authors also use the Survey of Health Services Utilization and Expenditures (SHSUE) for 1963 and 1970, covering 73 primary sampling units, to measure regular source of care, clinic use, and out-of-pocket prescription expenditures among poor and non-poor households.
new_fields.institutional_context: In 1965, the Office of Economic Opportunity (OEO) launched the Community Health Center program as part of the War on Poverty, funding local organizations to provide free or sliding-scale primary care, prescriptions, home visits, and transportation in poor neighborhoods. Unlike Medicare and Medicaid, CHCs directly delivered care rather than subsidizing private providers. The initial 1965–1974 rollout was characterized by 'great administrative confusion' at the OEO: grants were awarded through an arbitrary, application-driven process to whichever 'leading-edge' local organizations assembled proposals, producing quasi-random variation in which counties received CHCs and when. By 1974, 117 counties had CHCs. The 1975 Special Health Revenue Sharing Act subsequently shifted allocation to follow the Index of Medical Underservice, changing the selection process and targeting rural areas, which distinguishes the early rollout period from later expansions.

title: Earnings Losses of Displaced Workers

new_fields.research_question: What is the magnitude and temporal pattern of earnings losses experienced by high-tenure workers who separate from their employers, and do these losses predate separation, persist over the long term, and vary by industry or reemployment sector? The analysis seeks to isolate the causal earnings impact of job loss from pre-existing differences between separators and stayers.
new_fields.data_description: The authors construct a longitudinal administrative data set covering a 5 percent sample of the Pennsylvania wage and salary workforce. The file merges quarterly earnings records from unemployment insurance administrative data spanning 1974 through 1986 with firm-level information including employment levels, employment growth, geographic location, and 4-digit SIC industry. Worker-level variables are limited to year of birth, sex, and firm tenure since 1974. The analysis sample consists of prime-age high-tenure workers born between 1930 and 1959 who were employed at the same firm since at least 1974, yielding 9,568 separators and 14,028 nondisplaced workers studied over separations occurring between 1980 and 1986. The unit of observation is a worker-quarter, with separators further split into 'mass-layoff' and 'nonmass-layoff' subsamples based on firm employment declines.
new_fields.institutional_context: Identification leverages worker separations from distressed Pennsylvania firms during the economically turbulent early-to-mid 1980s, a period when the state's western half suffered double-digit unemployment while the eastern half grew with the mid-Atlantic region. To sharpen the interpretation of separations as involuntary job loss rather than quits or dismissals for cause, the authors exploit firm-level employment changes: separators from firms whose employment in the year after the worker's departure fell more than 30 percent below their late-1970s peak are classified as 'mass-layoff' displacements. Comparing the quarterly earnings trajectories of these displaced workers with those of otherwise similar high-tenure workers who remained at their firms—both before and after the separation quarter—enables the authors to trace earnings dynamics around the displacement event and distinguish displacement effects from pre-existing worker heterogeneity.

title: Children and Gender Inequality: Evidence from Denmark

new_fields.research_question: How does the arrival of children affect the labor market trajectories of women relative to men, and how much of overall gender inequality in earnings can be attributed to these child-related effects? The paper further asks through what mechanisms (occupation, sector, firm choice) these penalties operate and whether they are transmitted across generations from parents to daughters.
new_fields.data_description: The study uses Danish administrative register data covering the full population, with linked information on earnings, hours worked, labor force participation, wage rates, occupation, sector, firm characteristics, and family links across generations. Records on hours worked extend back to 1964, enabling intergenerational analysis, while the main estimation sample covers the period 1980–2013. The unit of observation is the individual-year, with annual frequency. Key outcomes include annual earnings, labor force participation, hours, wage rates, occupational rank, managerial status, and indicators for working in family-friendly firms (e.g., public sector, firms with mothers in management). Linked parent-child records allow matching estimated child penalties of daughters to the labor supply histories of their maternal and paternal grandparents.
new_fields.institutional_context: Denmark provides a setting with generous family policies—job-protected parental leave, extensive publicly provided child care, and relatively egalitarian gender norms—and one of the highest female labor force participation rates in the world (~80%), with virtually no participation gap. Despite these policies, a substantial gender earnings gap (15–20%) persists, comparable to that of the United States. The analysis leverages the sharp timing of the birth of the first child as a within-person shock: women and men evolve along parallel trajectories prior to childbirth and diverge immediately after, allowing the researchers to isolate the causal impact of parenthood. The authors also exploit sibling sex-mix variation (as in Angrist and Evans 1998) as an alternative source of exogenous variation in family size, and compare parents to individuals who never have children as a comparison group.

title: Family Health Behaviors

new_fields.research_question: How do severe health shocks experienced by one family member causally affect the preventive health care consumption and health-related behaviors of their spouses, adult children, and other network members such as coworkers? Through what mechanisms—information learning about one's own health risks versus salience and attention—do these spillovers operate?
new_fields.data_description: The study uses Danish administrative register data covering the entire adult Danish population from 1980 to 2011. The data include medication prescriptions (notably cholesterol-lowering statins), contacts with medical care professionals, inpatient and outpatient hospitalizations, death records with cause of death, and links across family members (spouses, adult children, parents-in-law, sons/daughters-in-law) and coworkers. Key outcomes include consumption of statins, diagnostic testing (e.g., cholesterol screening, radiology for cancer screening), smoking-related measures, and prescription opioid use. The unit of observation is the individual family member in households hit by a health shock, tracked in event time relative to the shock. The primary shocks analyzed are non-fatal heart attacks and strokes, with a complementary analysis of fatal events (including cancer deaths).
new_fields.institutional_context: Identification leverages the plausibly random timing, within a short window, of sudden and severe health events—non-fatal heart attacks and strokes, and fatal shocks such as spousal death—whose exact year of occurrence is unlikely to be predictable. Affected households experiencing a shock in year τ are compared to households that will experience the same type of shock a few years later (τ+Δ), providing a counterfactual of ex ante similar but not-yet-treated households. The Danish setting is particularly well suited because universal administrative registers allow linking individuals to spouses, adult children, in-laws, and coworkers, and because statins—a widely prescribed disease-specific preventive medication for cardiovascular risk—provide a concrete measurable behavioral response. Variation in pre-shock risk profiles, prior cholesterol testing, geographic distance to in-laws, and coworker similarity is used to probe mechanisms.

title: Lifetime Earnings and the Vietnam Era Draft Lottery: Evidence from Social Security Administrative Records

new_fields.research_question: What is the causal effect of military service during the Vietnam era on veterans' long-term civilian earnings? In particular, do Vietnam-era veterans earn less than comparable nonveterans a decade after discharge, once selection into military service based on unobserved civilian earnings potential is accounted for?
new_fields.data_description: Earnings data come from the Social Security Administration's Continuous Work History Sample (CWHS), a 1% sample of Social Security numbers. Two earnings series are used: FICA-taxable earnings (including self-employment) from 1964-1984, censored at the Social Security taxable maximum, and uncensored W-2 total compensation from 1978 onward. SSA programmers matched dates of birth to the CWHS, and lottery numbers were matched to birthdates using Selective Service tables. Due to IRS disclosure rules, data are released as cell aggregates defined by year of earnings, year of birth, race, and groups of five consecutive lottery numbers, including means, variances, fractions at/above the taxable maximum, fractions with zero earnings, and cell counts. The sample covers men born 1950-1953 (who turned 19 in their year of induction risk), by race (white/nonwhite).
new_fields.institutional_context: During the Vietnam War, the U.S. conducted five draft lotteries (1970-1974) to determine priority for conscription. Each man of draft age was assigned a Random Sequence Number (RSN) from 1 to 365 based on his birthdate in a televised public drawing. The Defense Department later announced an eligibility ceiling (RSN 195 in 1970, 125 in 1971, 95 in 1972); only men with RSNs below the ceiling were at risk of being drafted. Because RSNs were randomly assigned to birthdates, draft-eligibility status is independent of individual characteristics that affect civilian earnings, even though actual induction depended on subsequent physical and mental screening, and many men with low RSNs volunteered to improve service terms. The lottery thus generated randomly assigned variation in conscription risk that strongly influenced veteran status without being correlated with earnings potential.

title: Using Geographic Variation in College Proximity to Estimate the Return to Schooling

new_fields.research_question: What is the causal effect of an additional year of schooling on labor market earnings? In particular, do conventional estimates that treat education as exogenous understate or overstate the true return to schooling, especially for individuals whose educational attainment is shaped by access-related constraints?
new_fields.data_description: The analysis uses the National Longitudinal Survey of Young Men (NLSYM), a longitudinal survey of men aged 14-24 in 1966 followed through 1981. Key variables include completed years of schooling, hourly wages (used in log form), labor market experience, region of residence, race, family background characteristics (parental education, family structure), standardized test scores (Knowledge of the World of Work), and indicators for residence near a two-year or four-year college in 1966. The primary earnings outcome is measured in 1976 when respondents were 24-34 years old. The unit of observation is the individual young man, with the working sample comprising several thousand respondents with valid wage and schooling data.
new_fields.institutional_context: Identification exploits geographic variation in the availability of colleges near where young men grew up. In 1966, some respondents lived in local labor markets that contained an accredited four-year college (or a two-year college), while others lived in areas without nearby higher-education institutions. Growing up near a college substantially lowers the cost of attending — by allowing students to live at home and avoid tuition at commuter or public institutions — and is shown to raise educational attainment, particularly among men from lower socioeconomic backgrounds whose schooling decisions are most sensitive to costs. Because college proximity plausibly affects earnings only through its impact on schooling (after controlling for region, urban status, and family background), this geographic variation provides exogenous shifts in education that are arguably unrelated to a young man's underlying ability or tastes for schooling.

title: Estimating Average and Local Average Treatment Effects of Education When Compulsory Schooling Laws Really Matter

new_fields.research_question: What are the earnings returns to an additional year of compulsory schooling, and does the average treatment effect of schooling for a broad population differ from the local average treatment effect for narrowly affected subgroups? Specifically, how much do wages rise for individuals induced to stay in school by increases in the minimum school-leaving age in the UK?
new_fields.data_description: The analysis uses microdata from the British and Northern Irish General Household Surveys (GHHS), primarily spanning 1984-1998, with extensions to 2006 in alternative specifications. The unit of observation is an individual respondent, aggregated into cells by birth cohort and region (Great Britain vs. Northern Ireland) and weighted by cell size. The sample covers individuals aged 28-64 (alternative: 28-60), born between 1921 and 1951, who were age 14 between 1935 and 1965. Key variables include age at which the respondent left full-time education (schooling measure) and log annual earnings (outcome). Baseline samples contain roughly 55,000 observations for Great Britain and about 8,900 for Northern Ireland. Regressions include a quartic birth-cohort polynomial, age controls (quartic polynomial or age dummies), and standard errors clustered by birth cohort and region.
new_fields.institutional_context: Identification exploits sharp, nationally mandated increases in the minimum school-leaving age in the United Kingdom: Great Britain raised the leaving age from 14 to 15 in 1947, and Northern Ireland did so in 1957. These reforms created a discrete change across birth cohorts—those turning 14 just before the reform could legally leave school at 14, while those turning 14 just after were compelled to remain until 15. Unlike comparable reforms in the U.S. and Canada that bound only a small share of students, the UK changes affected roughly 40-50 percent of the cohort population, making the compliant group close to the overall population. The staggered timing between Great Britain and Northern Ireland provides a second source of variation, enabling cross-region comparisons of cohorts facing different leaving-age regimes at the same point in time, while cohort and age polynomials absorb smooth trends in earnings and schooling.

title: Zero Returns to Compulsory Schooling in Germany: Evidence and Interpretation

new_fields.research_question: What is the causal effect of an additional year of compulsory secondary schooling on earnings in Germany? Do labor market institutions, the apprenticeship training system, or the structure of the German schooling system explain why returns to compulsory schooling in Germany might differ from those documented in other countries?
new_fields.data_description: The analysis uses West German data covering individuals born roughly between 1925 and 1970 who attended secondary school during the period 1948-1970. The authors combine several data sources, including the German Micro Census (accessed via ZUMA and IZA), social security statistics calculated by Stefan Bender, and survey data obtained from the Zentralarchiv für Empirische Sozialforschung at the University of Köln (the 'QaC' sample). Key variables include years of schooling, secondary school track attended (Hauptschule, Realschule, Gymnasium), earnings/wages, employment status, self-employment, and apprenticeship completion. The unit of observation is the individual worker, with cohort of birth and state (Bundesland) of schooling as the key assignment dimensions. Samples are constructed to allow comparison of cohorts exposed and unexposed to the 9th grade extension across West German states.
new_fields.institutional_context: After World War II, the lowest track of German secondary school (Hauptschule) ended after grade 8. Beginning with Hamburg and Berlin in 1949, West German states progressively added a mandatory 9th grade, with the reform rolled out at different times across the eleven West German states and fully in place only by 1970. Education policy is set at the state (Bundesland) level within federal framework agreements, so the timing of the 9th-grade introduction varied substantially across states while curricula remained broadly comparable. Because roughly 75% of secondary students initially attended the basic track, about 60% of students in affected cohorts should have been directly bound by the extension. This staggered, state-by-cohort variation in the school-leaving age—combined with Germany's distinctive tracked schooling system and apprenticeship training—provides the variation used to identify schooling effects on earnings.

title: Economic Impacts of New Unionization on Private Sector Employers: 1984-2001

new_fields.research_question: What are the causal effects of new unionization on private sector employers in the United States, specifically on business survival, employment, output, productivity, and wages? Does the legal recognition of a union — which compels employers to bargain in good faith — translate into measurable economic costs for firms, or have unions become too weak to extract significant rents?
new_fields.data_description: The analysis combines several establishment-level datasets covering U.S. private sector establishments that faced union organizing drives during 1984-1999, with outcomes tracked through 2001. Union representation election data come from the National Labor Relations Board (NLRB), and contract expiration data come from the Federal Mediation and Conciliation Service (FMCS). Business survival, employment, and output outcomes are measured using a commercial database derived from telephone listings (InfoUSA). For manufacturing establishments, employment, wages, output, and productivity come from the U.S. Census Bureau's Longitudinal Research Database (LRD). The unit of observation is the establishment that experienced an NLRB representation election. Key variables include union vote share, election outcome, post-election business survival (mean rate ~0.40 over ~8 years), production hours, output, output per worker, and wages, measured over 1- to 15-year horizons after the election.
new_fields.institutional_context: Under the National Labor Relations Act (NLRA), most new unionization in the U.S. private sector occurs through a secret-ballot election administered by the NLRB. Following a card drive in which at least 30 percent of workers sign authorization cards, the NLRB defines the bargaining unit and conducts an on-site election. A simple majority — 50 percent plus one vote — is required for the union to win legal recognition, after which the employer is legally required to bargain in good faith with the certified union. If the union falls one vote short, the employer faces no such obligation and future organizing attempts are rare. This sharp 50-percent vote-share threshold generates quasi-random variation in union recognition among establishments with closely contested elections, allowing comparisons between near-winners and near-losers that are otherwise similar in unobserved characteristics correlated with profitability, growth, and managerial quality.

title: The Effects of Extended Unemployment Insurance over the Business Cycle

new_fields.research_question: How do the labor supply disincentive effects of extending unemployment insurance benefit durations vary over the business cycle? Specifically, does the moral hazard cost of longer UI durations (measured by effects on nonemployment and benefit durations) differ between booms and recessions, and how does this compare with the changing coverage benefits (exhaustion rates) that UI extensions provide during downturns?
new_fields.data_description: The authors use German administrative social security data covering the universe of unemployment spells and subsequent employment outcomes for mature workers, measured at daily frequency. The sample spans roughly the mid-1980s through 2008, yielding about 20 years of claimant cohorts. Key variables include exact age at UI claim (the running variable), potential UI benefit duration, actual UI benefit duration, nonemployment duration, UI exhaustion status, and worker demographics and industry. The unit of observation is an individual unemployment spell. Estimates are computed separately by calendar year and by year-by-industry cells, and then correlated with aggregate and industry-level business cycle indicators (e.g., unemployment rates). The analysis focuses on mature workers with stable labor force attachment around age thresholds that determine potential benefit duration.
new_fields.institutional_context: Germany's UI system assigns potential benefit duration as a deterministic step function of the claimant's exact age at the start of the unemployment spell, with sharp jumps in maximum entitlement at specific age cutoffs (producing differences of several months of benefits for workers just above versus just below an age threshold). Crucially, unlike the U.S. system of trigger-based extended benefits and emergency compensation, these German age-based potential duration rules are fixed by statute and do not vary with local or national labor market conditions. This makes the age-threshold variation in potential UI duration exogenous to the business cycle, allowing the authors to estimate labor supply and benefit-duration responses to UI extensions separately in each year and correlate those year-specific estimates with independently measured cyclical indicators.

title: Incentive Effects of Social Assistance: A Regression Discontinuity Approach

new_fields.research_question: How does the generosity of social assistance benefits affect labour market outcomes (such as employment) and non-labour outcomes (such as marital status and living arrangements) among childless individuals? The paper seeks to quantify the behavioural incentive effects of welfare transfers for a population — single non-parents — for whom standard labour supply reasoning applies most cleanly.
new_fields.data_description: The analysis uses Canadian survey microdata, including Census data and labour force survey files, covering the period surrounding the 1989 Quebec welfare reform. The unit of observation is the individual adult, with particular focus on childless men. Key variables include employment status, earnings, marital status, and living arrangements (e.g., co-residence with parents), along with age (in months, to exploit the age-30 threshold), province of residence, and demographic controls. Residents of other Canadian provinces serve as an additional comparison sample. The sample spans years before and after August 1989, when the age-based benefit differential was abolished, enabling both cross-sectional analysis around the age cutoff and before/after comparisons across provinces.
new_fields.institutional_context: Prior to August 1989, Quebec's social assistance program (governed by the 1969 Loi sur l'aide sociale) paid childless recipients under age 30 only about $185 per month, versus $507 for those aged 30 and over — a 145% jump in benefits upon turning 30. Only cash benefits varied by age; in-kind benefits (dental, medical) did not. Eligibility was verified monthly. This sharp age-based benefit schedule, unique among Canadian provinces, creates a discrete jump in welfare generosity at exactly age 30 while other policies and the broader economic environment vary smoothly. A December 1988 reform (effective August 1, 1989) eliminated the age-based differential, providing an additional temporal policy change. Canada's program also differs from the US in that singles and non-parents are eligible for benefits.

title: How Do Extended Benefits Affect Unemployment Duration? A Regression Discontinuity Approach

new_fields.research_question: How does a large extension of the maximum duration of unemployment benefits affect the duration of unemployment spells and job search? Does the effect differ between men and women, particularly in light of differential access to early retirement pathways after benefit exhaustion?
new_fields.data_description: The analysis uses two Austrian administrative data sources: the Austrian social security database and the Austrian unemployment insurance register. These records cover the universe of unemployment spells and provide complete work histories of individuals from 1972 onward, including precise information on age at entry into unemployment and place of residence. Key variables include unemployment duration, job search duration, age at unemployment inflow, district of residence, previous employment tenure, industry of prior employment, and benefit receipt. The unit of observation is an individual unemployment spell. The sample focuses on the non-steel inflow (over 80% of job seekers) around the program's 1988–1993 implementation window, and separate analyses are conducted for men and women to explore interactions with early retirement rules (age 54 for women, 59 for men).
new_fields.institutional_context: In June 1988, Austria enacted the Regional Extended Benefits Program (REBP), which raised the maximum duration of unemployment benefits from 30 weeks to 209 weeks for job seekers meeting all of: age 50 or older at spell start, a long continuous work history, residence for at least 6 months in one of 28 designated labor market districts, and spell beginning after June 1988 (or ongoing then). The 28 eligible districts were selected by the social affairs minister, targeting regions with high steel-sector employment concentration (tied to restructuring of nationalized steel industries), not regions with high unemployment per se. The program ran until August 1993. Eligibility thus jumped sharply at two boundaries: at exactly age 50, and at the geographic border between treated and non-treated districts—providing two distinct sources of variation in benefit access among otherwise comparable workers.

title: Dams

new_fields.research_question: How can a set of metaheuristics be coordinated across distributed computational nodes so that each node adaptively selects, at runtime and based only on local information exchanged with its neighbors, which metaheuristic to apply in order to approach the performance of a globally optimal (oracle) distributed strategy? Specifically, can a simple local rule combining exploitation of the best locally observed metaheuristic with exploration of alternatives match or outperform existing sequential and distributed adaptive parameter-control strategies?
new_fields.data_description: The study is methodological and algorithmic rather than empirical on real-world data. The authors evaluate their proposed Select Best and Mutate (SBM) algorithm, within the Distributed Adaptive Metaheuristic Selection (DAMS) framework, through computational experiments on the OneMax benchmark problem. The distributed environment is modeled as an unweighted graph G=(V,E) where nodes represent computational entities (machines, processors, or processes) and edges represent bidirectional communication links. Each node holds a local population P, a local state S, a current metaheuristic M, and a set M of available atomic metaheuristics (e.g., mutation operators with different rates). Performance is measured by comparing SBM against sequential adaptive strategies and other distributed adaptive strategies across multiple experimental configurations varying network topology, metaheuristic sets, and problem size.
new_fields.institutional_context: The setting is a distributed/parallel computing environment (multi-core CPUs, GPGPUs, grids, P2P networks) in which multiple atomic metaheuristics—treated as black-box operators with fixed input/output specifications—can be executed concurrently on different nodes that communicate only with neighbors in a graph. This distributed structure creates the key design problem: parameter control must be decentralized because no global observer exists. The authors exploit this constraint by organizing computation into three layers (distributed communication, metaheuristic selection, atomic execution), enabling each node to select a metaheuristic based on locally aggregated performance information propagated from neighbors. The OneMax problem serves as a controlled benchmark whose known structure allows isolating the effect of the adaptive selection rule from problem-specific confounds, and an 'oracle' distributed schedule provides a reference point for evaluating how closely local decisions approximate globally optimal coordination.

title: Do Rural Banks Matter? Evidence from the Indian Social Banking Experiment

new_fields.research_question: Does expanding commercial bank branches into previously unbanked rural areas reduce rural poverty and raise output in developing countries? The paper seeks to identify the causal effect of rural bank branch expansion on poverty reduction and on the sectoral composition of output (agricultural versus non-agricultural) in India.
new_fields.data_description: The authors construct a panel dataset covering the sixteen major Indian states over 1961-2000 (covering >95% of India's population). Bank data come from a branch-level Reserve Bank of India dataset recording, for every branch opened since 1805, the opening date, rural/urban status, and number of pre-existing branches at the location; this is used to build measures of branches per 100,000 persons in banked, unbanked, and rural unbanked locations. Poverty is measured using headcount ratios (rural and urban) from India's regular household expenditure surveys since the 1950s. Additional variables include state-level output, real male agricultural wages, rural credit and savings shares, and household debt composition by source from decadal surveys (1951-1991). Initial financial development is measured by 1961 bank branches per 100,000 persons.
new_fields.institutional_context: India's social banking experiment, following 1969 bank nationalization, aimed to extend formal credit to rural areas. A central policy lever was the 1:4 branch licensing rule imposed by the Indian Central Bank in 1977: a commercial bank could open a branch in a location that already had one or more branches only if it simultaneously opened four branches in unbanked locations. The rule was abandoned in 1990 with financial liberalization. Because states with lower initial (1961) financial development had more unbanked locations, the 1977-1990 rule mechanically directed disproportionately more rural branches to financially less-developed states, reversing the pre-1977 and post-1990 pattern in which branches tended to follow existing financial development. These policy-induced trend breaks in 1977 and 1990 in the relationship between initial financial development and branch expansion provide the identification leverage.

title: The Potato's Contribution to Population and Urbanization: Evidence from a Historical Experiment

new_fields.research_question: How did the arrival of a highly nutritious New World staple crop in the Old World affect long-run population growth and urbanization during the 18th and 19th centuries? The goal is to causally quantify the contribution of a large, exogenous improvement in caloric and nutritional availability to demographic change and the rural-to-urban transition.
new_fields.data_description: The authors assemble a country-level panel covering the Old World (Eastern Hemisphere, with Western Europe and extensions) from roughly 1000 to 1900 AD, observed at long time intervals spanning pre- and post-1700. Key outcome variables are total population and urbanization (city population share), drawn from standard historical demographic sources (e.g., Maddison; Bairoch-style urban data). The key treatment proxy is land suitability for cultivating potatoes, constructed from FAO/GAEZ-type geographic and climatic data. Controls include overall agricultural suitability, suitability for Old World staples (rice, wheat) and New World staples (maize, sweet potatoes), as well as ruggedness and elevation. The unit of observation is the country-period, allowing comparisons of levels and growth rates before (1000–1700) and after (1700–1900) potato adoption.
new_fields.institutional_context: Potatoes were domesticated in the Andes and were unknown in the Old World until the Columbian Exchange following the European discovery of the Americas in 1492. Their diffusion as a field crop across Eurasia and Africa occurred gradually, becoming widespread only after around 1700. Because potatoes are nutritionally superior to existing Old World staples—providing nearly all essential vitamins and minerals and far more calories per acre—their introduction constituted a major positive shock to nutrition and agricultural productivity. Crucially, potatoes thrive only in specific climatic and geographic conditions (cool temperatures, rugged terrain, higher elevations), so some regions of the Old World could adopt them as a staple while others could not. The combination of a sharp, externally-driven timing of arrival and pre-existing geographic heterogeneity in cultivation suitability generates plausibly exogenous variation in nutritional improvement across regions and over time, well before modern sanitation or medicine emerged.

title: Why Are Indian Children So Short? The Role of Birth Order and Son Preference

new_fields.research_question: Why are Indian children so much shorter than children in sub-Saharan Africa, despite India's higher income and better performance on other health indicators? Specifically, does cultural eldest-son preference, by shaping parents' fertility decisions and how they allocate health and nutrition resources across children of different birth orders and genders, explain a substantial portion of India's child height deficit?
new_fields.data_description: The authors use survey data on over 168,000 children under age five from India and 25 sub-Saharan African countries, primarily from Demographic and Health Surveys (DHS) and India's National Family Health Survey. The unit of observation is the child. Key outcomes include height-for-age z-scores (using the WHO reference population), weight-for-age, and child hemoglobin. The data also include a broad array of prenatal inputs (antenatal care, maternal nutrition) and postnatal health inputs (breastfeeding, vaccinations). Covariates include birth order, sibling gender composition, mother and household characteristics, religion, and state/region of residence. The authors supplement this with Indian Human Development Survey data to study household income/expenditure and child height, and Penn World Table GDP data for cross-country income comparisons. The sample spans multiple survey waves covering roughly the 1990s through the 2000s.
new_fields.institutional_context: Identification leverages cultural and religious variation in the strength of eldest-son preference across populations that otherwise share many characteristics. India's patrilocal and patrilineal Hindu kinship system—where aging parents live with and bequeath property to the eldest son, and where Hindu religious texts require a male heir for post-death rituals—generates strong eldest-son preference. This preference varies systematically: it is weaker in matrilineal regions (Kerala and the eight Northeast states), in states with less male-skewed sex ratios, among Muslims (relative to Hindus), and in neighboring South Asian countries like Bangladesh and Pakistan. The setting also features endogenous fertility-stopping behavior, where parents continue childbearing until a son is born. These cross-group differences in son-preference intensity, combined with within-family variation in sibling gender composition and birth order, provide the variation used to test whether son preference drives the steep birth-order gradient in child height.

title: Child Penalties Across Countries: Evidence and Explanations

new_fields.research_question: How does the arrival of the first child affect the labor market earnings trajectories of women relative to men, and how do these parenthood-related earnings gaps compare across countries with different family policies and gender norms? To what extent can cross-country differences in long-run earnings gaps between mothers and fathers be explained by parental leave policies, child care provision, and prevailing gender norms?
new_fields.data_description: The authors assemble comparable longitudinal micro-data on earnings and fertility for six countries: Denmark, Sweden, Austria, Germany, the United Kingdom, and the United States. For Denmark, Sweden, and Austria, they use full-population administrative registers; for Germany they use the GSOEP, for the US the PSID, and for the UK the BHPS. The unit of observation is an individual-year, with annual frequency. The main outcome is gross labor earnings (excluding taxes and transfers), specified in levels to retain zeros from non-participation; extensive-margin employment is also examined. The sample is restricted to individuals having their first child between ages 20 and 45 and observed each year from 5 years before to 10 years after first childbirth (with relaxed observation requirements for PSID and BHPS). Elicited gender-norm measures come from the International Social Survey Program.
new_fields.institutional_context: Identification exploits the sharp, datable occurrence of the first childbirth for each parent, enabling comparison of earnings trajectories of mothers and fathers before versus after this life event, while flexibly controlling for age (life-cycle) and calendar-year effects. Because individuals become parents at different ages, variation in time-since-birth is separable from age and year effects. The six countries span very different institutional environments—Scandinavian welfare states with extensive public child care and generous parental leave (Denmark, Sweden), German-speaking countries with long leave but more traditional family norms (Austria, Germany), and liberal English-speaking labor markets with limited family policy (UK, US). The paper also draws on quasi-experimental evidence from Austrian parental leave reforms and child care expansions studied in related work, and on cross-country variation in survey-elicited gender norms about working mothers.
