title: The Effects of Class Size on Student Achievement: New Evidence from Population Variation

new_fields.research_question: Does reducing class size in elementary schools causally improve student achievement, and if so, by how much? The question centers on whether naturally occurring, idiosyncratic differences in class size translate into measurable differences in standardized test performance across cohorts of students.
new_fields.data_description: The study uses long panels of administrative data from the Connecticut Department of Education covering 649 elementary schools. The data include grade-level enrollment counts, kindergarten cohort sizes, class sizes as reported by schools, and district-level class-size rules (maximum and minimum class size policies). Student achievement is measured using standardized test scores, normalized by the standard deviation of scores on each test. Observations are at the grade-by-school-by-cohort level, with cohorts tracked across kindergarten through grade 6. The panels are sufficiently long to allow fitting of a quartic time trend separately for each grade within each school to isolate idiosyncratic population variation. Additional controls include student, parent, and community characteristics, plus school and cohort fixed effects.
new_fields.institutional_context: Two features of Connecticut elementary schooling generate exogenous variation in class size. First, natural randomness in birth timing—combined with discrete school-entry cutoff rules (children born between January 1 and December 31 of a given year enter the same grade) and the integer nature of classrooms—produces idiosyncratic fluctuations in cohort size that translate directly into class-size differences when the number of classrooms per grade is fixed. Second, Connecticut school districts impose maximum and minimum class-size rules, so that a small change in enrollment crossing a threshold triggers the addition or removal of a classroom, causing a sharp, discontinuous drop or jump in class size (e.g., a cohort of 26 with a cap of 25 splits into two classes of 13). These features allow class size to vary independently of parental sorting, school choices, and compensatory policies.

title: Measuring the Impacts of Teachers I: Evaluating Bias in Teacher Value-Added Estimates

new_fields.research_question: Do estimates of teachers' contributions to student achievement, constructed from test-score residuals after controlling for prior scores and demographics, provide unbiased forecasts of how a teacher would affect students' test scores? Specifically, are these value-added estimates contaminated by non-random sorting of students to teachers on unobserved determinants of achievement?
new_fields.data_description: The analysis uses administrative records from a large urban U.S. school district linking students to teachers in grades 3-8 for math and English, covering roughly 1988-2009. Key variables include student standardized test scores, demographics, prior-year achievement, classroom and teacher identifiers, and school characteristics. These school-district records are matched at the individual level to U.S. federal income tax records (W-2s, 1040s, 1098/1098-T information returns, SSA files) using date of birth, gender, name, and ZIP code, yielding an 88.6% match rate across about 1.37 million students. The unit of observation for value-added estimation is the student-subject-year, collapsed to classroom- and teacher-year means; the matched tax data provide parental characteristics and later adult outcomes used in companion analyses.
new_fields.institutional_context: Identification exploits quasi-experimental variation arising from teacher turnover across schools and grades: when a high- or low-value-added teacher enters or exits a particular school-grade-subject cell, the mean characteristics and achievement of students taught in that cell shift, generating changes in teaching quality that are arguably orthogonal to persistent student unobservables within a school. Comparing changes in cohort-level test scores to changes in mean teacher value-added across consecutive cohorts in the same school-grade-subject provides a validation test for forecast bias. The setting relies on the institutional fact that teacher assignment to schools changes over time due to hiring, retirement, and reassignment, creating staggered shocks to teacher quality within narrowly defined cells that would not be expected if sorting on unobservables drove the estimates.

title: Why the Apple Doesn't Fall Far: Understanding Intergenerational Transmission of Human Capital

new_fields.research_question: Does a parent's level of education causally affect their children's educational attainment, or do observed intergenerational correlations in schooling reflect selection on ability and other family characteristics? Distinguishing these channels matters for assessing whether education policies generate spillovers onto the next generation.
new_fields.data_description: The authors use a unique Norwegian administrative dataset linking parents to children, drawing on registry data from Statistics Norway. Key variables include completed years of education for parents and children, parental earnings, birth year, and municipality of residence during schooling. The analysis exploits cohorts of parents born between roughly 1947 and 1958 who were potentially affected by a compulsory schooling reform rolled out across municipalities from 1960 to 1972. The unit of observation is the parent-child pair, with children's ultimate educational attainment observable even after leaving the parental home. Municipality-level controls (income, education levels, age structure, size, county) are also used. The dataset allows the authors to separately examine mother-son, mother-daughter, father-son, and father-daughter relationships.
new_fields.institutional_context: In 1959, the Norwegian Parliament mandated a reform of compulsory schooling that increased required education from seven to nine years and standardized the curriculum nationwide. Implementation was staggered across municipalities between 1960 and 1972, with all municipalities required to comply by 1973. Municipalities submitted plans to a Ministry of Education committee to receive federal funding for teachers and buildings; the committee sought representativeness conditional on plan quality. Prior research and the authors' own checks find no systematic relationship between the timing of adoption and municipality characteristics such as average earnings, taxable income, education levels, or age structure, once county fixed effects are included. This staggered rollout generates variation in parental schooling across birth cohorts and municipalities that is plausibly exogenous to parental ability, providing leverage for identifying the causal effect of parental education on children's outcomes.

title: Intensive Math Instruction and Educational Attainment: Long-Run Impacts of Double-Dose Algebra

new_fields.research_question: What are the long-run effects of assigning low-skilled 9th graders to an intensive algebra course that doubles instructional time, alters peer composition, and emphasizes problem-solving skills? Specifically, how does this intensive math instruction affect credits earned, test scores, high school graduation, and college enrollment, and do these effects vary by student reading skills?
new_fields.data_description: The study uses longitudinal administrative data from Chicago Public Schools (CPS) tracking students from 8th grade through college. The sample focuses on the first two cohorts of first-time 9th graders entering high school in fall 2003 and fall 2004. Key variables include 8th grade Iowa Tests of Basic Skills (ITBS) math and reading scores (used as the running variable), course enrollment and credits earned in high school, classroom peer composition and teacher assignments, high school test scores, high school graduation, and college enrollment outcomes. The unit of observation is the individual student. Data also capture classroom implementation details such as whether double-dose students had the same teacher across both algebra periods, consecutive scheduling, and overlap of class rosters.
new_fields.institutional_context: In fall 2003, Chicago Public Schools implemented a double-dose algebra policy in response to high 9th grade algebra failure rates following earlier curricular reforms that eliminated remedial courses. Under the policy, first-time 9th graders scoring below the national median on the 8th grade ITBS math test were required to enroll in two periods of algebra—a regular algebra class plus an algebra support/problem-solving class—receiving 90 minutes of daily math instruction instead of the usual 45. CPS provided specific curricula (Agile Mind, Cognitive Tutor) and professional development for double-dose teachers, and recommended that students have the same teacher for both periods, scheduled consecutively, with overlapping class rosters. The sharp test-score cutoff for assignment, used strictly for the 2003 and 2004 cohorts before adherence weakened, generates exogenous variation in treatment assignment around the national median threshold.

title: A Little Now for a Lot Later: A Look at a Texas Advanced Placement Incentive Program

new_fields.research_question: Does a program that provides cash payments to both students and teachers for passing scores on Advanced Placement exams, combined with teacher training and curriculum support, increase AP course enrollment, AP exam taking, and longer-term outcomes such as SAT/ACT performance and college matriculation in low-income, minority-majority high schools? Do such incentives distort behavior by diverting effort away from non-AP activities, and through what mechanisms do they operate?
new_fields.data_description: The analysis uses aggregate school-level data from Texas high schools, with cohorts observed before and after adoption of the Advanced Placement Incentive Program (APIP), which began in 1996 and expanded to over 40 schools. Key outcome variables include counts of students taking AP or International Baccalaureate exams, AP course enrollment, numbers of students achieving high SAT/ACT scores, and college matriculation (particularly at Texas colleges). Data come from the Texas Education Agency, AP Strategies (the nonprofit administering the program), and the College Board. Additional qualitative evidence comes from guidance counselors at participating schools. The unit of observation is the school-cohort. The sample covers schools that adopted the APIP and comparison schools that had committed to adoption but had not yet implemented it, spanning the mid-1990s through the early 2000s.
new_fields.institutional_context: The Advanced Placement Incentive Program (APIP), administered by the Dallas-based nonprofit AP Strategies, pays cash rewards to both students and teachers for each passing score (3 or higher) on AP exams, alongside teacher training by the College Board and pre-AP curriculum via 'vertical teams.' Lead teachers receive $3,000–$10,000 annual bonuses plus performance pay; AP teachers receive $100–$500 per passing student score; students also receive cash rewards. The program targets low-income, minority-majority Texas districts. Crucially, because administrators lacked capacity to launch the program simultaneously in all interested schools, rollout was staggered across schools that had already committed to adoption. This staggered implementation, combined with within-school cohort comparisons before and after adoption, provides variation in AP participation unrelated to individual student motivation, while schools in the queue but not yet implementing serve as a natural comparison group.

title: Into College, Out of Poverty? Policies to Increase the Postsecondary Attainment of the Poor

new_fields.research_question: Does reducing the monetary cost of college—through grants, scholarships, tax subsidies, or bundled financial-and-support programs—causally increase college entry, persistence, and degree completion among low-income students? Which design features (simplicity, transparency, linkage to academic support or performance incentives) make such cost reductions more effective at raising postsecondary attainment for the poor?
new_fields.data_description: The paper is a review synthesizing experimental and quasi-experimental estimates from the prior literature rather than a single new dataset analysis. Descriptive statistics cited come from the October Current Population Survey (authors' calculations of college-going rates for 23-year-olds in 1968 and 2005, and BA completion for 25-26 year olds in 2005), the College Board's Trends in Student Aid and Education Pays reports (2005) for Pell Grant and Stafford Loan volumes (e.g., $13.6 billion in Pell Grants and $55 billion in Stafford loans in 2004-05), and earnings series for full-time workers by education level from 1972-2005 in constant 2003 dollars. Reviewed studies cover federal Pell Grants, Stafford Loans, state merit-aid programs, tax credits, and private/foundation scholarships (Gates, I Have a Dream, Kalamazoo Promise), with outcomes including enrollment, retention, and degree completion.
new_fields.institutional_context: The U.S. postsecondary aid system offers multiple discrete sources of variation in college prices. Federal Pell Grants are means-tested, flowing almost exclusively to families below roughly $40,000 in income, while Stafford Loans have their own eligibility rules. States subsidize public-university tuition and, since the early 1990s, more than a dozen states have launched broad-based merit-aid programs awarding full tuition to residents meeting a minimum high-school GPA threshold (commonly 3.0). Federal Hope and Lifetime Learning tax credits, tuition deductions, Coverdell accounts, and 529 plans create additional price variation skewed toward higher-income families. Foundation and place-based programs (Gates Millennium Scholars, I Have a Dream, Kalamazoo Promise) and randomized scholarship-plus-services demonstrations provide further quasi-random or randomized shifts in college costs that can be exploited to identify causal effects on attainment.

title: The Impacts of Environmental Regulations on Industrial Activity: Evidence from the 1970 and 1977 Clean Air Act Amendments and the Census of Manufactures

new_fields.research_question: Do federally mandated county-level air pollution regulations reduce industrial activity among polluting manufacturers? Specifically, how do stricter regulatory designations affect employment, capital stock, and output growth in pollution-intensive industries relative to less-regulated areas?
new_fields.data_description: The analysis combines two main data sources covering 1967-1987. Regulatory data consist of annual pollutant-specific nonattainment/attainment designations for each of the 3,070 U.S. counties for four criteria pollutants (carbon monoxide, ozone, sulfur dioxide, and total suspended particulates), compiled by the author from the Code of Federal Regulations and EPA pollution monitors. Manufacturing data come from the 1967, 1972, 1977, 1982, and 1987 Censuses of Manufactures microdata (Longitudinal Research Database), comprising approximately 1.75 million plant-level observations with detailed information on county of location, employment, capital stock, investment, shipments/output, and input usage. The unit of observation is the manufacturing plant, and outcomes are measured as plant-level growth in employment, capital stock, and shipments. Appendix data include federal air quality standards for each pollutant.
new_fields.institutional_context: The 1970 and 1977 Clean Air Act Amendments established uniform national ambient air quality standards for four criteria pollutants and required the EPA to annually classify every U.S. county as either 'nonattainment' or 'attainment' for each pollutant based on whether local concentrations exceeded the federal threshold. Plants emitting a regulated pollutant in nonattainment counties faced substantially stricter oversight: state-of-the-art abatement equipment requirements, emissions permits, emission ceilings on existing sources, and (after 1977) a requirement that new emissions be offset by reductions elsewhere in the same county. In attainment counties, abatement requirements were weaker and small or existing plants were largely unregulated. Non-emitters were unregulated in both. This pollutant-by-county assignment generates cross-sectional and longitudinal variation in regulatory stringency that differentially affects otherwise similar plants depending on location and emissions profile, while enforcement by EPA and states made the designations binding.

title: Are Consumers Myopic? Evidence from New and Used Car Purchases

new_fields.research_question: Do consumers fully incorporate expected future fuel costs into their willingness-to-pay when purchasing new and used cars, or do they undervalue (act myopically toward) these future costs relative to the up-front purchase price? Specifically, how much does a change in gasoline prices shift equilibrium prices and market shares of vehicles across different fuel-economy classes, and what implicit discount rate does this imply?
new_fields.data_description: The primary dataset consists of individual automobile transaction records from approximately 20 percent of all new car dealerships in the United States, covering January 1, 1999 through June 30, 2008. Data were collected by a major market research firm and include every new and used car transaction at sample dealers during the period. For each transaction, the authors observe the exact vehicle purchased (make, model, model year, trim, engine characteristics, fuel economy/MPG), the transaction price paid (net of manufacturer rebates and trade-in credits), location, purchase timing, and buyer demographics. These transaction data are combined with data on gasoline prices and information on vehicle characteristics such as MPG, enabling analysis of prices, market shares, and unit sales across fuel-economy quartiles for both new and used cars at the transaction level.
new_fields.institutional_context: Identification exploits substantial temporal and geographic variation in retail gasoline prices between 1999 and 2008, a period spanning both low and sharply rising fuel prices. Because the stock of vehicle models available at any moment is fixed in the short run (manufacturers cannot quickly redesign fuel economy), fluctuations in gasoline prices generate exogenous shifts in the expected future operating cost of owning cars of different fuel economies, while leaving the up-front capital cost of the vehicle largely unaffected in the very short run. Comparing how equilibrium transaction prices and market shares of high-MPG versus low-MPG vehicles move with gasoline prices—within narrowly defined car models and controlling for location and time—allows the researchers to recover how consumers trade off up-front vehicle prices against ongoing fuel costs, and thus to back out implicit discount rates applied to future fuel expenditures.

title: The Effect of Driving Restrictions on Air Quality in Mexico City

new_fields.research_question: Did the 1989 Mexico City policy banning most vehicles from circulating one weekday per week based on license plate numbers reduce urban air pollution? The paper also investigates behavioral responses—whether the ban caused drivers to shift to public transit or instead led to changes in vehicle ownership and fleet composition that could offset intended air-quality gains.
new_fields.data_description: The primary data are hourly air pollution readings from Mexico City's Automated Environmental Monitoring Network (Red Automática de Monitoreo Ambiental), covering five pollutants: carbon monoxide, nitrogen dioxide, ozone, nitrogen oxides, and sulfur dioxide. The network began in 1986 with between 5 and 15 monitoring stations per pollutant. The same network provides hourly temperature, humidity, and wind speed. The empirical analysis focuses on 1986–1993, a symmetric 8-year window around the November 20, 1989 policy introduction, with observations at the station-hour level restricted to stations operating in 1986. Complementary data include gasoline sales, vehicle registrations, bus and subway ridership, taxi registrations, and advertised used-vehicle prices for taxis and transit vans in the Mexico City metropolitan area.
new_fields.institutional_context: On November 20, 1989, the Mexico City government introduced Hoy No Circula (HNC), which prohibits most private vehicles from circulating one weekday per week, assigned by the last digit of the license plate, between 5:00 a.m. and 10:00 p.m. The program initially covered 2.3 million vehicles (about 460,000 per day) across the metropolitan area. Exemptions applied to taxis, buses, emergency vehicles, LPG-fueled commercial vehicles, and perishable-goods transporters. Enforcement by city police was vigorous from day one: violators faced 48-hour vehicle impoundment and fines equivalent to about US$200, and license-plate-based enforcement made violations easy to detect. Compliance was reportedly near universal. The sharp, date-specific rollout creates a clean temporal break in driving behavior that can be exploited to identify pollution effects, using earlier-year seasonal patterns as a counterfactual.

title: What Do Emissions Markets Deliver and to Whom? Evidence from Southern California's NOx Trading Program

new_fields.research_question: Does replacing prescriptive facility-level emissions standards with a market-based cap-and-trade system for nitrogen oxides reduce facility-level emissions more than the prescriptive regime would have? And are any emissions reductions achieved under the market-based regime distributed equitably across neighborhoods with different socio-economic and demographic characteristics, or are pollution burdens concentrated in low-income and minority communities?
new_fields.data_description: The authors assemble facility-level NOx emissions data for industrial stationary sources in California. Treated facilities are those required to participate in Southern California's RECLAIM program, administered by the South Coast Air Quality Management District (SCAQMD). Control facilities are similar industrial sources located in other California non-attainment counties that remained under prescriptive standards. Emissions data were obtained with assistance from the California Air Resources Board and SCAQMD. The panel spans years before and after RECLAIM's 1994 launch, allowing comparison of emissions trajectories across regulatory regimes. The authors additionally link facilities to neighborhood-level socio-economic and demographic characteristics (e.g., income, minority share) from census data in order to examine the distributional incidence of emissions changes across communities surrounding regulated plants.
new_fields.institutional_context: Following the 1990 Clean Air Act Amendments, extreme ozone non-attainment areas were required to use economic incentive programs to meet federal ambient air quality standards. In 1994, SCAQMD launched the Regional Clean Air Incentives Market (RECLAIM), which replaced more than 40 prescriptive command-and-control rules for NOx (and SO2) with a tradable permit system covering large industrial facilities in the Los Angeles basin. Crucially, only a subset of industrial facilities in California non-attainment counties were moved from the prescriptive regime into RECLAIM: participation was determined by location within SCAQMD's jurisdiction and by source-size thresholds. Similar facilities elsewhere in California's non-attainment areas remained under the prescriptive standards, providing a comparison group exposed to the same federal air-quality pressure, statewide economic conditions, and technological trends but a different regulatory instrument.

title: The Economic Impact of Hurricane Katrina on its Victims: Evidence from Individual Tax Returns

new_fields.research_question: What are the long-term economic and social consequences of Hurricane Katrina on the individuals who lived in New Orleans prior to the storm? Specifically, how did the disaster affect victims' location choices, wage and total income, employment, unemployment receipts, retirement account withdrawals, marriage, divorce, and fertility over the subsequent years?
new_fields.data_description: The authors use a panel drawn from the universe of U.S. individual tax returns (IRS Form 1040 filings) spanning 1999 to 2010, with the unit of observation being tax-filing households observed annually. Tax returns provide filing addresses (allowing identification of pre-storm New Orleans residents), and records are linked across years to form a twelve-year household panel. Variables include wage and salary income, self-employment income, unemployment insurance receipts, retirement account distributions, adjusted gross income, marital status, number of dependent children, homeownership proxies, and age. Supplementary data for selecting comparison cities come from the 2000 U.S. Decennial Census and the 2001–2005 American Community Survey. Regional Economic Information Systems data are used for aggregate unemployment insurance statistics. The sample covers all pre-Katrina New Orleans filers and a random subsample of filers from matched control cities.
new_fields.institutional_context: Hurricane Katrina struck the U.S. Gulf Coast in late August 2005 with essentially no advance warning, killing nearly 2,000 people, destroying over 200,000 homes, and causing upwards of $100 billion in property damage. It displaced a large share of New Orleans residents, many of whom remained geographically dispersed years later. The disaster is treated as a large, unanticipated shock to the affected population. Victims received substantial government and private support: over $100 billion in direct disaster relief, sharp increases in unemployment insurance payments, an expanded Work Opportunity Tax Credit covering Katrina-affected areas, a special exemption allowing penalty-free early withdrawals from retirement accounts for affected residents, and over $4 billion in charitable donations. Because New Orleans is demographically and economically unique, the authors select comparable U.S. cities using pre-2005 Census and ACS characteristics and apply propensity-score reweighting on pre-storm household attributes to construct a counterfactual.

title: Does Air Quality Matter? Evidence from the Housing Market

new_fields.research_question: Does air quality get capitalized into housing prices? Specifically, this paper seeks to identify the causal effect of reductions in total suspended particulates (TSPs) on county-level residential property values, moving beyond cross-sectional correlations that have historically produced weak and unstable estimates of the hedonic price gradient for clean air.
new_fields.data_description: The authors assemble county-level microdata for the United States covering 1970-1990. County attainment/non-attainment status for each year was hand-collected from the Code of Federal Regulations (the first such compilation). County air pollution measurements (total suspended particulates, TSPs) come from the EPA's Air Quality Subsystem Database, obtained via a Freedom of Information Act request. Property value data and county demographic/economic characteristics are drawn from the 1972, 1983, and 1994 County and City Data Books, supplemented with the 1980 and 1990 Census five-percent PUMS files. The unit of observation is the county, and key variables include mean TSP concentrations (mg/m3), median housing values, regulatory status, and covariates such as income, education, and population density. The analysis focuses on changes across the 1970s and 1980s decades.
new_fields.institutional_context: The 1970 and 1977 Clean Air Act Amendments marked the federal government's first major intervention in air pollution regulation. The EPA established national ambient air quality standards for pollutants including total suspended particulates (TSPs) and assigned each U.S. county to either 'non-attainment' or 'attainment' status based on whether measured pollution concentrations exceeded federally-determined maximum allowable thresholds. Polluters located in non-attainment counties were subject to substantially stricter federal regulatory oversight—including mandatory State Implementation Plans specifying abatement actions—than those in attainment counties. Because assignment to non-attainment status is a discrete function of whether a county crosses a federal pollution threshold, and the resulting regulatory pressure generated larger pollution reductions in non-attainment counties (7-10 mg/m3 in the 1970s, 4-5 mg/m3 in the 1980s relative to attainment counties), the regulation generates quasi-random variation in air quality changes that is plausibly orthogonal to unobserved county-level housing demand and supply shocks.

title: Environmental Regulations, Air and Water Pollution, and Infant Mortality in India

new_fields.research_question: Can environmental regulations effectively reduce air and water pollution in a developing country with weak regulatory institutions, and do such pollution reductions translate into improvements in infant health? Additionally, why might air pollution regulations succeed while water pollution regulations fail in the same institutional setting?
new_fields.data_description: The authors construct a novel city-level panel dataset for India covering 1986–2007, combining air pollution, water pollution, environmental regulation adoption, and infant mortality data. Air pollution data cover approximately 140 cities, with measurements of particulate matter (PM, diameter <100μm), sulfur dioxide (SO2), and nitrogen dioxide (NO2), drawn from the Central Pollution Control Board. Water pollution data cover 424 cities across 162 rivers, including biochemical oxygen demand, dissolved oxygen, and fecal coliform counts. The authors compiled city-level records of environmental regulation adoption dates (Supreme Court Action Plans, Mandated Catalytic Converters, National River Conservation Plan)—a dataset not previously assembled by the government or researchers. Infant mortality rates at the city level are also included. Supplementary data include literacy rates and newspaper coverage (Times of India) as proxies for public demand for environmental quality.
new_fields.institutional_context: India's environmental regulatory framework originated with the Water Act of 1974 and Air Act of 1981, which created the Central and State Pollution Control Boards. Following the 1984 Bhopal Disaster, public interest litigation and judicial activism expanded dramatically. The paper exploits the staggered adoption across cities of three major regulatory interventions: (1) Supreme Court Action Plans, promulgated by India's supreme court starting in the late 1990s, mandating city-specific air pollution abatement; (2) Mandated Catalytic Converters, requiring new automobiles in designated cities to have catalytic converters; and (3) the National River Conservation Plan, the flagship water policy targeting industrial effluent reduction and sewage treatment along specific river segments. The cross-city and cross-time variation in when these policies took effect, combined with differences in enforcement mechanisms (judicial versus executive, with or without dedicated funding), provides the comparative setting for evaluating regulatory effectiveness in a weak-institutions context.

title: The Impact of Pollution on Worker Productivity

new_fields.research_question: Does ambient ozone pollution reduce the productivity of workers engaged in physically demanding outdoor tasks, even at concentrations below federal air quality standards? The study seeks to isolate the effect of pollution on the intensive margin of labor — output per unit of time worked — separate from any labor supply response, thereby quantifying a previously undocumented environmental productivity effect.
new_fields.data_description: The authors use a proprietary daily panel dataset from an electronic payroll tracking system (PET Tiger, by Orange Enterprises) at a single ~500-acre farm in California's Central Valley that grows blueberries and grapes during the 2009 and 2010 growing seasons. The worker-day-level data include unique worker IDs, pieces harvested, field location, crop type, piece-rate contract terms (time-plus-pieces or time-plus-all-pieces, with a binding $8/hour minimum wage), clock-in/out times, and gender. These productivity records are merged with hourly ozone concentrations, temperature, and other meteorological and air-quality variables from California Air Resources Board monitoring stations. The unit of observation is a worker-day, enabling measurement of both labor supply (hours, attendance) and intensive-margin productivity (pieces per hour).
new_fields.institutional_context: Two institutional features enable credible causal identification. First, daily fluctuations in ground-level ozone near the farm are plausibly exogenous to local economic activity: ozone is not directly emitted but forms from nonlinear photochemical reactions of NOx and VOCs transported from distant urban centers (Los Angeles, San Francisco), so daily variation is driven by weather and regional transport rather than local conditions. Second, agricultural workers exhibit highly inelastic short-run labor supply — they arrive and leave in crews, spend the day outdoors regardless of air quality, and have little scope for avoidance behavior, which the authors verify using data on attendance and hours. Piece-rate compensation ensures that measured output closely reflects productive capacity, while the minimum-wage floor creates a known kink addressed through censored regression specifications.

title: The Causal Effect of Environmental Catastrophe on Long-Run Economic Growth: Evidence from 6,700 Cyclones

new_fields.research_question: Do tropical cyclones have a causal effect on long-run economic growth, and if so, how large and persistent are the income losses? The paper asks whether national economies recover from environmental catastrophes through rebuilding, migration, or wealth transfers, or whether disaster exposure permanently depresses income trajectories. It also investigates how cumulative exposure shapes cross-country patterns of development and the implied cost of climate change.
new_fields.data_description: The authors construct a novel global dataset of tropical cyclone exposure for every country over 1950-2008, covering approximately 6,700 storms and 4,174 cyclone-by-country events. Cyclone exposure is measured using ground-, ship-, aerial-, and satellite-based meteorological observations combined with cyclone physics models, producing annual nationally-averaged maximum wind speed (m/s) at 1°x1° pixel resolution aggregated to country level. These physical measures are merged with country-year macroeconomic data on GDP per capita growth and other macro outcomes. The unit of observation is country-year, with panel coverage spanning nearly six decades. Additional variables include country fixed effects, country-specific trends, year fixed effects, and lagged cyclone exposure distributions used to capture delayed impacts over a 20-year horizon.
new_fields.institutional_context: Identification leverages the stochastic nature of tropical cyclone formation, trajectory, and intensity, which are governed by ocean and atmospheric dynamics. Conditional on a country's geographic location, year-to-year variation in whether cyclones form, where they travel, and how intense they become is effectively random, producing exogenous within-country variation in annual disaster exposure. While long-run average cyclone climatology is a fixed geographic feature of countries (and thus correlated with other persistent characteristics), the specific timing and severity of strikes in any given year is not. This allows the authors to compare a country's growth to its own pre-strike trajectory, after absorbing country fixed effects, country-specific trends, and global year shocks, isolating the causal effect of cyclone strikes from confounding geographic, institutional, or global macroeconomic factors.

title: Regression Discontinuity Designs in Economics

new_fields.research_question: This paper is a methodological review rather than an empirical study with a single causal question. It asks: under what conditions can treatment effects be credibly identified in non-experimental settings where treatment status changes sharply at a known cutoff of an observed assignment variable, how should such estimates be interpreted, and what practical procedures yield reliable estimates? It synthesizes when such designs succeed or fail based on agents' ability to manipulate the assignment variable.
new_fields.data_description: As a survey/user-guide, the paper does not analyze a single dataset but draws on examples from the applied economics literature published from the 1960s through the late 2000s. Illustrative applications referenced include Thistlethwaite and Campbell (1960) on merit award test-score cutoffs and academic outcomes; Van der Klaauw (2002) on financial aid thresholds; Angrist and Lavy (1999) on class-size rules (Maimonides' rule) in Israeli schools; Black (1999) on school district boundary discontinuities and housing prices; and studies on welfare, unemployment insurance, disability programs, Medicaid eligibility thresholds, remedial education cutoffs, close-election vote shares for median voter tests, and union certification election thresholds. Key variables across examples include an assignment/forcing variable X, a cutoff c, a binary treatment D, and outcomes Y, typically at the individual, student, household, firm, or electoral-district level.
new_fields.institutional_context: The methodological setting exploited throughout the paper is one in which an administrative or institutional rule deterministically (or probabilistically) assigns a treatment once an observed continuous variable crosses a known threshold: test scores determining scholarship or remedial-education placement, income or age thresholds determining program eligibility (Medicaid, disability, UI), enrollment cutoffs triggering class-size caps under Maimonides' rule, vote-share thresholds of 50% determining electoral victory or union certification, and geographic boundaries separating school districts. Identification rests on the assumption that agents cannot precisely manipulate their position relative to the cutoff, so units just above and just below are comparable. This local randomization arises from institutional cutoff rules combined with imprecise control, making baseline covariates balanced across the threshold and allowing tests analogous to those used for randomized experiments.

title: Enjoying the Quiet Life? Corporate Governance and Managerial Preferences

new_fields.research_question: How does weakening the disciplining threat faced by corporate managers affect firm and plant outcomes such as worker wages, plant creation and destruction, productivity, and profitability? What do these responses reveal about managerial preferences — specifically, whether managers pursue empire building or instead prefer a 'quiet life'?
new_fields.data_description: The analysis uses a unique match between the Longitudinal Research Database (LRD), which provides plant-level data on the U.S. manufacturing sector (wages for production and white-collar workers, employment, plant births and deaths, capital, output, and productivity), and Compustat, which provides firm-level balance sheet and stock market information. Observations are at the plant-year level for manufacturing plants, linked to their parent firms, and at the firm-year level for aggregate outcomes. The sample spans roughly the late 1970s through the early 1990s, covering the period over which U.S. states enacted second- and third-generation antitakeover statutes. Key variables include plant wages by worker type, plant creation/destruction rates, total factor productivity, return on capital, firm size, and capital expenditures, along with each firm's state of incorporation and each plant's state of location.
new_fields.institutional_context: Beginning in the mid-1980s, U.S. states enacted a wave of second- and third-generation antitakeover statutes — most notably business combination laws — that sharply reduced the threat of hostile takeovers for firms chartered in the legislating state. These laws were adopted by different states at different times between roughly 1984 and 1991, creating staggered changes in the strength of external governance. Crucially, the statutes apply based on a firm's state of incorporation, a purely legal designation often unrelated to where the firm actually operates. Because about three-quarters of firms in the sample own plants outside their state of incorporation, one can compare plants located in the same state but belonging to firms incorporated in different states, absorbing local economic and political shocks that might otherwise be correlated with the timing of legislation.

title: Bank Mergers and Crime: The Real and Social Effects of Credit Market Competition

new_fields.research_question: Do reductions in local banking competition causally affect credit conditions, local real economic activity, and subsequent property crime rates in affected neighborhoods? Specifically, how do consolidations among large banks alter interest rates, loan sizes, construction, property prices, neighborhood demographics, and downstream social outcomes such as burglary and property crime?
new_fields.data_description: The authors combine several micro-level datasets. Commercial loan and property transaction data come from COMPS.com, covering 22,642 U.S. commercial real estate transactions between January 1992 and March 1999 across 11 states plus DC, with detailed geocoded property location, prices, loan terms, capitalization rates, and participant identities. Crime data at the neighborhood level come from CAP Index, Inc., supplemented with FBI Uniform Crime Reports at the county level (burglary, property crime, homicide). Construction activity is from F.W. Dodge (McGraw-Hill). Demographic and income data come from the U.S. Census. Bank merger data cover mergers of non-failing banks with at least $1 billion in assets during the 1990s. State bank branching deregulation dates are from Phil Strahan. Observations are at the neighborhood (within-county), county, and state levels.
new_fields.institutional_context: Identification leverages mergers between large (>$1 billion assets), non-failing U.S. commercial banks during the 1990s as plausibly exogenous shocks to local banking competition within neighborhoods. Because small commercial real estate lending is geographically localized due to information and agency frictions, merger-induced changes in local loan market concentration generate variation in credit terms within counties. The large size and health of merging banks makes it implausible that local neighborhood economic conditions drive the mergers, while prior literature (Berger et al. 1998) shows that merger-induced competitive distortions persist roughly three years before new entry restores equilibrium. As a complementary source of variation, the authors exploit the staggered timing of U.S. state-level deregulation of bank branching restrictions, which increased credit market competition in the opposite direction, providing an additional lever for identifying the effects of banking competition on credit, real activity, and crime.

title: Common Risk Factors in the Returns on Stocks and Bonds

new_fields.research_question: Do a small number of common risk factors explain the cross-section and time-series variation in average returns on stocks and bonds? Specifically, can systematic variation in returns across portfolios sorted on firm size and book-to-market equity, along with bond-market return patterns, be captured by shared sources of priced risk that link equity and fixed-income markets?
new_fields.data_description: The paper uses monthly returns on U.S. stocks from NYSE, AMEX, and NASDAQ (CRSP) combined with accounting data from COMPUSTAT to compute book-to-market equity and firm size (market capitalization). Stocks are sorted into portfolios by size and book-to-market to form test assets and mimicking factor portfolios (SMB for size and HML for value). The analysis also uses monthly returns on U.S. government and corporate bond portfolios spanning different maturities and default-risk categories, with factors capturing a term-structure premium (TERM) and a default premium (DEF). A broad market equity return factor (excess return on the value-weighted market) is also included. The sample covers roughly 1963–1991 at the monthly frequency, with portfolios as the unit of observation.
new_fields.institutional_context: Identification exploits the cross-sectional dispersion in average returns associated with firm characteristics (size and book-to-market) and with bond characteristics (maturity and default risk). By constructing mimicking portfolios that go long and short stocks ranked on these attributes, the authors isolate common sources of co-movement in returns that proxy for underlying state variables or distress/term/default risks. The institutional setting is the integrated U.S. capital market in which equities and bonds are priced, so that factors built from bond markets (term and default spreads) can be tested as priced risks in equities, and stock-based size/value factors can be tested in bonds. This shared pricing environment allows joint time-series regressions of portfolio excess returns on the candidate factors to assess which risks are commonly compensated across both asset classes.

title: Event Studies in Economics and Finance

new_fields.research_question: Do quarterly corporate earnings announcements convey new information to equity markets, such that the magnitude and sign of unexpected earnings are reflected in contemporaneous changes in the firm's stock price? Specifically, are positive earnings surprises associated with equity price increases and negative surprises with price decreases around the announcement date?
new_fields.data_description: The illustrative application uses quarterly earnings announcements for the 30 firms comprising the Dow Jones Industrial Index over a five-year period from January 1989 to December 1993, covering the fourth quarter of 1988 through the third quarter of 1993, yielding 600 firm-quarter announcements. For each announcement, three items are compiled: the announcement date (from Datastream), the actual reported earnings (from Compustat), and the mean analyst earnings forecast from the Institutional Brokers Estimate System (I/B/E/S), taken from the last month of the quarter, which proxies for the market's earnings expectation. Daily stock returns are used, with a 41-day window (20 days before, day of, and 20 days after the announcement) and a 250-trading-day pre-announcement estimation period. Announcements are classified as good, no, or bad news using a 2.5% surprise threshold.
new_fields.institutional_context: The setting exploits mandatory quarterly earnings disclosures by publicly traded U.S. firms, governed by Financial Accounting Standards Board (FASB) and Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) reporting regulations designed to ensure that financial statements are informative about firm value. Because announcement dates are publicly scheduled and the unexpected component of earnings can be measured as the deviation of reported earnings from analysts' pre-announcement consensus forecasts (I/B/E/S), each announcement provides a discrete, dated information release to investors. Under market rationality, any new information embedded in the disclosure should be impounded rapidly into equity prices on or immediately around the announcement day. This narrow, well-defined informational release—together with a pre-announcement window over which normal return behavior can be characterized—provides the setting for attributing short-horizon equity price movements to the earnings news itself.

title: The Econometrics of Financial Markets

new_fields.research_question: Do quarterly earnings announcements convey value-relevant information to equity investors, and does the equity-price response vary with the magnitude and sign of the unexpected component of the announcement (good news, no news, bad news)? The study seeks to quantify the short-window causal impact of the announcement itself on firm equity value.
new_fields.data_description: The illustrative sample covers the thirty firms in the Dow Jones Industrial Index over the five-year period from January 1989 to December 1993, yielding 600 quarterly earnings announcements (Q4 1988 through Q3 1993). For each firm-quarter the authors compile the announcement date (from Datastream), actual announced earnings (from Compustat), and the mean analyst earnings forecast taken in the last month of the quarter (from I/B/E/S) as a proxy for market expectations. The unit of observation is a firm-quarter announcement. Daily stock returns are used at a one-day sampling interval, with a 41-day window around the announcement (20 pre-event days, the event day, and 20 post-event days) and a 250-trading-day pre-announcement window used to fit normal-return benchmarks such as the constant-mean-return and market models.
new_fields.institutional_context: Identification exploits the discrete, publicly observable release of quarterly earnings figures, whose timing is determined by FASB and SEC disclosure regulations rather than by investors. Because rational, informationally efficient markets should impound news into prices essentially immediately, comparing realized short-horizon returns around the announcement to a statistically modeled benchmark of returns that would have prevailed absent the announcement isolates the price impact attributable to the news. Announcements are further classified by their surprise relative to the consensus I/B/E/S forecast: actual earnings exceeding expectations by more than 2.5% are labeled good news, those falling more than 2.5% short are bad news, and those within a 5% band around expectations are no news (189, 238, and 173 cases respectively), providing cross-sectional variation in the information shock.

title: Investor Sentiment and the Cross-Section of Stock Returns

new_fields.research_question: Does broad investor sentiment at the beginning of a period predict subsequent cross-sectional differences in stock returns, particularly for stocks whose valuations are more subjective and harder to arbitrage? The paper asks whether waves of sentiment lead to initial mispricing of small, young, volatile, unprofitable, non-dividend-paying, extreme-growth, and distressed firms that later corrects, and whether such predictability is distinct from compensation for systematic risk.
new_fields.data_description: The study uses U.S. monthly stock returns from CRSP between 1963 and 2001, with firm-month as the unit of observation. Firm characteristics used to sort stocks include market equity (size), firm age, return volatility, profitability (earnings), dividend-paying status, book-to-market ratio, sales growth, and external financing activity, constructed from CRSP and Compustat. The authors assemble several time-series proxies for investor sentiment drawn from prior literature (e.g., closed-end fund discount, NYSE turnover, number and first-day returns of IPOs, equity share in new issues, dividend premium) and construct a composite sentiment index as the first principal component of these proxies. Each proxy is orthogonalized against a set of macroeconomic condition variables. The sample also incorporates a qualitative narrative of U.S. market sentiment episodes from 1961 through the late-1990s Internet bubble.
new_fields.institutional_context: Identification exploits time variation in aggregate U.S. investor sentiment across roughly four decades (1961–2001), a period spanning multiple speculative episodes including the late-1960s growth-stock craze, the 1970s 'Nifty Fifty,' biotech and technology booms, and the late-1990s Internet bubble, as well as intervening low-sentiment periods. Because sentiment-driven demand shocks in the presence of binding arbitrage constraints are predicted to disproportionately affect stocks with highly subjective valuations and high arbitrage costs, the authors treat shifts in beginning-of-period sentiment as a source of conditioning variation that should produce predictable, sign-flipping cross-sectional return patterns across firm-characteristic deciles. To separate sentiment-based mispricing from rational risk compensation, the sentiment proxies are purged of contemporaneous macroeconomic influences, and the resulting orthogonalized measures align closely with historical anecdotal accounts of bubbles and busts.

title: Financial Dependence and Growth

new_fields.research_question: Does the development of a country's financial sector causally promote economic growth by lowering the cost of external finance to firms? Specifically, do industrial sectors that are technologically more dependent on external financing grow disproportionately faster in countries with more developed financial markets and institutions, compared to sectors that can fund themselves internally?
new_fields.data_description: The study combines industry-level data across a large cross-section of countries during the 1980s with firm-level data from the United States used to construct an industry-specific measure of external financial dependence (the difference between capital investment and internally generated cash flow from operations, computed from U.S. listed firms under the assumption that U.S. capital markets are frictionless). Country-level financial development is measured using indicators such as the size of domestic credit markets and stock market capitalization, along with accounting standards. Outcome variables include real industry growth rates, investment intensity, and average firm size by industry-country pair. Controls include country-level proxies for overall economic development and human capital, plus the ex ante share of financially dependent industries in each economy.
new_fields.institutional_context: Identification exploits the idea that an industry's need for external finance is a technological characteristic that persists across countries, while countries differ exogenously in how well-developed their financial systems are. Cross-country variation in financial development is argued to be largely predetermined — shaped historically by colonial origin and the legal tradition (common law versus civil law) imposed by colonizers, as documented by La Porta, Lopez-de-Silanes, Shleifer and Vishny. This allows the authors to compare how much faster externally dependent industries grow relative to less dependent ones, across countries with different financial systems, while absorbing country and industry fixed effects. Accounting standards serve as a more exogenous proxy for financial development to address concerns that markets might endogenously develop in anticipation of industry financing needs.

title: Finance and the Sources of Growth

new_fields.research_question: Does the level of banking sector development causally affect real per capita GDP growth, and through which channels—total factor productivity growth, physical capital accumulation, or private saving rates? The paper seeks to distinguish whether banks promote growth primarily by improving the allocation of resources (raising productivity) or by mobilizing savings and fostering capital accumulation.
new_fields.data_description: The analysis uses a cross-country dataset covering 63 countries over 1960–1995. Two samples are constructed: a pure cross-section with variables averaged over 1960–1995, and a panel with data averaged over seven non-overlapping 5-year periods between 1960 and 1995. Key variables include real per capita GDP growth, real per capita physical capital stock growth (using disaggregated Penn-World Tables 5.6 capital stock data), total factor productivity growth (computed under Mankiw 1995 and Bils–Klenow 1996 human-capital specifications), and gross private saving as a share of gross private disposable income (1971–1995, from a World Bank initiative by Loayza et al. 1998). Banking sector development is measured as private credit by deposit-money banks relative to GDP, with correct deflation of financial stocks. Legal-origin classifications (English, French, German, Scandinavian), extended from LLSV's 49 to 63 countries, are also used.
new_fields.institutional_context: Identification exploits the historical origin of countries' legal systems. Most countries acquired their legal traditions—English common law, or French, German, or Scandinavian civil law—through colonization or occupation centuries ago, making legal origin plausibly exogenous to contemporary economic growth. LaPorta, Lopez-de-Silanes, Shleifer, and Vishny (1997, 1998) document that legal origin shapes laws governing bank credit, the enforcement of financial contracts, and corporate information disclosure standards, and subsequent work (Levine, Loayza, and Beck 1998; Levine 1998, 1999) shows these legal-system features substantively explain cross-country differences in banking sector development. Because legal origin plausibly affects growth only through its influence on the contracting and financial environment, it provides exogenous variation in banking development. In the panel setting, country-specific unobserved heterogeneity and reverse causality are addressed by exploiting the time-series variation and using lagged levels and differences of the regressors as internal instruments.

title: Why Has CEO Pay Increased So Much?

new_fields.research_question: What explains the large increase in CEO compensation in the United States between 1980 and 2003? Specifically, to what extent can the roughly sixfold rise in CEO pay be accounted for by the contemporaneous growth in the market value of large firms, as opposed to agency problems, governance failures, or changes in incentive structures? The paper also asks how CEO pay levels vary cross-sectionally with firm size and across countries.
new_fields.data_description: The paper uses data on U.S. CEO compensation for large publicly traded firms, drawing on compensation data shared by Carola Frydman and Kevin J. Murphy, covering CEO pay levels over the period from approximately 1970 through 2003, with particular focus on 1980–2003. Key variables include total CEO compensation, firm market capitalization (equity plus debt), earnings (EBIT), and firm rank by size. The unit of observation is the firm-year for large U.S. companies, particularly the top 500 firms. Supplementary international evidence on CEO pay and firm size is drawn from prior studies (e.g., Abowd and Bognanno; Conyon and Murphy) to examine cross-country differences in executive compensation relative to firm size. The calibration focuses on top-ranked CEOs and their firms.
new_fields.institutional_context: The setting is the U.S. market for top executives, conceptualized as a competitive assignment market in which heterogeneous CEOs are matched to heterogeneous firms, with more talented CEOs running larger firms because their marginal productivity scales with firm size. Between 1980 and 2003, market capitalizations of large U.S. corporations rose approximately sixfold, providing substantial cross-sectional and time-series variation in firm size. This variation, combined with the assignment structure, pins down equilibrium pay levels: a given CEO's compensation depends on both own-firm size and the aggregate size of large firms in the economy. Cross-country differences in the growth of firm market values (e.g., Europe vs. the U.S.) provide additional variation used to assess whether compensation tracks firm size. The calibration leverages extreme value theory applied to the upper tail of the talent and firm size distributions.

title: Anchoring on Credit Spreads

new_fields.research_question: Do historical, non-informative signals—specifically the level of credit spreads prevailing when a firm last borrowed—influence the interest rate a firm pays on a new loan today, beyond what current fundamentals justify? The paper investigates whether past deal terms exert a behavioral pull on current borrowing costs, generating systematic premia or discounts unrelated to creditworthiness.
new_fields.data_description: The analysis uses syndicated loan data, focusing on firms that borrow repeatedly from banking syndicates. Key variables include loan-level credit spreads (above LIBOR), loan origination dates, credit ratings (AAA through CCC), lead arranger identities, covenants, fees, loan size, and maturity. The sample spans multiple years including a detailed look at borrowers that took loans in 2005–2007 and again in 2008 (around the financial crisis). The unit of observation is a loan (or pair of consecutive loans for the same firm). Firm-level financial variables such as profitability, leverage, valuation ratios, and past/future stock returns are also used to check for creditworthiness differences. Aggregate credit spread indices by rating category provide the market-level benchmark against which firm-specific past spreads are compared.
new_fields.institutional_context: The syndicated loan market features bilateral negotiation between a borrower and a lead-arranger bank, with substantial information asymmetry and match-specific surplus that produces a range of feasible interest rates rather than a single competitive price. Because any given loan's spread is negotiated, psychological reference points—particularly the spread a firm paid on its previous loan, or the prevailing aggregate spread at that prior origination—can enter bargaining. Variation across firms in the timing of their last loan, combined with large fluctuations in aggregate credit spreads (notably the 2008 crisis, when spreads rose ~35%), creates quasi-random differences in historical 'anchors' across otherwise similar borrowers. Features such as whether the lead arranger changed, whether the firm is rated, and the number of prior lead arrangers provide variation in anchor salience and lender competition used to identify the behavioral mechanism.

title: Growing Out of Trouble? Corporate Responses to Liability Risk

new_fields.research_question: How do firms adjust their investment, financing, and payout decisions when they experience an exogenous increase in the risk of large, adverse future shocks to their business prospects? Specifically, do heightened future liability risks lead firms to pursue growth and diversification, and to what extent are such responses driven by shareholder interests versus managerial agency motives?
new_fields.data_description: The authors assemble a firm-year panel of 2,209 U.S. firms spanning more than 100 SIC industries from 1980 to 2006. Firm financial and accounting variables (size, market-to-book, leverage, cash flows, payouts, Altman z-score, capital expenditures) come from standard corporate databases, supplemented with acquisition-level data including target characteristics, takeover premia, and acquirer announcement abnormal returns. Governance and ownership measures (external governance indices, managerial equity stakes, institutional ownership) and CEO turnover data are also used. A custom extract from the Center for Disease Control's National Occupational Exposure Survey provides industry-level worker exposure to 121 chemicals newly identified as carcinogens during the sample. The unit of observation is the firm-year, with industry-by-year variation in newly identified carcinogen exposure providing the key shock.
new_fields.institutional_context: Under the U.S. workers' compensation system, employers are strictly liable for job-related illnesses, but sick workers and their families can also sue employers directly for negligence, dual capacity, or willful misconduct, potentially yielding large damage awards, legal fees, and insurance costs. When a chemical already present in a firm's workplace is newly identified as a carcinogen by regulatory or scientific bodies, firms whose workers have historically been exposed face a sudden, plausibly exogenous increase in expected future legal liability — with asbestos (which bankrupted 85+ firms and cost defendants an estimated $200–265 billion) as the salient worst-case scenario. Because the identification of new carcinogens is driven by scientific discovery and is plausibly unrelated to the exposed firms' current cash flows or investment opportunities, it generates cross-industry, time-varying variation in liability risk exposure that can be compared against otherwise similar unexposed firms.

title: Tax Incentives and the Decision to Purchase Health Insurance: Evidence from the Self-Employed

new_fields.research_question: How sensitive is the decision to purchase health insurance to its after-tax price? Specifically, does reducing the after-tax cost of health insurance through tax deductibility increase the probability that self-employed individuals obtain coverage, and what is the implied price elasticity of the discrete insurance purchase decision?
new_fields.data_description: The analysis uses the Current Population Survey (CPS) March supplements, a nationally representative U.S. household survey of over 50,000 households that collects prior-year health insurance status. The sample spans roughly 1985-1989, covering the years surrounding the 1986 federal tax reform. The unit of observation is the individual worker, distinguishing self-employed from wage-and-salary employed persons, and further stratified by family structure (single vs. married) and income. Key variables include health insurance coverage status (a discrete purchase indicator), self-employment status, earned income, marital status, and demographic controls. The authors combine CPS data with the NBER TAXSIM calculator to construct individual-specific marginal tax rates and after-tax prices of health insurance, incorporating payroll taxes, itemization status, and medical-expense deductibility rules. Because the CPS lacks insurance expenditure data, the analysis focuses on the discrete coverage decision.
new_fields.institutional_context: The Tax Reform Act of 1986 (TRA86) introduced a new federal tax subsidy for health insurance purchases by self-employed individuals. Prior to TRA86, self-employed workers who did not itemize paid for health insurance entirely with after-tax dollars, while employer-provided insurance for wage-and-salary workers was already excluded from taxable income. Beginning in 1986, self-employed persons could deduct 25 percent of their health insurance premiums from taxable income, substantially lowering their after-tax price of coverage. Crucially, the tax incentives for health insurance among employed workers changed very little around TRA86, so wage-and-salary workers serve as a natural comparison group absorbing economywide trends (service-sector shift, rising health costs, widening income distribution). Variation in the magnitude of the tax-price reduction also differs across self-employed workers by marginal tax bracket and marital status, providing additional cross-sectional variation within the self-employed population around the reform.

title: Education and Health: Evaluating Theories and Evidence

new_fields.research_question: Does additional schooling causally improve health outcomes and health behaviors, and if so, through which mechanisms (income, occupation, cognitive/decision-making skills) does education translate into better health? The paper also asks how large the monetary value of health returns to education is relative to earnings returns, and whether education policies should be considered health policies.
new_fields.data_description: The primary data come from multiple years of the U.S. National Health Interview Survey (NHIS), a large nationally representative survey containing self-reported health status, diagnosed acute and chronic conditions (heart disease, stroke, hypertension, cancer, diabetes, asthma, etc.), mental health measures, functional limitations, and a wide range of health behaviors (smoking, drinking, obesity, exercise, illegal drug use, seat belt use, smoke detectors, preventive care such as flu shots, mammograms, pap smears, colonoscopies). Five-year mortality is obtained by linking NHIS respondents to death certificates via the National Death Index. The unit of observation is the individual aged 25 and above (post-schooling). Controls include single-year age dummies, race, and gender. International comparisons use Barro-Lee cross-country education data paired with life expectancy.
new_fields.institutional_context: This paper is a review and synthesis rather than a single quasi-experimental study. It surveys the literature on the education-health gradient across many countries (US, Canada, Israel, Western and Eastern Europe including Russia, Bangladesh, Korea, China) and time periods, drawing on initiatives such as Healthy People 2010 in the US and UK health-inequality reduction targets that systematically monitor education-based health disparities. The authors document basic correlations using NHIS regressions and then evaluate competing theoretical mechanisms linking schooling to health—including income effects, occupational choice, access to care, knowledge, and differences in cognitive and decision-making patterns—by reviewing studies that exploit compulsory schooling laws, school-construction programs, and other sources of exogenous variation in educational attainment to assess causality.

title: Medicaid and Mortality: New Evidence from Linked Survey and Administrative Data

new_fields.research_question: Does expanding public health insurance eligibility to low-income near-elderly adults reduce their mortality? The paper seeks to quantify the causal effect of gaining Medicaid coverage on all-cause and cause-specific mortality among adults likely to become newly eligible, overcoming limitations of prior work that could not link individual eligibility characteristics to objective health outcomes.
new_fields.data_description: The authors construct a novel linked dataset combining the 2008–2013 American Community Survey (ACS), a large-scale federal survey with roughly 4 million respondents per year, with administrative Medicaid enrollment records and the Census Numident file containing date-of-death information through 2017 for individuals with Social Security Numbers. Supplemental cause-of-death analysis uses the Mortality Disparities in American Communities (MDAC) project, which links the 2008 ACS to National Death Index death certificates. The unit of observation is the individual-year. Key variables include family income relative to the Federal Poverty Level, citizenship, receipt of social assistance, state of residence, Medicaid enrollment, and annual mortality. The primary sample focuses on adults aged 55–64 in 2014 with characteristics indicating likely eligibility (income below 138% FPL), with additional analyses for other age and income groups.
new_fields.institutional_context: The Affordable Care Act (ACA) expanded Medicaid eligibility in 2014 to all adults in families with incomes below 138% of the Federal Poverty Level, whereas previously coverage was generally limited to pregnant women, disabled adults, and very low-income parents. A 2012 Supreme Court decision made the expansion optional for states: 29 states and DC expanded in 2014, 7 expanded over subsequent years, and others did not expand. This generated geographic variation in whether otherwise-similar low-income adults became newly eligible for Medicaid depending solely on their state of residence. Approximately 13.6 million adults gained Medicaid coverage under the ACA. The authors exploit the state-level adoption decisions, combined with pre/post timing around 2014, to compare mortality trajectories of likely-eligible individuals in expansion versus non-expansion states.

title: The Effect of Health Insurance Coverage on the Use of Medical Services

new_fields.research_question: What is the causal effect of health insurance coverage on the utilization of medical services—specifically emergency department visits and inpatient hospital admissions—among young adults? The paper aims to isolate the effect of being uninsured (versus privately insured) on healthcare consumption, distinguishing it from unobserved differences between insured and uninsured populations.
new_fields.data_description: The analysis combines three data sources. First, the National Health Interview Survey (NHIS) from 1997 to 2007, restricted to respondents aged 18 to 20 (approximately 24,260 observations), provides information on insurance coverage type (private, Medicaid, uninsured, other), demographics, schooling, smoking, and self-reported utilization. Second, a census of emergency department records from Arizona, California, Iowa, New Jersey, and Wisconsin. Third, hospital inpatient discharge records from Arizona, California, Iowa, New York, Texas, and Wisconsin. Key variables include insurance status, an indicator for age above 19, counts and characteristics of ED visits and inpatient admissions (including severity, diagnosis, and hospital ownership type—public, private nonprofit, for-profit). The unit of observation is the individual in the NHIS and the hospital/ED visit in the administrative records.
new_fields.institutional_context: Identification exploits a sharp rule in private health insurance contracts: many plans cover dependents only through age 18, or through the end of the month in which the dependent turns 19, unless the dependent is enrolled as a full-time student. As a consequence, a substantial share of young adults abruptly lose private insurance coverage upon their nineteenth birthday, producing a 5 to 8 percentage point jump in the probability of being uninsured precisely at age 19. Because this change is driven by contractual eligibility rules rather than by individual choice or by concurrent changes in employment, school attendance, or health behaviors (which the authors show do not change discontinuously at 19), it provides quasi-experimental variation in insurance status that is plausibly unrelated to other determinants of healthcare utilization.

title: Medicare Spending, The Physician Workforce, and Beneficiaries’ Quality of Care

new_fields.research_question: Does higher Medicare spending per beneficiary translate into higher-quality care for the elderly, and does the composition of the local physician workforce (generalists versus specialists) shape both the level of spending and the quality of care delivered? The paper seeks to understand whether intensive, costly care crowds out the provision of inexpensive, evidence-based effective care.
new_fields.data_description: The unit of observation is the U.S. state. Quality of care is measured using twenty-four process-of-care indicators developed by the Medicare Quality Improvement Organization (QIO) for 2000–2001, covering six conditions (AMI, breast cancer, diabetes, heart failure, pneumonia, stroke), plus a subset of four indicators available for both 1995 and 1999 from the Dartmouth Atlas. Medicare fee-for-service reimbursement per beneficiary is calculated from Medicare claims via the Dartmouth Atlas, adjusted for inflation (CPI), state cost-of-living, and age/sex/race. End-of-life utilization (hospital days and ICU admission in the last six months of life) also comes from claims. Patient satisfaction is drawn from the 1992–1995 Medicare Current Beneficiary Survey. Physician and RN workforce counts per capita come from the 2003 Area Resource File combined with 2000 Census population.
new_fields.institutional_context: Medicare beneficiaries receive strikingly different care across U.S. states, even though Medicare is a national program. For example, administration of beta-blockers within 24 hours of a heart attack varied from 50% in Alabama to 86% in New Hampshire in 2000. The QIO measures capture interventions with strong scientific consensus and few contraindications (e.g., mammography, HbA1c monitoring, warfarin for atrial fibrillation), so cross-state variation is unlikely to reflect patient risk. End-of-life spending has been shown to be weakly linked to underlying sickness, outcomes, or satisfaction, allowing it to serve as a marker of practice style. The geographic distribution of generalists versus specialists, together with the Balanced Budget Act of 1997 and state-level HMO penetration, provides variation in the mix of providers and resources that plausibly drives both spending intensity and the use of effective care.

title: The Causal Effect of Education on Earnings

new_fields.research_question: What is the causal effect of an additional year of schooling on individual earnings, and how does it differ from the observed correlation between education and wages? The paper further asks whether estimated returns vary across individuals (heterogeneous returns) and whether the average return differs for disadvantaged subgroups induced to acquire more schooling by institutional features of the education system.
new_fields.data_description: The chapter is a survey that draws on a broad set of US and international microeconomic datasets used in the education-earnings literature, including the 1940-1980 Decennial Censuses, Current Population Surveys (notably March CPS 1994-1996 and the February 1990 CPS supplement on educational attainment), and specialized surveys of twins and siblings. Key variables are log hourly or annual earnings, years of completed schooling (or degree-based attainment after 1990), age, potential labor market experience (age - schooling - 6), race, and family background measures. The unit of observation is the individual worker, typically aged 16-66 with positive earnings. Illustrative regressions in the chapter use pooled CPS samples of roughly 100,000 men and 95,000 women to estimate Mincerian human capital earnings functions.
new_fields.institutional_context: Identification of the causal return to schooling in the studies reviewed exploits institutional features of education systems that shift schooling attainment for reasons plausibly unrelated to individual earning ability. Examples include compulsory schooling laws and minimum school-leaving ages, variation in the age at which children start school combined with quarter-of-birth patterns, geographic proximity to colleges, regional differences in tuition and school quality, and policy-induced changes in school construction or access. A second strand uses within-family comparisons among siblings and identical twins to net out shared family background and genetic endowments. A third uses family background variables (parental education, family structure) as controls or excluded instruments. These sources of variation are argued to generate schooling differences that are not driven by unobserved ability, enabling recovery of the causal schooling-earnings relationship.
