title: The Impact of Air Pollution on Infant Mortality: Evidence from Geographic Variation in Pollution Shocks Induced by a Recession

new_fields.research_question: What is the causal effect of ambient particulate matter (total suspended particulates) air pollution on infant mortality rates, and through what biological pathway (e.g., fetal exposure affecting birth weight and neonatal survival) does this effect operate? The study also asks whether the pollution–infant mortality relationship is nonlinear and whether effects differ by race and sex.
new_fields.data_description: The authors assemble county-level data for U.S. counties covering 1980–1982 (with attention to the 1980–82 window). Air pollution data come from EPA monitor readings of total suspended particulates (TSPs), aggregated to annual county-level concentrations (mg/m3). Infant health outcomes come from comprehensive U.S. Vital Statistics natality and mortality records, providing counts of live births and infant deaths per 100,000 live births, disaggregated by timing of death (within one day, within one month, post-neonatal), cause of death (including accidents/homicides as placebo), race (black vs. overall), and sex, as well as birth weight. The data are merged with county-level covariates on parental characteristics, maternal health and medical history, prenatal care utilization, Medicaid and transfer payments, income, and demographics.
new_fields.institutional_context: Identification exploits the 1981–82 U.S. recession, which generated sharp, geographically uneven reductions in industrial activity. Heavily industrialized counties (e.g., Pittsburgh, PA) experienced large manufacturing plant shutdowns that produced dramatic declines in TSPs concentrations, while neighboring counties experienced moderate air-quality improvements, and counties without pollution-intensive manufacturing saw little change. This recession-induced geographic variation in pollution shocks over a narrow 1980–82 window is argued to be orthogonal to changes in other determinants of infant mortality (parental characteristics, prenatal care, Medicaid, etc.), providing quasi-random variation in air quality that is not confounded by the slow-moving socioeconomic factors that plague cross-sectional comparisons. Comparing infant mortality changes in counties with large pollution reductions to those with small reductions thus isolates the pollution effect.

title: Medicare Spending, the Physician Workforce, and Beneficiaries' Quality of Care

new_fields.research_question: Does higher Medicare spending per beneficiary translate into higher-quality care for beneficiaries, or does costly intensive care crowd out effective, evidence-based care? How does the composition of the physician workforce — generalists versus specialists — shape both Medicare spending levels and the quality of care delivered to beneficiaries?
new_fields.data_description: The unit of observation is the U.S. state. Quality is measured using 24 process-of-care indicators from the Medicare Quality Improvement Organization (QIO), computed at the state level by Jencks and colleagues for 2000–01 (e.g., beta-blockers at AMI discharge, mammography, HbA1c monitoring, eye exams for diabetics). A subset of four measures is also available for 1995 and 1999 from Dartmouth Atlas Medicare claims data. State-level Medicare fee-for-service reimbursement per beneficiary is computed from Medicare claims and adjusted for CPI inflation, state cost-of-living, and age/sex/race composition. Additional variables include days in hospital and ICU admission in the last six months of life, patient satisfaction from the 1992–1995 Medicare Current Beneficiary Survey, Medicare HMO penetration, AMI discharges/mortality, and per-capita counts of specialists, general practitioners, and registered nurses from the 2003 Area Resource File.
new_fields.institutional_context: Medicare reimbursement levels and the use of effective clinical procedures vary widely across U.S. states for reasons largely unrelated to patient need — for example, beta-blocker use within 24 hours of AMI admission ranged from 50% in Alabama to 86% in New Hampshire in 2000. These geographic differences reflect local practice styles, health care infrastructure, and the underlying mix of providers (generalists versus specialists, nurses, hospital beds) rather than patient sickness, as prior Dartmouth Atlas research documents for end-of-life care. This cross-state variation in spending intensity and workforce composition — combined with quality indicators chosen because they are inexpensive, evidence-based, and rarely contraindicated (so risk adjustment matters little) — provides the setting for examining whether marginal Medicare dollars buy better care. The Balanced Budget Act of 1997's curtailment of home health spending provides an additional source of within-state change between 1995 and 1999.

title: The Central Role of Noise in Evaluating Interventions That Use Test Scores to Rank Schools

new_fields.research_question: Does Chile's P-900 program—a package of infrastructure improvements, instructional materials, teacher training, and after-school tutoring targeted at low-performing publicly-funded schools—causally raise fourth-grade student test scores? How much of the program's apparent positive impact reflects a true treatment effect versus spurious mean reversion arising from transitory noise in school-level average test scores used to assign treatment?
new_fields.data_description: The authors use school-level data from Chile's SIMCE (Sistema de Medición de la Calidad de la Educación) standardized achievement tests administered to the population of fourth-graders, covering public and publicly-subsidized private schools across Chile's 13 administrative regions. Key variables include each school's mean fourth-grade scores in language, mathematics, and a combined measure, as well as fourth-grade enrollments and P-900 program participation status. The primary outcomes are school-level gain scores over 1988–1990 and 1988–1992. The 1988 combined mean score is the pre-program assignment variable; 1990 was the first full treatment year, and 1992 captures up to three years of exposure. Data were provided by Chile's Ministry of Education. The unit of observation is the school. Very small or inaccessible schools (accounting for under 10% of enrollments) were excluded from testing and program eligibility.
new_fields.institutional_context: In 1990, Chile launched the 900 Schools Program (P-900) to assist its lowest-achieving publicly-funded primary schools. Program assignment had two stages. First, the Ministry of Education computed each school's 1988 fourth-grade mean test scores, ranked schools within each of the 13 administrative regions, and established a region-specific cutoff; schools whose mean fell below their region's cutoff were selected. Second, regional teams reviewed lists and removed some schools (very small/inaccessible ones, or those with managerial problems). Selected schools received infrastructure repairs, textbooks and classroom materials, weekly teacher training workshops (from 1992), and after-school tutoring for struggling third- and fourth-graders. Assignment was fixed through 1992. The sharp, region-specific cutoff rule based on a pre-program mean score—combined with known imprecision (noise and sampling variation) in those scores, especially at small schools—creates the identifying variation the authors exploit.

title: The Impact of the Mariel Boatlift on the Miami Labor Market

new_fields.research_question: Does a sudden, large increase in the supply of low-skilled immigrant labor to a local labor market reduce the wages and raise the unemployment rates of less-skilled native workers, including blacks and earlier immigrants from the same ethnic group? The paper examines how quickly and how fully a city's labor market can absorb an unexpected, exogenous supply shock of unskilled workers.
new_fields.data_description: The analysis uses individual-level micro-data from the merged outgoing rotation group samples of the Current Population Survey (CPS) for 1979-1985, covering roughly 1,200 Miami-area respondents per month. Key variables include hourly wages, unemployment status, labor force participation, occupation, education, age, gender, and ethnicity (with Cubans separately identified in the CPS questionnaire). The unit of observation is the working-age individual (16-61). Supplementary data come from the 1980 Decennial Census, the March 1985 CPS Mobility Supplement (which identifies post-1980 Cuban entrants), and Census Bureau county population estimates. Comparison cities are Atlanta, Los Angeles, Houston, and Tampa-St. Petersburg. Outcomes are computed separately for white non-Hispanics, black non-Hispanics, Cubans, and other Hispanics.
new_fields.institutional_context: On April 20, 1980, Fidel Castro unexpectedly announced that Cubans wishing to emigrate could leave from the port of Mariel. Between May and September 1980, approximately 125,000 Cuban refugees arrived in the United States via a flotilla of privately chartered boats, with about half settling permanently in Miami. This influx raised Miami's labor force by roughly 7% and increased the stock of Cuban workers there by about 20%, with a disproportionate concentration in less-skilled occupations given the relatively low education levels of the Mariel arrivals. Because the Boatlift resulted from an unforeseen political decision in Cuba rather than from Miami labor demand conditions, it provides a plausibly exogenous supply shock concentrated in a single metropolitan area, allowing comparisons of Miami's labor market outcomes before and after 1980 against other metropolitan areas unaffected by the shock.

title: Empirical Strategies in Labor Economics

new_fields.research_question: This chapter is a methodological survey rather than a single empirical study, but it organizes its discussion around recurring causal questions in labor economics: what are the effects of schooling, union membership, immigration, military service, and class size on labor market outcomes such as earnings? The overarching question is how to credibly estimate such counterfactual causal effects when omitted variables and selection bias threaten simple comparisons.
new_fields.data_description: As a Handbook chapter, the piece draws on a wide range of US micro datasets used in labor economics rather than a single sample. It reviews and tabulates usage of public-use files including the PSID, NLS, CPS, SEO, and decennial Census, as well as primary researcher-collected surveys, customized public-use extracts, administrative records, and administrative-survey linkages. A bibliometric table compiled by the authors classifies articles in eight leading economics journals from 1965-1969 through 1994-1997 by data type (theory, micro cross-section, panel, experiment, time series, aggregate cross-section). The chapter also discusses measurement error evidence for key labor variables (earnings, hours, schooling, union status), survey sampling weights, and allocation flags for imputed values.
new_fields.institutional_context: The chapter's methodological backdrop is the shift in labor economics toward an 'experimentalist' perspective in which credible causal inference is grounded in settings that approximate random assignment. Identification is argued to come from policy changes, administrative rules, natural events, or institutional features that generate variation in treatments (schooling, union coverage, immigrant inflows, conscription, class size) plausibly unrelated to unobserved determinants of outcomes. Illustrative settings include compulsory-schooling laws and quarter-of-birth variation affecting education; the Mariel boatlift and other immigration shocks; Vietnam-era draft lotteries affecting military service; and administrative class-size rules such as maximum-class-size thresholds. These institutional levers, together with randomized social experiments (e.g., training evaluations), provide the exogenous variation that the surveyed empirical strategies exploit to recover causal parameters of interest to labor economists.

title: Minimum Wage Effects Across State Borders: Estimates Using Contiguous Counties

new_fields.research_question: How do minimum wage increases affect earnings and employment in low-wage sectors, particularly restaurants, in the United States? Do negative employment effects found in prior national-level studies reflect true disemployment or spatial heterogeneity in employment trends that is unrelated to minimum wage policy? Are adjacent local areas valid counterfactuals for evaluating these effects?
new_fields.data_description: The primary data source is the Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages (QCEW), which provides near-census quarterly county-level payroll and employment data by detailed industry, derived from ES-202 unemployment insurance filings covering roughly 98% of workers. The sample spans 1990 through 2006 (sixteen and a half years) at the county-quarter level. Key outcome variables are average earnings and employment in the restaurant industry, and additionally in the broader accommodation and food services sector and the retail sector; manufacturing is used as a placebo industry with few minimum wage workers. The main analytical unit is pairs of contiguous counties that straddle state borders. Supplementary use is made of the Current Population Survey to characterize the minimum-wage workforce. State and federal minimum wage levels over time provide the policy variation.
new_fields.institutional_context: Identification leverages policy discontinuities at U.S. state borders: state minimum wages frequently differ from those of adjacent states and from the federal floor, and these differentials change over time as individual states raise their minimums above the federal level or as federal increases (e.g., 1996–1997) compress differentials. Because labor markets, costs of living, and economic conditions tend to be similar across a state line within a local area, counties on opposite sides of a border that face different statutory minimum wages offer a natural local comparison. Between 1990 and 2006, numerous such cross-border minimum wage differentials arose and shifted, generating many local natural experiments. By 2005, seventeen states plus D.C. had minimums above the federal level, while no Southern state did, producing substantial geographic variation in the binding wage floor that can be exploited using adjacent county pairs.

title: The Effect of the Minimum Wage on the Fast-Food Industry

new_fields.research_question: How do federal minimum wage increases affect wages, employment, prices, and wage dispersion in a low-wage industry? Specifically, the paper asks whether raising the mandated wage floor reduces employment at firms more bound by the increase, whether it leads to price pass-through, and whether employers take up a newly authorized youth training wage.
new_fields.data_description: The authors conducted an original longitudinal telephone survey of fast-food restaurants in Texas, covering Burger King, Wendy's, and Kentucky Fried Chicken outlets drawn systematically from metropolitan Yellow Pages listings (January 1990). The first wave, administered December 12-18, 1990, obtained 167 responses (57% response rate); the second wave, conducted July 8-August 2, 1991, obtained 330 responses (56% overall, 66% for re-contacted firms), with 110 firms observed in both waves. A reliability re-interview of 30 firms occurred in August 1991. Variables include starting wage, full- and part-time wages, employment, prices of standardized items (french fries, soda), workforce demographics (share black, Hispanic), and subminimum wage utilization. County/city-level labor market controls (unemployment rate, city size) were merged from the 1988 County and City Data Book. Unit of observation: the restaurant.
new_fields.institutional_context: Identification exploits two federal statutory increases in the U.S. minimum wage under amendments to the Fair Labor Standards Act: from $3.35 to $3.80 on April 1, 1990, and from $3.80 to $4.25 on April 1, 1991. The amendments also introduced a youth subminimum ("training") wage equal to 85% of the minimum ($3.62 after April 1991) available for teenage workers for up to six months, with minimal training requirements after the first 90 days. Texas was selected because it is a large low-wage state with no binding state minimum wage overriding the federal floor and no state subminimum, making the federal changes fully binding. The fast-food industry was chosen because wages cluster at the minimum (one-third of sampled restaurants paid exactly $3.35 before April 1990, and 76% paid exactly $4.25 after April 1991), and the industry is competitive with high turnover and many teenage hires, generating strong cross-firm variation in exposure to the mandated increase.

title: The Labor Demand Curve is Downward Sloping: Reexamining the Impact of Immigration on the Labor Market

new_fields.research_question: How does an influx of immigrant workers affect the wages and employment opportunities of competing native workers with similar skills? Specifically, to what extent do increases in labor supply within narrowly defined skill groups—defined by both education and work experience—reduce the wages of native workers in those same groups?
new_fields.data_description: The analysis uses U.S. Public Use Microdata Samples (PUMS) from the 1960, 1970, 1980, and 1990 Decennial Censuses, combined with pooled 1999, 2000, and 2001 Annual Demographic Supplements of the Current Population Survey (treated as a '2000' cross section). The sample is restricted to men aged 18–64 in the civilian labor force. Immigrants are defined as foreign-born noncitizens or naturalized citizens; all others are natives. Workers are sorted into four education categories (high school dropouts, high school graduates, some college, college graduates) and into five-year work-experience intervals (1–40 years), where experience is approximated as age minus assumed school-leaving age. The unit of observation is the education-by-experience-by-year skill cell. Key variables include the foreign-born share of the labor force in each cell and native wages/employment outcomes.
new_fields.institutional_context: Large-scale immigration to the United States resurged following the 1965 Amendments to the Immigration and Nationality Act, producing sizable but highly uneven inflows across decades. Crucially, immigrant arrivals are not balanced across skill groups: even within a given education category (e.g., high school dropouts), the influx disproportionately augments some work-experience cells and not others, and the pattern of this imbalance shifts across Census years from 1960 to 2000. Because similarly educated workers with different experience levels are imperfect substitutes in production, and because the national size of native workforces within narrow education-experience cells is relatively fixed and less susceptible to internal migration responses than local labor markets, the cross-cell, over-time variation in immigrant supply shocks provides a credible source of identifying variation absent in earlier city-level comparisons.

title: Identification and Estimation of Local Average Treatment Effects

new_fields.research_question: Under what conditions can one nonparametrically identify an average causal effect of a binary treatment on an outcome when treatment is not randomly assigned but an exogenous variable shifts selection into treatment? Specifically, when there is no subpopulation with zero probability of treatment, which average treatment effect parameter is identified, and for which subgroup does it apply?
new_fields.data_description: This is a theoretical/methodological paper rather than an empirical study with a single dataset. The framework assumes a random sample of individuals for whom the researcher observes a triple (Y_i, D_i, Z_i): an outcome Y_i, a binary treatment/participation indicator D_i, and an exogenous variable Z_i with discrete (or general) support. Potential outcomes Y_i(0), Y_i(1) and potential treatment status D_i(z) for each value z in the support of Z are defined as counterfactuals. Illustrative applications discussed include Angrist's (1990) use of the Vietnam-era draft lottery to study veteran-status effects on earnings, and Angrist and Krueger's (1991) quarter-of-birth analysis of schooling and earnings. No new data are collected; the paper derives identification and asymptotic distribution results applicable to such observational settings.
new_fields.institutional_context: The identification strategy leverages settings often called 'natural experiments,' in which an exogenous variable — independent of potential outcomes but correlated with treatment take-up — induces variation in participation. Canonical examples include the Vietnam-era draft lottery, where randomly assigned lottery numbers based on date of birth determined conscription priority and thereby shifted the probability of military service, and quarter-of-birth variation combined with compulsory schooling laws, which induced differences in years of education. The key institutional ingredients are (i) an exogeneity/exclusion restriction so the shifter affects outcomes only through treatment, and (ii) a monotonicity property: the shifter moves everyone's treatment status in the same direction, ruling out 'defiers.' Under these conditions, the average treatment effect is identified for the subpopulation of 'compliers' whose treatment status is responsive to the exogenous shifter.

title: Consequences of Employment Protection? The Case of the Americans with Disabilities Act

new_fields.research_question: Does mandating that employers provide accommodations for disabled workers and prohibiting wage or hiring discrimination against them affect the employment outcomes of disabled individuals? Specifically, do such protections raise or lower employment levels of the intended beneficiaries, and do effects differ by age group, firm size, or region?
new_fields.data_description: The analysis uses micro-data from the Current Population Survey (CPS), principally the March Annual Demographic Files, covering years surrounding the early 1990s (roughly 1988-1997). Key variables include weeks worked, employment status, hours, earnings/wages, age, sex, education, state of residence, and self-reported disability status (work-limiting health conditions). The unit of observation is the working-age individual. Samples are stratified by disability status, sex, and age groups (e.g., 21-39 vs 40-58). Supplementary data come from firm-size information in the CPS and potentially EEOC discrimination charge statistics. Outcomes are compared between disabled and non-disabled workers before and after federal protections took effect, with variation exploited across firm-size thresholds and across states with pre-existing protections.
new_fields.institutional_context: The Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA), passed in 1990 and taking effect in July 1992, prohibits employment discrimination against qualified individuals with disabilities and requires employers to provide 'reasonable accommodations' unless doing so imposes undue hardship. The law generated a sharp change in the legal environment facing employers of disabled workers, raising the effective cost of hiring, firing, or failing to accommodate them. Importantly, the ADA applied only to firms with 25 or more employees initially (later lowered to 15 in 1994), creating variation across firm sizes. It also preempted a patchwork of state-level disability laws, so states with weaker pre-ADA protections experienced a larger change than those that already mandated accommodations. These sources of variation—timing of the federal mandate, firm-size thresholds, and cross-state differences in prior legal regimes—generate comparisons between affected and less-affected workers and employers.

title: Identification and Estimation of Treatment Effects with a Regression Discontinuity Design

new_fields.research_question: What are the causal impacts of a conditional cash transfer program targeted at poor rural households on education, health, nutrition, and consumption outcomes? Specifically, does providing cash and nutritional supplements to mothers, conditional on children's school attendance and health clinic visits, improve schooling enrollment, reduce child illness, reduce stunting, and increase dietary diversity among beneficiary households relative to comparable non-beneficiary households?
new_fields.data_description: The evaluation uses panel (repeated observations) household survey data collected by IFPRI covering approximately 24,000 households in 506 localities across 7 Mexican states. Households were interviewed periodically between November 1997 and November 1999, spanning the pre- and post-implementation period of PROGRESA. The unit of observation is the rural household (with child- and individual-level outcomes nested within). Key outcome variables include school enrollment (by gender and grade level), child labor, incidence of illness, adult sick/disability days, child stunting (ages 12–36 months), caloric consumption, and dietary composition (fruits, vegetables, meat). Complementary qualitative data were gathered via focus groups and workshops with beneficiaries, local leaders, program officials, health clinic workers, and teachers. A cost analysis of administrative expenditures relative to program transfers was also conducted.
new_fields.institutional_context: PROGRESA was a large-scale Mexican anti-poverty program launched in the late 1990s that provided cash transfers and nutritional supplements to mothers in extremely poor rural households, conditional on children's regular school attendance and visits to health centers. The program used a two-stage targeting process: localities were first selected based on a census-based marginality index, and within eligible localities households were selected using socioeconomic criteria. Crucially, the program was phased in gradually across localities, and in the early stages of rollout, researchers exploited this staggered implementation by randomly assigning the timing of program entry across eligible localities. This created a set of early-treated beneficiary localities and not-yet-treated comparison localities that were eligible but whose benefits had not yet begun, providing the basis for comparing outcomes between treatment and control households before and after implementation.

title: Does Electoral Accountability Affect Economic Policy Choices? Evidence from Gubernatorial Term Limits

new_fields.research_question: Do incentives created by re-election eligibility shape the economic policy choices of incumbent politicians? Specifically, does a governor's ability to stand for re-election causally affect state-level fiscal and tax policy outcomes, and are any such effects mediated through political competition and reputation-building?
new_fields.data_description: The paper uses a panel of U.S. states covering gubernatorial terms, with state-year as the unit of observation. Key variables include state taxes (total taxes per capita, sales taxes, income taxes), state spending per capita, workers' compensation measures, and minimum wages, along with political variables such as the governor's party, whether the incumbent is eligible to run again, and state political and demographic controls (income, population, federal grants). The sample spans multiple decades of post-war U.S. state fiscal data, allowing the authors to compare policy choices made by the same governors when they are eligible versus ineligible for re-election across states with differing term-limit rules.
new_fields.institutional_context: U.S. state constitutions impose heterogeneous restrictions on how many consecutive terms a governor may serve. In some states governors face no binding limit and can seek re-election indefinitely; in others, governors are constitutionally barred from running again after one or two terms. This creates variation within a governor's tenure: a two-term-limited governor faces voters in her first term but is a 'lame duck' in her second, while governors in unrestricted states always face electoral accountability. Because these constitutional rules were set long before the sample period and differ across states for historical reasons, they generate plausibly exogenous variation in whether an incumbent's future career depends on voter approval, allowing the authors to isolate the effect of electoral accountability on policy choices.

title: E-ZTax: Tax Salience and Tax Rates

new_fields.research_question: Does reducing the visibility of a tax to payers lead governments to set higher tax rates over time? Specifically, when the act of paying a tax becomes less noticeable to consumers, how do equilibrium tax rates, consumer price responsiveness, and the political cycle of tax-setting change?
new_fields.data_description: The author assembles a novel panel data set covering 123 toll facilities across the United States, documenting the full history of toll rates and the date of electronic toll collection (ETC) installation at each facility over several decades. Where available, the data also include annual facility-level measures of toll traffic volume, toll revenue, and the share of traffic and revenue paid via ETC. The unit of observation is the toll facility-year. The paper additionally uses original survey evidence on drivers' awareness of the toll amounts they pay, comparing cash payers to ETC users (including regular commuters), to validate the salience interpretation. Local electoral calendar data are used to study political-cycle effects on toll changes.
new_fields.institutional_context: Toll authorities in the U.S. adopted electronic toll collection systems (e.g., E-ZPass in the Northeast, I-Pass in Illinois, FasTrak in California) at staggered points in time over several decades, with some facilities still not having adopted by the end of the sample. ETC allows tolls to be automatically deducted as vehicles pass through plazas, so drivers no longer actively count out cash—plausibly reducing the salience of the toll amount, as confirmed by survey evidence showing markedly lower toll awareness among electronic payers. This staggered, within-facility rollout of ETC provides variation in tax salience that is plausibly unrelated to underlying demand for toll revenue, enabling the author to compare toll rate trajectories before and after ETC adoption across facilities adopting at different times.

title: Measuring the Output Responses to Fiscal Policy

new_fields.research_question: How do the output effects of government spending shocks differ between recessions and expansions in the US economy? Specifically, are fiscal multipliers larger when the economy has slack, and do multipliers vary across disaggregated spending components (e.g., military versus nonmilitary)? How does accounting for predictable components of fiscal shocks (anticipation by professional forecasters) alter the estimated size of these multipliers?
new_fields.data_description: The authors use quarterly US macroeconomic data, primarily covering the post-WWII period (since 1946) through the late 2000s. Core variables include log real government purchases (federal, state, and local consumption and investment), log real government receipts net of transfers, and log real GDP in chained 2000 dollars, deflated by the GDP deflator. The paper also disaggregates government spending into components including military and nonmilitary spending. To measure anticipated fiscal shocks, the authors collected and digitized quarterly forecasts from the University of Michigan's RSQE macroeconometric model, the Survey of Professional Forecasters (SPF), and the Federal Reserve Board's Greenbook forecasts prepared for FOMC meetings. Recession/expansion regimes are defined using a seven-quarter moving average of real GDP growth, calibrated so the economy is in recession about 20 percent of the time, consistent with NBER dating.
new_fields.institutional_context: Identification builds on Blanchard and Perotti (2002), exploiting institutional lags in the US federal budgeting process: discretionary government spending decisions cannot respond to output innovations within a single quarter because appropriations, procurement, and implementation take time. This delay allows unanticipated shocks to government purchases to be isolated from contemporaneous output and tax shocks via a recursive ordering (G, T, Y). The nondiscretionary response of taxes to output is pinned down using external estimates of fiscal output elasticities. To address concerns that VAR innovations may still reflect anticipated policy, the authors incorporate professional forecasts (RSQE, SPF, Greenbook) to purge fiscal surprises of predictable components. Critically, the paper exploits variation in the state of the US business cycle—periods of slack versus expansion—to allow both contemporaneous covariances and dynamic propagation of shocks to switch smoothly between recessionary and expansionary regimes.

title: Tax Structures in Developing Countries: Many Puzzles and a Possible Explanation

new_fields.research_question: Why do developing countries collect substantially less tax revenue relative to GDP than rich countries, and why do they rely on corporate income taxes, tariffs, and seignorage rather than personal income and consumption taxes? Can a unified explanation based on firms' ability to evade taxation by exiting the formal financial sector account for these systematic differences in tax structure, as well as related policies like tariff protection, inflation, and state ownership of banks?
new_fields.data_description: The paper assembles cross-country data comparing tax structures between poor and rich countries. Key variables include total tax revenue as a share of GDP, the composition of revenue across personal income tax, corporate income tax, consumption/value-added taxes, tariffs, and seignorage, as well as statutory maximum tax rates (VAT, personal income, corporate) and inflation rates. Estimates of the size of the informal (underground) economy as a share of GDP are drawn from Schneider and Enste (2000), reporting a median of 37% in developing countries (ranging from 13% in Hong Kong/Singapore to 76% in Nigeria) versus about 15% in OECD countries. The unit of observation is the country. The analysis uses 18 rich-country and 25 poor-country observations in simple cross-sectional regressions of revenue/GDP on statutory tax rates.
new_fields.institutional_context: The setting is the sharp divergence between developing and developed economies in tax administration capacity, driven by the depth of the formal financial sector. In rich countries, firms rely heavily on banks, creating paper trails (transaction records, accounting data) that enable enforcement of income, payroll, and consumption taxes. In poor countries, weak financial sectors mean firms can operate entirely in cash, disappearing into a large informal economy and escaping taxation altogether. Governments therefore face a disintermediation constraint: taxing firms too heavily pushes them out of the financial sector and erodes the tax base. This asymmetry makes capital-intensive firms—more dependent on bank finance—the natural locus of taxation, and rationalizes complementary policies (tariffs protecting capital-intensive sectors, inflation taxing the cash economy, state-owned banks securing information access, red tape hindering informal entry) as mechanisms to protect the taxable base.

title: Do Political Parties Matter? Evidence from U.S. Cities

new_fields.research_question: Do the partisan affiliations of elected mayors (Democrat vs. Republican) causally affect local policy outcomes in U.S. cities, including the size of local government, the allocation of public spending across functions, and crime rates? The paper also investigates whether any such partisan effects are moderated by city-level homogeneity and inter-jurisdictional competition consistent with Tiebout sorting.
new_fields.data_description: The authors construct a new panel dataset of 4,543 direct mayoral elections held between 1950 and 2005 in over 400 U.S. cities with populations of at least 25,000 as of 2000. For each election, the data record the party affiliation of candidates and vote margins, enabling identification of close Democrat-vs-Republican contests. These election records are linked to city-level policy outcomes including per-capita local government expenditures, per-capita tax revenues, public employment, the composition of spending across functions (e.g., police, fire, parks and recreation), and violent and property crime rates. The data also include city demographic characteristics such as racial composition, adult educational attainment, family income, and census block-group income dispersion, plus a Herfindahl-based measure of jurisdictional competition within metropolitan areas. The unit of observation is the city-election (or city-term).
new_fields.institutional_context: U.S. mayoral elections with direct two-party (Democrat vs. Republican) competition provide the identifying setting. In cities where a Democrat narrowly defeats a Republican (or vice versa), the identity of the winning party is plausibly as-good-as-random because narrow margins of victory generate quasi-experimental variation in who holds office, while underlying city characteristics (voter ideology, demographics, income) vary continuously across the victory threshold. This allows comparisons of subsequent policy outcomes in cities where Democrats barely won versus barely lost. The institutional environment of American local government is also distinctive: cities are small and relatively homogeneous compared with congressional districts, and metropolitan areas are fragmented into many competing jurisdictions, enabling Tiebout-style residential sorting and inter-city competition that may constrain partisan policy choices by mayors.

title: MPs for Sale? Returns to Office in Postwar British Politics

new_fields.research_question: Do politicians personally profit financially from holding legislative office, and if so, through what channels? Specifically, how much does winning a seat in the UK House of Commons increase a politician's lifetime wealth, and does this financial return differ across political parties with different organizational and funding structures?
new_fields.data_description: The authors assembled an original dataset on the estates (wealth at death) of British politicians who entered the House of Commons between 1950 and 1970 and have since died. The data include both successful MPs and parliamentary candidates who ran unsuccessfully. Beyond wealth at death, the dataset records rich candidate-level covariates including age, pre-politics occupation, schools and universities attended, titles of nobility, and election vote margins. The authors also collected information on post-election career outcomes, notably directorships held at publicly traded firms. The unit of observation is the individual politician (MP or losing candidate), with party affiliation (Conservative vs. Labour) a key dimension of analysis. Wealth data come from probate records of deceased politicians.
new_fields.institutional_context: In postwar Britain, parliamentary seats were allocated through first-past-the-post elections in single-member constituencies, producing many narrowly decided races where the outcome between winner and loser was effectively determined by small, arguably random vote differences. This quasi-random assignment of office in close contests allows comparison of otherwise similar candidates who barely won versus barely lost. The institutional setting is further characterized by permissive rules on MPs' outside employment: members could serve as corporate directors and paid parliamentary consultants while in office, with only limited disclosure requirements before 1996. The two major parties differed sharply in organization: Labour was funded and dominated by trade unions that secured exclusive loyalty from sponsored MPs, while Conservatives drew diffuse financial support, leaving their MPs free to sell services to competing outside firms.

title: Elections and the Regression Discontinuity Design: Lessons from Close U.S. House Races, 1942–2008

new_fields.research_question: Do bare winners and bare losers of close U.S. House elections constitute valid counterfactuals for one another, such that the incumbency (or incumbent-party) advantage can be credibly estimated by comparing narrowly won and narrowly lost races? The paper asks whether pretreatment characteristics of candidates are balanced in the immediate neighborhood of the 50% vote-share threshold, and if not, what this implies for estimates of incumbency effects in the postwar U.S. House.
new_fields.data_description: The authors construct an original dataset on U.S. House of Representatives elections and candidates covering 1942–2008, with the candidate-race as the unit of observation. Key variables include Democratic vote share and margin of victory (the forcing variable), winner/loser status, pretreatment covariates such as candidate political experience, prior officeholding, incumbency status of the previous officeholder, campaign financial resources (fundraising and spending), and Congressional Quarterly's pre-election race ratings. The data also include information on national partisan tides, open-seat indicators, and, for a hand-collected subsample of very close races, detailed information on initial vote counts, recounts, and subsequent tallies used to assess whether outcome reversals occur post-Election Day. Comparisons are drawn against the replication data from Lee (2008).
new_fields.institutional_context: The identification strategy exploits U.S. plurality-rule House elections, where a candidate is seated if and only if they obtain more votes than their opponent, generating a sharp 50% threshold in two-party vote share that deterministically assigns 'treatment' (winning the seat, or a party holding the seat). In principle, races decided by razor-thin margins should resemble a local lottery, since the exact final vote tally contains a non-trivial random component. The paper scrutinizes this premise by examining whether candidates and parties can effectively influence close outcomes through pre-Election Day activities (resource deployment, candidate quality, organizational strength, responsiveness to national partisan tides) or post-election processes (recounts, challenges). The setting — postwar U.S. House contests, 1942–2008 — provides thousands of races spanning varying partisan environments in which to test whether the threshold genuinely produces as-if-random assignment among near-tie elections.

title: The Long and Short of the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement

new_fields.research_question: What are the short-run labor market adjustment costs and long-run productivity gains from a reciprocal trade liberalization between two industrialized economies? Specifically, how do reductions in domestic import tariffs and foreign (partner-country) tariffs affect plant- and industry-level employment, earnings, and labor productivity in the liberalizing country?
new_fields.data_description: The study uses Canadian manufacturing data at the 4-digit Canadian SIC level, covering 213 industries, combined with plant-level micro data from Statistics Canada (accessed via the Micro-Economic Studies and Analysis Division). Industry outcomes include employment and earnings of production and nonproduction workers, skill upgrading, earnings inequality, hours worked, plant size, and labor productivity. Carefully constructed policy-mandated bilateral tariff series measure Canadian tariffs against the U.S. and U.S. tariffs against Canada, as well as tariffs against the rest of the world, along with effective tariff rates and nontariff barriers. Comparable industry-level data for the United States, Japan, and the United Kingdom are used to control for industry-specific shocks. The pre-policy period is 1980–1986 and the post-policy period is 1989–1996, with 1988 serving as the baseline year.
new_fields.institutional_context: The Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement (FTA), implemented on January 1, 1989, mandated annual reciprocal tariff reductions between Canada and the United States while leaving tariffs against the rest of the world unchanged. In 1988, average Canadian manufacturing tariffs against the U.S. were 8.1 percent (16 percent effective), with one in four 4-digit industries protected by tariffs above 10 percent; average U.S. tariffs against Canada were around 4 percent. The depth of mandated tariff cuts varied substantially across narrowly defined industries, providing cross-industry variation in policy exposure. Unlike liberalization episodes in developing countries, the FTA was not bundled with broader market reforms or triggered by a macroeconomic crisis, making it a relatively clean policy shock. Pre-FTA tariffs were set on a Most Favored Nation basis (except the 1965 Auto Pact), and the reciprocal structure generated both import- and export-liberalizing variation.

title: The Return to Protectionism

new_fields.research_question: What were the short-run effects of the 2018 U.S. import tariff increases and foreign retaliatory tariffs on U.S. trade quantities, prices, and aggregate and regional real income? Specifically, how much of the tariff was passed through to import and export prices, and how were gains and losses distributed across consumers, producers, the government, and U.S. counties with different sectoral specializations and political compositions?
new_fields.data_description: The authors build a monthly panel data set covering 2017:1–2019:4. U.S. statutory import tariffs at the HS-8 level are compiled from 14 USITC schedule revisions issued in 2018, while retaliatory tariffs at the HS-6 level are assembled from official documents of China, Canada, Mexico, and WTO notifications (EU, Russia, Turkey), combined with WTO MFN rates. Monthly U.S. Census Bureau administrative trade data provide values, quantities, and duties collected at the HS-10 level (products) by partner country (country-product pairs are 'varieties') for the universe of U.S. imports and exports. Unit values and duty-inclusive unit values are computed from these flows. The data are aggregated into products (HS-10) and sectors (4-digit NAICS), and county-level specialization patterns are used for regional analysis.
new_fields.institutional_context: In 2018 the United States, reversing decades of trade liberalization, enacted several waves of tariff increases, raising average tariffs from 2.6% to 16.6% on 12,043 products covering $303 billion (12.7%) of annual imports, targeting specific products and countries (notably China, steel/aluminum exporters, washing machines, solar panels). Major partners—China, Canada, Mexico, the EU, Russia, and Turkey—responded with retaliatory tariffs raising rates from 7.3% to 20.4% on 8,073 U.S. export products worth $127 billion (8.2% of exports), disproportionately targeting agricultural goods. Tariff changes were announced by the USTR and partner finance ministries and implemented within weeks, producing sharp, plausibly exogenous within-product variation across countries and over time. This abrupt, product-country-specific variation, uncorrelated with prior trends or anticipation, provides the identifying variation for estimating trade elasticities and pass-through.

title: Policy Uncertainty, Trade, and Welfare: Theory and Evidence for China and the United States

new_fields.research_question: Did the reduction in U.S. trade policy uncertainty faced by Chinese exporters following China's 2001 WTO accession cause higher growth in Chinese exports to the U.S.? The paper quantifies how the removal of the annual threat of losing Most Favored Nation (MFN) status—shifting applied tariffs from low MFN rates to much higher column-2 rates—affected industry-level export growth and welfare.
new_fields.data_description: The empirical analysis uses Chinese exports to the U.S., E.U., and Japan at the HS-6 industry level, primarily comparing 2000 and 2005, with additional pre-accession years (1996, 1999) and a full yearly panel spanning 1996-2005. Key variables include: log changes in export values; applied U.S. MFN tariffs and column-2 'threat' tariffs (used to construct a profit-loss uncertainty measure with elasticity of substitution σ=3, with σ=2,4 and Broda-Weinstein HS-10 elasticities as robustness); transport costs; nontariff barrier indicators (anti-dumping, countervailing duties, China-specific safeguards, Multi-Fiber Agreement quotas); and NBER-CES U.S. capital-labor intensity. Comparison groups include Taiwan and other WTO members without U.S. PTAs (Japan, Korea, Norway, Switzerland, EU-15). Tariff data come from TRAINS.
new_fields.institutional_context: Prior to WTO accession in January 2002, China's MFN status in the U.S. was subject to annual Congressional renewal, creating a persistent threat that applied tariffs would revert to much higher column-2 (Smoot-Hawley-era) rates. House vote shares to revoke MFN hovered around 33-40 percent in 1996-2000. WTO accession bound the U.S. to MFN treatment, eliminating this renewal threat and thus sharply reducing policy uncertainty, even though applied tariffs changed little. The cross-industry variation in the gap between applied MFN and column-2 tariffs generates differential exposure to this uncertainty shock. Taiwan, which acceded to the WTO shortly after China but was never subject to annual MFN renewal, provides a comparison group. The Multi-Fiber Agreement textile quota phase-out (completed by 2005) is a contemporaneous policy change controlled for separately.

title: Trade, Foreign Investment, and Industrial Policy for Developing Countries

new_fields.research_question: Do developing countries gain from abandoning policy neutrality in trade, foreign direct investment, and cross-industry resource allocation by imposing tariffs, subsidies, and tax breaks beyond those justified by optimal taxation or revenue needs? Specifically, does promoting particular sectors or attracting FDI through 'hard' interventions raise welfare and growth via Marshallian externalities, learning-by-exporting, or knowledge spillovers, and are 'soft' policies addressing coordination failures more effective?
new_fields.data_description: This paper is a theoretical and empirical literature review rather than an original empirical study. It synthesizes evidence from existing micro- and macro-level studies covering the second half of the twentieth century, drawing on: (i) industry case studies of protected sectors (e.g., US steel rails, Japanese semiconductors); (ii) cross-industry panel studies relating productivity growth to tariffs, quotas, and production subsidies; (iii) cross-country studies linking average protection levels and trade volumes to GDP growth, including country-specific analyses of South Korea and Taiwan; and (iv) firm- and plant-level micro studies of FDI spillovers, export promotion, input linkages, and labor market effects. Key variables referenced include tariff levels, trade-to-GDP shares, productivity growth, firm productivity heterogeneity, and FDI inflows with associated horizontal and vertical spillovers.
new_fields.institutional_context: The setting is the post-1970s wave of trade and FDI liberalization across developing countries, during which governments simultaneously deployed selective interventions—export subsidies, infant-industry tariff protection, FDI tax breaks, and sector-targeted support—alongside market opening. The paper treats these deviations from policy neutrality ('industrial policy') as the object of study, motivated by theoretical rationales including Marshallian externalities, inter-industry spillovers, rents in advanced sectors, sector-specific coordination failures, and information spillovers from discovery of new profitable activities. Specific country experiences (South Korea, Taiwan, Japan's semiconductor industry, US steel rails) and cross-country variation in tariffs, trade shares, and FDI regimes provide the institutional backdrop. The review also situates findings within new heterogeneous-firm trade theory, where complementary policies on firm entry, exit, labor flexibility, and infrastructure condition the effects of liberalization.

title: Institutions Rule: The Primacy of Institutions over Geography and Integration in Economic Development

new_fields.research_question: How much of the cross-national variation in income levels can be explained by the quality of domestic institutions (property rights, rule of law), geographic endowments (climate, location), and openness to international trade, and which of these 'deep determinants' has the dominant causal effect on long-run economic development? The paper also seeks to disentangle the indirect channels through which geography and trade may shape incomes via their influence on institutional quality.
new_fields.data_description: The analysis uses cross-country data on income, institutions, geography, and trade openness. The dependent variable is GDP per capita on a PPP basis for 1995. Institutional quality is measured using perceptions-based indices of property rights and the rule of law. Geography is proxied by distance from the equator, share of land area in the tropics, and average temperature. Integration is measured by the trade-to-GDP ratio. The unit of observation is the country, and analyses are run on three samples: a 64-country sample from Acemoglu, Johnson, and Robinson (2001), an 80-country sample with settler mortality data (preferred sample), and a 140-country sample using linguistic-heritage variables as alternative institutional proxies.
new_fields.institutional_context: Identification exploits two sources of plausibly exogenous variation. For institutional quality, the authors use log mortality rates of European colonial settlers (from Acemoglu, Johnson, and Robinson 2001): in colonies where disease environments made European settlement feasible, colonizers built property-rights-protecting institutions that persisted, whereas hostile disease environments led to extractive institutions. For trade integration, the authors use the Frankel-Romer (1999) constructed trade share, derived from a gravity model of bilateral trade based on country size, geographic distance, and other geographic characteristics — generating predicted trade/GDP ratios uncorrelated with income-determining factors other than trade. In robustness checks, the share of the population speaking English or a Western European language (Hall and Jones 1999) serves as an alternative exogenous source of variation in institutional quality for the larger 140-country sample.

title: Relationship-Specificity, Incomplete Contracts, and the Pattern of Trade

new_fields.research_question: Does a country's ability to enforce written contracts shape its comparative advantage in international trade? Specifically, do countries with stronger contract enforcement export relatively more in industries whose production depends heavily on relationship-specific intermediate inputs, and how does this channel compare in magnitude to traditional factor endowments like physical capital and skilled labor?
new_fields.data_description: The unit of observation is a country-industry pair covering exports in 1997. Bilateral/total trade flow data come from Feenstra (2000), converted from 4-digit SITC codes to the BEA's 1997 Input-Output industry classification, yielding 222 industries (182 when factor intensities are required). Factor endowments (human capital as log ratio of high-school completers to non-completers, and log capital per worker, both 1992) come from Antweiler and Trefler (2002); skill and capital intensities of production come from Bartelsman and Gray (1996). Judicial quality is measured by Kaufmann, Kraay, and Mastruzzi's (2003) 'rule of law' index (1997-1998), with robustness checks using Gwartney and Lawson (2003) and World Bank (2004). Contract intensity of each good is constructed from the 1997 U.S. I-O Use Table combined with Rauch's (1999) classification of inputs by whether they are sold on organized exchanges or reference-priced. The sample covers up to 146 countries.
new_fields.institutional_context: Identification exploits cross-country variation in judicial quality/contract enforcement interacted with cross-industry variation in the importance of relationship-specific inputs. The theoretical setting draws on the hold-up literature (Klein-Crawford-Alchian; Williamson; Grossman-Hart; Hart-Moore): when intermediate inputs require customized, relationship-specific investments and contracts are imperfectly enforceable ex post, suppliers underinvest ex ante, raising production costs. Countries with stronger judicial systems mitigate this hold-up problem, generating a cost advantage that is larger in industries more intensive in relationship-specific inputs. Whether an input is relationship-specific is proxied by whether it is traded on an organized exchange (thick market, little specificity) or only reference-priced in trade publications (intermediate specificity), versus neither (highly specific). To address reverse causality from trade patterns to legal institutions, the paper leverages exogenous variation in judicial quality stemming from countries' colonial legal origins (common vs. civil law traditions).

title: Robust Nonparametric Confidence Intervals for Regression-Discontinuity Designs

new_fields.research_question: How can researchers construct confidence intervals for average treatment effects at a cutoff that remain valid when the bandwidth used for local polynomial estimation is chosen via mean squared error minimization or cross-validation? Specifically, how can one correct the coverage distortions that arise because standard inference procedures produce intervals whose empirical coverage falls well below nominal levels when bandwidths are 'large'?
new_fields.data_description: The paper is primarily methodological and theoretical, deriving asymptotic distributional approximations for local polynomial estimators at boundary points. Empirical illustrations and simulations draw on datasets previously used in the applied literature, including household data from the Progresa/Oportunidades conditional cash transfer program in Mexico (used in the Supplemental Material's empirical illustration). The simulation study is empirically motivated, calibrated to realistic data generating processes. Key variables in the generic setting are an outcome Y, a continuous running/forcing variable X with a known cutoff (normalized to zero), and a binary treatment indicator T = 1(X ≥ 0). The unit of observation is an individual unit i with a random sample (Y_i, X_i) of size n. Companion R and STATA software packages implement the proposed procedures.
new_fields.institutional_context: The setting exploits situations where treatment assignment is determined by whether an observed continuous score or forcing variable crosses a known threshold, creating a discontinuous jump in treatment probability at the cutoff. Units just above and just below the cutoff are assumed comparable in terms of smoothly varying unobserved confounders, so that the jump in outcomes at the threshold identifies the local average treatment effect. The paper covers four canonical variants: sharp designs (deterministic assignment at the cutoff), fuzzy designs (probabilistic assignment), and their kink counterparts (where the slope, rather than the level, of the treatment assignment changes at the cutoff). The original motivating example is Thistlethwaite and Campbell's (1960) study of academic awards given to students scoring above a test-score threshold. Applications span economics, political science, and education.

title: Does Hazardous Waste Matter? Evidence from the Housing Market and the Superfund Program

new_fields.research_question: What are the local welfare effects of cleaning up hazardous waste sites on surrounding communities? Specifically, do federally sponsored remediation of the most polluted hazardous waste sites generate benefits—reflected in higher residential property values, rents, housing supply, population, and in-migration of households that value environmental quality—that justify the substantial public expenditures on cleanup?
new_fields.data_description: The authors assemble what they describe as the most comprehensive dataset ever compiled on the U.S. Superfund program. It covers all approximately 1,400 Superfund hazardous waste sites as of 2000, along with the 290 sites that narrowly missed placement on the initial 1983 National Priorities List (NPL), for a total of roughly 690 candidate sites. For each site, the data include the EPA's Hazard Ranking System (HRS) score (0–100 scale). The housing market outcomes are measured at the Census-tract level in 1980 (before the first NPL was released), 1990, and 2000, and include residential property values, rental rates, housing supply (new construction), total population, and demographic characteristics of residents. Data on cleanup costs (averaging $43 million per site) were obtained from Katherine Probst.
new_fields.institutional_context: The 1980 CERCLA (Superfund) legislation authorized the EPA to identify the nation's most dangerous hazardous waste sites and place them on the National Priorities List (NPL) for long-run remedial cleanup. Facing budget constraints permitting only 400 cleanups, the EPA in 1982 developed the Hazard Ranking System (HRS), a scoring rule from 0 to 100 based on toxicity, exposure pathways (groundwater, surface water, air), proximity to humans, and affected population size. The EPA applied the HRS to the 690 most dangerous candidate sites (winnowed from roughly 15,000 referrals). After scoring, the EPA set the cutoff at 28.5—the score dividing the 400th and 401st ranked sites—and placed only sites above this threshold on the initial 1983 NPL. Because the 28.5 threshold was chosen after scoring was completed, scores could not be manipulated, creating quasi-random assignment to cleanup eligibility near the cutoff.

title: Did Highways Cause Suburbanization?

new_fields.research_question: To what extent did the construction of new limited-access highways between 1950 and 1990 cause the decline in central city populations in U.S. metropolitan areas? The paper seeks to quantify the causal contribution of urban highway infrastructure to suburbanization, distinguishing it from alternative explanations such as Tiebout sorting, racial preferences, and central city blight.
new_fields.data_description: The analysis uses a panel of 139 U.S. metropolitan statistical areas (MSAs) with at least 100,000 residents and central cities of at least 50,000 residents in 1950, observed decennially from 1950 to 1990. Key variables include constant-geography (1950-definition) central city population, total MSA population, and demographic controls (non-white share, high school graduation rates) from U.S. Census data. Highway data come from the PR-511 dataset combined with digital maps of the interstate system, enabling construction of county-year-level interstate mileage. The primary treatment variable is the number of highway 'rays'—limited-access segments connecting central business districts to areas outside the central city—measured in each MSA-year. A 1947 federal interstate highway plan provides the planned-rays measure. The unit of observation is the MSA (in long differences) or MSA-decade (in panel regressions).
new_fields.institutional_context: The Federal Aid Highway Act of 1944 directed the formation of a national interstate highway system designed to connect distant metropolitan areas, serve national defense, and link to Canada and Mexico—explicitly not to facilitate local commuting. A 1947 plan approved by the federal roads commissioner designated 37,324 miles of highways based on 1940 population, manufacturing, agriculture, military installations, and a 1941 War Department strategic network. Major federal funding only arrived with the 1956 Federal Aid Highway Act, which committed the federal government to pay 90% of construction costs and expanded the plan to 41,000 miles. Because the 1947 plan was designed for interregional trade and defense rather than responding to local commuting demand or MSA growth trends, planned rays provide variation in highway placement across MSAs that is plausibly unrelated to local suburbanization pressures, while strongly predicting actual highway construction by 1990.

title: The Welfare Economics of Land Use Planning

new_fields.research_question: What are the magnitudes of the benefits (environmental amenities such as open space and restrictions on industrial land use) and costs (higher land and housing prices from restricted developable land) of restrictive urban land use regulation, and how are these net welfare effects distributed across household income groups in an urban area facing strong development pressure?
new_fields.data_description: The study uses micro-level housing and household data for Reading, UK, collected in the second and third quarters of 1984. Housing structure details and asking prices come from a 15% sample of Estate Agents' property particulars for owner-occupied homes, yielding 433 observations used to estimate a Box–Cox hedonic price function. Property locations were geocoded from Ordnance Survey maps and aerial photographs, which also provided local land use information. Neighbourhood characteristics were drawn from the Small Area Statistics of the Census of Population and local authority records. Household income, demographic composition, transaction prices (where available), and other household details were collected through a household survey with a 48% response rate after follow-up, producing 206 households used to estimate an Almost Ideal Demand System for land, structure, and planning-produced amenities.
new_fields.institutional_context: The analysis exploits the UK's Town and Country Planning System, whose modern form emerged from 1930s anti-ribbon-development legislation and has long prioritised containment of urban sprawl via mechanisms such as green belts and restrictions on industrial land use and development. Reading was selected because, by a variety of measures, it faces some of the most restrictive land use planning in Britain, making it a setting where planning sharply constrains developable land supply while producing local amenities (e.g., open space, separation from industrial uses). This restrictive regulatory regime creates measurable variation in amenity provision and land availability across locations within a single urban area that otherwise approximates the assumptions of classic monocentric urban economic theory, enabling estimation of both the amenity benefits generated by planning and the costs imposed through reduced private residential land availability.

title: Estimating the Value of a New Transit Option

new_fields.research_question: Does the introduction of a new light rail transit line generate capitalized benefits in nearby property values, and if so, do these benefits operate through station-level access (price gradients) or through broader neighborhood-level appreciation? The paper further asks whether effects differ across single-family homes, condominiums, and commercial properties, and whether light rail functions primarily as a transportation amenity or as an economic development catalyst in medium-sized, lower-density U.S. cities.
new_fields.data_description: The study uses the full population of single-family residential, condominium (multi-family ownership), and commercial property transactions in Charlotte/Mecklenburg County, North Carolina, sold from 1994 through the post-opening period of the South Line light rail (which began operations in November 2007). Properties included are those proximate to the actual South Line corridor or to the Northeast and Southeast corridors that were considered but ultimately not selected. Transaction records include sale price, structural characteristics, and location, supplemented with distance measures to LRT stations and census/neighborhood controls. The unit of observation is an individual property sale. Both hedonic and repeat sales specifications are estimated, with propensity score matching used to construct alternative control groups.
new_fields.institutional_context: Charlotte's planning process for its first light rail alignment formally evaluated three candidate corridors—South, Northeast, and Southeast—throughout a multi-year process beginning in the late 1980s. A 1994 land use plan explicitly targeted five transit corridors, and in November 1998 county voters approved a half-cent sales tax to fund transit. In September 2000, the Metropolitan Transit Commission officially selected the South corridor as the first LRT alignment; the Northeast and Southeast corridors, though seriously considered as 'finalists' (and the Northeast was originally preferred), were not built. The South Line opened in November 2007. This publicly documented selection among ex ante comparable candidate corridors provides neighborhoods along the non-selected corridors as plausible counterfactuals for those along the treated South Line, enabling comparisons of property value trajectories before and after the announcement and opening.

title: Creative Destruction: Barriers to Urban Growth and the Great Boston Fire of 1872

new_fields.research_question: Do positive cross-plot externalities from building reconstruction constrain urban growth when landowners fail to internalize spillovers onto neighbors? Specifically, does widespread simultaneous reconstruction of outdated buildings raise land and building values both on reconstructed plots and on nearby untouched plots, and how large are the resulting capitalized economic gains relative to the value of destroyed structures?
new_fields.data_description: The authors construct a new plot-level panel covering all plots in the burned downtown Boston area and surrounding unburned areas in 1867, 1869, 1871, 1872, 1873, 1882, and 1894. The primary source is Boston city tax assessment records, which provide each plot's assessed land value, building value, land area, and occupant characteristics (including residential versus commercial use and occupant wealth/industry). Supplemental data on plot transactions come from Boston's Registry of Deeds, which the authors use to validate that assessed values track market sales prices in burned and unburned areas, before and after the Fire. Additional data capture road network changes, plot ownership, plot size, and industrial composition. The unit of observation is a plot-year; variables also include distance to the Fire boundary.
new_fields.institutional_context: In November 1872, a fire swept through Boston's downtown business district, burning for 22 hours and destroying 776 buildings, causing roughly $75 million in damages (about 11 percent of Boston's total assessed real estate and personal property). The fire's spread was driven by idiosyncratic factors—delayed alarms and sickness among the fire department's horses—before being halted by firefighting aid from surrounding towns, producing a sharp geographic boundary between destroyed and spared plots. Reconstruction occurred in an era before zoning regulations and strong building codes, managed largely by private landowners with limited municipal coordination; proposals for major road reconfiguration and stringent building codes were blocked by landowners, and insurance and capital inflows funded rebuilding. This sudden, externally-caused clearing of an otherwise growing downtown created forced simultaneous reconstruction of many adjacent plots, enabling comparisons between burned plots, nearby unburned plots at varying distances, and more distant control areas.

title: The Fundamental Law of Road Congestion: Evidence from US Cities

new_fields.research_question: How does the stock of road infrastructure (lane kilometers of interstate highways and major urban roads) causally affect vehicle kilometers traveled (VKT) in US metropolitan areas? What are the underlying mechanisms — changes in driving by incumbent residents, commercial/trucking activity, and in-migration — and does expanding public transit reduce VKT? The answers speak to whether building more roads or transit can alleviate urban traffic congestion.
new_fields.data_description: The analysis combines several US data sources at the metropolitan statistical area (MSA) level. Average annual daily traffic (AADT) and detailed descriptions of the road network come from the US Highway Performance and Monitoring System (HPMS) for 1983, 1993, and 2003. Individual and household travel behavior is drawn from the National Personal Transportation Survey (NPTS) for 1995 and 2001. These are augmented with data on truck traffic, public transit provision, sectoral employment, population, and physical geography. The unit of observation is the metropolitan area, observed roughly every decade, covering all MSAs in the continental United States. Key variables include lane-kilometers of interstate and other major roads, VKT, public transit capacity, and demographic/economic controls.
new_fields.institutional_context: Road capacity in US cities is not allocated randomly: highways may be expanded in growing cities experiencing rising travel demand, or alternatively directed to declining cities to prop them up, making contemporaneous road stocks endogenous to traffic. To break this simultaneity, the authors exploit historical and planning features that shaped where interstates and major roads were actually built but that plausibly do not directly determine current travel demand. Specifically, they use (i) the routes of major exploration expeditions between 1835 and 1850, (ii) the configuration of major rail routes in 1898, and (iii) the proposed routes of the interstate highway system from a 1947 preliminary plan. These long-predetermined network templates strongly predict the modern spatial distribution of highway lane-kilometers across MSAs, providing exogenous variation in road supply.

title: The Geographic Determinants of Housing Supply

new_fields.research_question: To what extent do exogenous geographic features — such as oceans, lakes, wetlands, and steep-sloped terrain — determine contemporaneous patterns of urban growth, housing prices, and the responsiveness of housing supply to demand shocks across U.S. metropolitan areas? How do these physical land constraints interact with, and shape, local land-use regulations, and what are the resulting metropolitan-specific housing supply elasticities?
new_fields.data_description: The paper constructs a novel metropolitan-area dataset on developable land using GIS processing of satellite and elevation data. Terrain slopes are computed from the USGS Digital Elevation Model at 90-meter resolution to identify land with slopes above 15% within a 50-km radius of each MSA central city centroid. Internal water bodies and wetlands are measured using the 1992 USGS National Land Cover Dataset at 30-meter resolution, and digital contour maps identify area lost to oceans and the Great Lakes. These are combined with the Wharton Residential Urban Land Regulation Index (Gyourko, Saiz, and Summers 2008), Census data on population, median house values, income, education, immigration, and industry (1970–2000), patents per capita, January sunshine hours, and tourist visits. The unit of observation is the MSA/NECMA, focusing on areas with population above 500,000.
new_fields.institutional_context: Identification exploits the fact that physical geographic features — ocean coastlines, the Great Lakes, inland water bodies, wetlands, and mountainous terrain with slopes above 15% — are predetermined natural features that exogenously restrict the supply of developable land around a city. Architectural guidelines treat slopes above 15% as effectively unbuildable for residential construction, a claim the author verifies in Los Angeles where such zones cover 48% of land area but house only 3.65% of the population. These natural constraints are plausibly exogenous to contemporary housing demand and prices, unlike land-use regulations, which are themselves endogenous to preexisting land values through homeowner political incentives (the homevoter hypothesis). The setting also allows use of exogenous regulatory shifters — local tastes for regulation — to disentangle physical from man-made supply constraints in determining metropolitan housing supply elasticities.

title: When Do Better Schools Raise Housing Prices? Evidence from Paris Public and Private Schools

new_fields.research_question: How does the academic performance of neighborhood public schools get capitalized into local housing prices, and does this capitalization depend on the local availability of private school alternatives? Specifically, do well-developed private school options weaken parents' willingness to pay a housing premium for access to higher-performing public schools?
new_fields.data_description: The authors use comprehensive administrative data on real estate transactions in the city of Paris over the period 1997–2004, combined with detailed data on public and private middle schools (collèges), including school performance indices and attendance zone maps. The unit of observation is a housing sale, with information on sale price, flat characteristics (size, floor, number of rooms, age of building, parking, etc.), location at the census block level, school year of transaction, and the public middle school catchment area to which the flat is assigned. Neighborhood socio-demographic characteristics come from census data. School performance is measured using multiple indicators. The final sample focuses on sales located within narrow bandwidths (250m, 300m, 350m) of public middle school attendance boundaries.
new_fields.institutional_context: Secondary schooling in Paris combines strict residence-based assignment to public middle schools with a well-developed, almost entirely publicly funded private school sector that operates under different admission rules not tied to residence. The French educational system is highly centralized: children attend collège from ages 11 to 14, and public school assignment is determined by administratively drawn catchment areas (school attendance zones) that create sharp spatial discontinuities in access to public schools of differing quality. These attendance boundaries often run along specific streets, so that otherwise comparable flats on opposite sides of the same street are assigned to different public middle schools. The coexistence of residence-based public assignment with a dense, affordable private school option provides a setting to examine how outside schooling options alter the value parents place on public school access through housing location.
