title: School Quality, Neighborhoods, and Housing Prices: The Impacts of School Desegregation

new_fields.research_question: How much do school characteristics—such as test scores and racial composition—causally affect residential housing prices, separate from the effects of correlated neighborhood amenities and peer composition? The paper also asks whether changes in school assignments feed back into neighborhood demographic composition.
new_fields.data_description: The authors use administrative real estate parcel and sales records from the Property Assessment and Land Record Management division of Mecklenburg County, North Carolina, covering single-family home sales from January 1994 through December 2001. After trimming the top and bottom 1% of prices, the sample contains 89,793 sales on 69,361 parcels. Each parcel has precise geographic coordinates, detailed structural attributes (bedrooms, bathrooms, acreage, 36-category building quality), assessor-defined neighborhood identifiers (1,048 neighborhoods), and census block group measures of median income and percent African American (from 1990 and 2000). The Charlotte-Mecklenburg School District provided annual school boundary maps and school locations for 1993–2001, plus school-level test proficiency rates and racial composition. Parcels are linked to assigned elementary, middle, and high schools and to distances to the nearest assignment boundary.
new_fields.institutional_context: From 1971 to 2001, Charlotte-Mecklenburg operated under the court-ordered Swann desegregation plan, which required busing and racial balancing so that each school's African American share stayed within 15 percentage points of the district average. To achieve balance, the district drew non-contiguous attendance zones that crossed neighborhood lines, so that homes within a few hundred feet of each other were often assigned to schools with very different test scores and racial compositions. Rapid population growth and demographic change forced the district to periodically redraw boundaries, especially when new schools opened—e.g., in 1997 roughly 30% of residential units were reassigned to different high schools, and in 1998 about 16–18% of units were reassigned at the elementary and middle school levels. These sharp boundary discontinuities and reassignment shocks provide plausibly exogenous variation in school assignments holding location fixed.

title: Do Stock Prices Influence Corporate Decisions? Evidence from the Technology Bubble

new_fields.research_question: Does non-fundamental variation in stock prices causally affect corporate real decisions—specifically capital investment, equity issuance, and cash savings? In particular, do elevated equity valuations relax financing constraints and thereby alter investment and financing behavior of firms whose fundamentals were not directly affected by the valuation run-up?
new_fields.data_description: The authors assemble a large firm-year panel of U.S. non-tech manufacturers (so-called 'old economy' firms) covering the 1971–2003 period, with the late-1990s tech run-up as the focal sub-period. Tech-linked manufacturers are identified and excluded using the U.S. Input–Output matrix plus additional screens. Key firm-level variables include capital investment, equity issuance, cash savings, cash flow, a market-based Tobin's Q (QMkt), and a projected 'fundamental Q' (FundQ) constructed from past profitability, sales growth, and industry fundamentals. Firms are additionally classified as financially constrained versus unconstrained using standard proxies. Comparison samples include tech firms and constrained/unconstrained non-tech firms. Aggregate indices (Dow Jones, Nasdaq, Industrial Production) are used for context. The unit of observation is the firm-year.
new_fields.institutional_context: The setting exploits the 1990s technology stock price run-up. While tech firms' valuations and investment may both reflect unobserved technology-driven revisions in expected profitability (making causal inference within tech difficult), the run-up spilled over into the equity prices of traditional 'old economy' manufacturers whose business fundamentals did not undergo comparable shifts. Contemporary productivity research (Jorgenson and Stiroh, 1999; Gordon, 2000) confirmed that traditional manufacturers were not expected to benefit from the tech innovation wave, and limits-to-arbitrage arguments (Shleifer and Vishny, 1997; Brunnermeier and Nagel, 2004) rationalize persistent mispricing spreading across sectors. This cross-sector spillover provides plausibly exogenous variation in non-tech firms' equity valuations, while heterogeneity between financially constrained and unconstrained non-tech firms offers a cross-sectional contrast for identifying whether mispricing affects real corporate policies.

title: The Impact of Medicaid on Labor Market Activity and Program Participation: Evidence from the Oregon Health Insurance Experiment

new_fields.research_question: What are the causal effects of Medicaid coverage on low-income adults' labor market outcomes (employment, earnings, likelihood of earning above the federal poverty level) and on their participation in other safety net programs such as SNAP, TANF, SSI, and SSDI? Do these indirect effects constitute meaningful additional costs or benefits of expanding public health insurance?
new_fields.data_description: The authors use 2009 administrative data covering approximately 75,000 adults on the Oregon Medicaid lottery list, with an analytic sample of 61,790 observations at the individual level. Annual earnings and receipt of Supplemental Security Income (SSI) and Social Security Disability Insurance (SSDI) come from Social Security Administration records, matched to lottery participants by name and date of birth (85% match rate, balanced across treatment and control). Receipt of SNAP (food stamps) and TANF (cash welfare) benefits, as well as Medicaid enrollment status, come from Oregon state administrative records. Pre-randomization (2007) values of outcomes are used as controls. Outcomes include indicators for any earnings/benefit receipt, dollar amounts of earnings and benefits, and whether earnings exceed the federal poverty level.
new_fields.institutional_context: In 2008, Oregon opened a limited Medicaid expansion for low-income uninsured adults (ages 19–64, below the federal poverty level, assets under $2,000, uninsured for six months, and not otherwise categorically eligible). Because demand far exceeded available slots, the state randomly drew roughly 30,000 names by lottery from a waiting list of about 90,000. Selected households could apply for Medicaid and enroll if they met eligibility criteria; ultimately the lottery raised Medicaid enrollment by about 25 percentage points without crowding out private coverage. This random allocation of the opportunity to apply for Medicaid creates exogenous variation in public insurance coverage that is unrelated to individuals' underlying labor supply or propensity to take up other transfer programs, enabling credible causal estimation.

title: Salience and Taxation: Theory and Evidence

new_fields.research_question: Do consumers respond less to commodity taxes when those taxes are not displayed in posted prices than to equivalent changes in posted prices themselves? More broadly, does the visibility of tax-inclusive prices affect demand responses, and what are the implications for tax incidence and deadweight loss when consumers fail to fully optimize with respect to taxes?
new_fields.data_description: Two complementary datasets are used. First, scanner data from a grocery store covering a three-week period in early 2006, recording quantities sold and revenues at the product level for cosmetics, hair care accessories, and deodorants (roughly 750 taxable products) in a treatment store, alongside non-tagged products in the same aisle and products in two control stores in nearby cities. A survey of grocery shoppers complements the scanner data by measuring consumer knowledge of which goods are subject to sales tax. Second, annual state-level panel data on total beer consumption by state from 1970 to 2003, linked to state excise tax rates on beer (included in posted prices) and general state sales tax rates (added at the register). The unit of observation is state-year for the alcohol analysis and product-store-week for the grocery analysis.
new_fields.institutional_context: Two settings provide exogenous variation in the salience of taxation. In U.S. retail, sales taxes (7.375 percent in the study's store) are typically excluded from shelf prices and added only at the register, making them less visible than the posted pretax price. The researchers implemented an intervention in which tax-inclusive price tags were posted below original shelf tags for treated product categories in one grocery store, while other categories in the same store and other nearby stores were left unchanged, generating variation in tax visibility across products and stores. The second setting exploits the fact that alcohol in the United States is subject to two distinct state taxes: excise taxes that are embedded in posted shelf prices, and general sales taxes that are applied at checkout. State-level legislative changes in these two tax rates between 1970 and 2003 provide variation in salient versus non-salient tax changes.

title: Workers' Compensation and Injury Duration: Evidence from a Natural Experiment

new_fields.research_question: Does raising the level of weekly cash benefits paid to injured workers lengthen the duration of time they spend away from work on injury-related leave? The study seeks to quantify how the generosity of wage-replacement payments shapes workers' incentives to return to work, separating this behavioral response from confounding differences across workers and injuries.
new_fields.data_description: The analysis uses administrative workers' compensation claims records from Kentucky and Michigan provided by the National Council on Compensation Insurance (NCCI). The unit of observation is an individual injury claim involving temporary total disability. Key variables include the duration of time out of work (spell length), the weekly benefit amount received, the pre-injury weekly wage, demographic and job characteristics (age, gender, marital status, industry), injury type and body part affected, and the date of injury. Samples cover claims filed in windows before and after statutory benefit changes in each state (Kentucky's change in mid-1980 and Michigan's in early 1982), allowing comparison of injury spells across injured workers subject to different benefit rules.
new_fields.institutional_context: Both Kentucky and Michigan enacted large increases in the maximum weekly workers' compensation benefit for temporary total disability claims. Because benefits equal a fixed replacement rate (typically two-thirds) of the pre-injury wage subject to a statutory cap, raising the cap sharply increased benefits for workers whose wages placed them above the old maximum but left benefits unchanged for lower-wage workers whose replacement rate was already below the cap. The reforms thus generated sudden, discrete jumps in benefit generosity that affected only high-wage injured workers, while low-wage workers injured in the same period serve as a natural comparison group unaffected by the statutory change. This policy-induced variation in benefits is plausibly unrelated to individual return-to-work decisions, creating a quasi-experimental setting.

title: NAFTA and the Local Labor Market

new_fields.research_question: Did the tariff reductions negotiated under the North American Free Trade Agreement reduce wage growth for U.S. workers employed in industries that compete with Mexican imports and for workers residing in localities whose employment is concentrated in such industries? Are these distributional effects heterogeneous across education groups and do they spill over to workers in nontraded sectors within vulnerable localities?
new_fields.data_description: The analysis uses U.S. Census microdata for 1990 and 2000 from the IPUMS project at the Minnesota Population Center, consisting of two repeated cross-sections of individual workers. The unit of observation is the individual worker, with variables including wages, education (less than high school, high school graduate, some college, college graduate), industry of employment (89 Census traded-goods industries plus nontraded sectors), occupation (blue-collar vs. white-collar), and geographic location identified by Consistent Public-Use Microdata Areas (conspumas). These are merged with industry-level U.S. tariffs on Mexican imports for 1990 and 2000, and with Mexican trade data used to construct revealed comparative advantage measures (Mexican exports to countries other than the U.S. relative to other countries' exports).
new_fields.institutional_context: NAFTA, signed in 1993 by the U.S., Canada, and Mexico, phased out tariffs on Mexican imports gradually starting in 1994, with most reductions occurring over ten years and some extending to fifteen years. Crucially, the negotiated schedule of tariff liberalization varied substantially across industries: some sectors had high initial tariffs that fell rapidly during 1990–2000, while others had low initial tariffs or slower phase-outs. This sector-specific variation in both initial protection levels and the speed of tariff drawdown, combined with geographic variation in industry composition across U.S. localities (conspumas), creates differential exposure to the trade shock. Tariffs between the U.S. and Canada had already been eliminated under the earlier Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement, so variation in exposure is driven specifically by Mexican tariff changes, weighted by Mexico's revealed comparative advantage to account for its actual export capacity.

title: Trade Integration, Market Size, and Industrialization: Evidence from China's National Trunk Highway System

new_fields.research_question: How does the connection of small peripheral regions to large metropolitan centers via large-scale inter-regional transport infrastructure affect the economic growth and industrial output of those peripheral regions? Specifically, do reductions in trade costs between ex ante asymmetric markets within a country diffuse industrial activity to the periphery, or reinforce the concentration of production in core metropolitan agglomerations?
new_fields.data_description: The analysis uses county-level data from China covering periods before and after the construction of the National Trunk Highway System (NTHS), with the bulk of network construction occurring between 1992 and 2007 (kick-off phase 1992-1997, rapid development 1998-2007). Key outcome variables include county-level GDP growth, industrial output growth, local government revenue growth, county population, urban population, and urbanization measures. The author combines these economic data with remote sensing data on land cover and elevation to compute construction cost parameters, and with geographic information on the NTHS network, provincial capitals, cities with urban registered populations above 500,000, and border crossings. The unit of observation is the Chinese county, distinguishing non-targeted peripheral counties from targeted metropolitan city nodes.
new_fields.institutional_context: China's National Trunk Highway System was approved in 1992 as a '7-5' network of seven horizontal and five vertical expressway axes, constructed at an estimated cost of US$120 billion and spanning roughly 35,000 km of four-lane limited-access toll ways, completed by the end of 2007. The stated policy objective was to connect provincial capitals, cities with urban registered populations above 500,000, and border crossings on a single continuous expressway network. Targeted metropolitan centers represented only 1.5% of land area and 17% of population but 60% of non-agricultural production pre-1997; the average peripheral-to-metropolitan GDP ratio was 1:25. As a by-product of linking targeted nodes, many small non-targeted peripheral counties along the routes were connected to major production centers, creating variation in connection status that was not explicitly targeted by the policy.

title: Valuation Ratios and the Long-Run Stock Market Outlook

new_fields.research_question: Can valuation ratios such as the price-dividend and price-earnings ratios predict future real stock price growth, and if so, why does predictability appear strong at long horizons but weak at short horizons? Specifically, is this horizon-dependent pattern explained by increased statistical power at long horizons in a linear setting, or by nonlinearities in the underlying data-generating process?
new_fields.data_description: The study uses annual data from Campbell and Shiller (1998) spanning 1871/1872–1997 for the S&P 500. The key series are the nominal S&P 500 stock price index, nominal dividends, and nominal earnings, each deflated by the consumer price index to obtain real stock prices, real dividends, and real earnings. The unit of observation is the year. Key constructed variables are the log price–dividend ratio (January real stock price divided by real dividends over the prior calendar year) and the log price–earnings ratio (January real stock price divided by real earnings over the prior calendar year), along with k-period log real stock price changes for horizons k = 1 to 10 years. Data are obtained from Robert Shiller's website.
new_fields.institutional_context: The setting is the long-run US equity market, where measures of fundamental value (dividends and earnings) are thought to anchor stock prices in the long run, implying mean reversion in valuation ratios. This stable long-run relationship between prices and fundamentals motivates using current valuation ratios to forecast subsequent multi-year stock price movements. The long historical span (over 125 years of annual S&P 500 data constructed by Shiller) encompasses multiple market cycles, allowing researchers to examine whether deviations of prices from dividend- or earnings-based fundamentals systematically reverse. The empirical puzzle—significant forecasting power at long horizons but not short—arises naturally in this context and motivates examining whether nonlinear mean-reversion (e.g., stronger reversion when valuation ratios are far from equilibrium) in the price–dividend and price–earnings ratios accounts for the horizon pattern.

title: The New Issues Puzzle

new_fields.research_question: Do firms that issue equity—either through initial public offerings or seasoned equity offerings—subsequently earn lower long-run stock returns than otherwise comparable non-issuing firms? If so, can this underperformance be explained by risk (beta), firm size, book-to-market effects, or long-term return reversals, and how does it vary with issuance volume over time?
new_fields.data_description: The authors assemble two samples of U.S. equity issuances during 1970-1990: 4,753 operating-company IPOs (excluding closed-end funds, REITs, and ADRs) and 3,702 seasoned equity offerings involving at least some primary shares (excluding utilities, SIC 491-494), conducted by 2,680 distinct firms. IPO data come from Investment Dealer's Digest, Going Public: The IPO Reporter, IDD Information Services, and Securities Data Company; SEO data come from the SEC's registered offering statistics tape, the Loderer-Sheehan-Kadlec sample, and Securities Data Co. Daily and monthly stock returns are taken from CRSP's Nasdaq and Amex-NYSE tapes. Key variables include post-issue buy-and-hold returns over three- and five-year windows, market capitalization, book-to-market ratios, betas, and Fama-French three-factor loadings. The unit of observation is the issuing firm-offering, each paired with a size-matched non-issuing firm.
new_fields.institutional_context: Identification leverages the discrete corporate decision to issue equity (IPO or SEO) as a firm-level event whose aftermath can be tracked against a control group of non-issuing firms with identical starting market capitalization. For each issuer, on every December 31 the authors rank all CRSP-listed common stocks that have not issued equity in the prior five years and select the firm with market cap closest to but just above the issuer as the matching benchmark, splicing in replacements if the match is delisted or itself issues stock. Post-issue buy-and-hold returns over three- and five-year windows are then compared between issuers and matched non-issuers. The 1970-1990 sample also exhibits sharp time-series variation in issuance volume, allowing the authors to exploit high- versus low-volume periods to examine whether underperformance is concentrated in hot-issue windows, consistent with a timing interpretation.

title: Minimum Wages and Employment: A Case Study of the Fast-Food Industry in New Jersey and Pennsylvania: Comment

new_fields.research_question: Does an increase in the state minimum wage reduce employment at fast-food restaurants subject to the higher wage floor, relative to establishments in a neighboring state where the minimum wage is unchanged? Specifically, did New Jersey's April 1992 minimum-wage increase from $4.25 to $5.05 lower fast-food employment compared to eastern Pennsylvania?
new_fields.data_description: The authors use administrative payroll records obtained from Burger King, Wendy's, Roy Rogers, and Kentucky Fried Chicken restaurants located in New Jersey and eastern Pennsylvania, covering the same zip-code sectional areas (first three digits) and chains sampled by Card and Krueger (1994). Payroll data were collected by the authors and the Employment Policies Institute from franchisees and parent corporations, yielding 235 restaurants (72 in PA, 163 in NJ) across 25 of 31 zip-code areas. The records report total hours worked by nonmanagement employees during pay periods spanning each of CK's two survey waves: February 15–March 4, 1992 (pre) and November 5–December 31, 1992 (post). Hours are converted to full-time equivalents assuming a 35-hour workweek. The unit of observation is the individual restaurant. Results are compared to CK's original telephone-survey data.
new_fields.institutional_context: On April 1, 1992, New Jersey raised its state minimum wage from $4.25 to $5.05 per hour (an 18.8 percent increase), while neighboring Pennsylvania's minimum wage remained at the federal floor of $4.25. Prior to this date, both states had been bound by the same federal minimum (which had risen to $4.25 on April 1, 1991). Because the fast-food industry employs a large share of low-wage workers likely to be affected by the wage floor, the geographically proximate Pennsylvania restaurants serve as a comparison group unaffected by the New Jersey change. This state-level policy change, combined with pre- and post-increase observations on restaurants in both states, provides the setting for evaluating the employment consequences of the minimum-wage hike.

title: Do Firms Want to Borrow More? Testing Credit Constraints Using a Directed Lending Program

new_fields.research_question: Are medium-sized firms in India credit constrained, in the sense that an exogenous expansion in the supply of bank credit leads them to increase investment and production rather than merely substitute cheaper credit for more expensive borrowing? Relatedly, what is the marginal product of capital for such firms, and how large is the gap between it and the interest rate paid?
new_fields.data_description: The authors assemble firm-level data collected directly from a single large Indian public sector bank, covering a sample of medium-sized, officially registered (but not publicly listed) Indian firms that borrow short-term working capital from the bank. Key variables include the firm's working capital credit limit and utilization from the bank, borrowing from other market sources, sales/revenue, profits, investment in plant and machinery, and interest costs. Observations are at the firm-year level, spanning years around the 1998 and 2000 regulatory changes. The sample is restricted to firms whose investment in plant and machinery places them near the eligibility thresholds (below Rs. 6.5 million, between Rs. 6.5 and 30 million, and between Rs. 10 and 30 million), enabling comparisons across groups whose priority-sector eligibility status changed.
new_fields.institutional_context: Indian banks are required to direct at least 40% of net credit to a 'priority sector' that includes small scale industry (SSI); failing this target forces them to park funds in low-yield government instruments, so the target is effectively binding. Eligibility for SSI-priority lending depends on a firm's investment in plant and machinery. In January 1998, the ceiling defining SSI was raised from Rs. 6.5 million to Rs. 30 million, newly granting priority status to a well-defined band of medium-sized firms. In January 2000, this reform was partially reversed: firms with investment between Rs. 10 and 30 million lost priority eligibility, while those between Rs. 6.5 and 10 million retained it. These two opposing reforms generate sharp, firm-specific changes in access to subsidized bank credit, with firms already inside the priority sector throughout serving as a natural comparison group.

title: Colonial Origins of Comparative Development: An Empirical Investigation

new_fields.research_question: What is the causal effect of domestic institutions—specifically the security of property rights and constraints on government expropriation—on long-run economic performance (GDP per capita) across former European colonies? The paper seeks to isolate exogenous variation in institutional quality to quantify how much of cross-country income differences can be attributed to institutions rather than to geography, culture, or reverse causation.
new_fields.data_description: The sample covers 75 former European colonies. The outcome is log GDP per capita (PPP-adjusted) in 1995. The key institutional proxy is the 'protection against risk of expropriation' index from Political Risk Services, averaged over 1985–1995, measuring security of property rights against government expropriation. The central explanatory measure is the mortality rate (per 1,000 per annum) of European soldiers, bishops, and sailors stationed in the colonies during the 17th–19th centuries, drawn primarily from the historical work of Philip D. Curtin. Additional controls include latitude, continent dummies (notably Africa), identity of the main colonizer, legal origin, climate, religion, natural resources, soil quality, ethnolinguistic fragmentation, and measures of the current disease environment (malaria prevalence, life expectancy, infant mortality, European-descent population share). Early institutional measures (circa 1900) and European settlement shares are also used.
new_fields.institutional_context: Identification exploits historical variation in the disease environment faced by Europeans attempting to colonize different regions. In locations where malaria and yellow fever produced very high mortality among Europeans (but not among immune indigenous populations), Europeans could not settle in large numbers and instead established 'extractive' colonial states designed to transfer resources to the metropole, with weak property rights and few checks on government power. In healthier locations, Europeans migrated and replicated European-style institutions emphasizing private property and constraints on the executive ('Neo-Europes' such as the US, Canada, Australia, New Zealand). These colonial institutions persisted through independence into the present. Settler mortality rates, recorded by historians from military and clerical records over 1600–1850, thus provide historically-determined variation in colonization strategy that shaped institutional trajectories independently of current economic conditions.

title: The Effects of the Unemployment Insurance Payroll Tax on Wages, Employment, Claims and Denials

new_fields.research_question: How does a payroll tax levied on employers, where the tax rate varies both across industries and across firms within the same labor market, affect workers' earnings and employment? Additionally, how does tying an employer's tax rate to its past layoff behavior affect employee turnover, unemployment insurance claim rates, and the rate at which claims are denied?
new_fields.data_description: The study uses longitudinal administrative earnings records from Washington State covering workers and firms before and after 1985, along with data from neighboring states Oregon and Idaho as comparison jurisdictions. Key variables include firm-level and industry-average unemployment insurance (UI) tax rates, tax bases, worker earnings, employment levels, UI claim rates, claim denial rates, and measures of seasonal and cyclical employment variation. Marginal tax cost measures (the share of an additional dollar of UI benefits paid by former employees that a firm pays in higher future taxes) are constructed for Washington, Oregon, and Idaho from 1972–1997. Aggregate data include state-level unemployment rates and insured unemployment rates. The analysis focuses on the 1984–1985 tax change period but uses data spanning roughly 1972 through the mid-1990s, with firms and workers as units of observation.
new_fields.institutional_context: From 1972 through 1984, all employers in Washington State paid the same UI payroll tax rate (3.0 or 3.3 percent), effectively eliminating experience rating for 13 years. The federal Tax Equity and Fiscal Responsibility Act of 1982 required all states to have a maximum UI tax rate of at least 5.4 percent by 1985. Because a uniform 5.4 percent rate would have massively over-taxed Washington firms, the state legislature was forced in March 1984 to reinstate experience rating starting in 1985, adopting a benefit-ratio system with tax schedules tied to the state UI trust fund balance. This produced a sudden, externally-imposed dispersion in firm tax rates (ranging from 2.5 to 5.4 percent in 1985, later widening to 0.6–5.42 percent by 1989), with changes plausibly exogenous to firm-level outcomes and neighboring states serving as unaffected comparisons.

title: The Distribution of School Spending Impacts

new_fields.research_question: How much do marginal increases in public K-12 per-pupil school spending causally affect student outcomes such as test scores, high school graduation, and college-going in the United States? How do these effects vary by spending type (capital vs. non-capital), student economic background, and baseline spending levels, and how generalizable are impacts across contexts?
new_fields.data_description: The authors compile a meta-analytic dataset from 31 'credibly causal' studies published over the past 25 years that examine the relationship between K-12 public school spending and student outcomes in the United States. For each study, the authors extract or re-compute a common parameter: the standardized effect of a $1000 per-pupil increase in school spending (sustained over four years, CPI-adjusted to 2018 dollars) on standardized student outcomes, including test scores, high school graduation rates, and college-going rates. Capital spending is amortized over the useful life of assets (~50 years) to make it comparable to non-capital spending flows. The unit of observation is a study-level effect estimate, with outcomes measured (where possible) four years after the spending change. Studies span varied U.S. policy contexts, geographic areas, and baseline spending levels.
new_fields.institutional_context: The meta-analysis restricts inclusion to studies exploiting quasi-random or quasi-experimental policy variation in school spending — for example, school finance reforms, court-ordered funding equalizations, capital bond referenda passing by narrow margins, and state aid formula changes. To be included, a study must demonstrate that its policy-induced spending variation is plausibly exogenous (unrelated to other determinants of student outcomes) and that the policy meaningfully shifted per-pupil spending (analogous to relevance and exogeneity conditions). This contrasts with older observational literature based on partial correlations between resources and outcomes, which are excluded. The institutional diversity — varying state legal contexts (e.g., adequacy lawsuits in Delaware, New York, Maryland, New Mexico, Illinois, Tennessee), funding reform types, and capital versus operational spending shocks — provides the cross-study variation that permits identification of marginal spending effects and heterogeneity analysis.

title: How Do Incumbents Respond to the Threat of Entry? Evidence from the Major Airlines

new_fields.research_question: How do incumbent firms adjust their pricing and capacity decisions when facing a heightened probability of future entry by a competitor, as opposed to actual entry? Do incumbents cut fares preemptively on routes where entry becomes imminent, and are such responses consistent with entry deterrence or accommodation motives?
new_fields.data_description: The authors use the U.S. Department of Transportation's DB1A ticket files (a 10% sample of all domestic tickets) from 1993:Q1 through 2004:Q4, aggregated to the route-carrier-quarter level. Key variables include average logged ticket fares and logged passenger counts for direct (predominantly nonstop) flights on routes defined by pairs of endpoint airports. The sample is restricted to routes among the 59 airports Southwest ever served, and to the seven major incumbent carriers (American, Continental, Delta, Northwest, TWA, United, US Airways). The analysis focuses on 704 routes where Southwest established presence in both endpoint airports, yielding over 19,000 route-carrier-quarter observations within a 25-quarter window (three years before to three years after the threatened-entry event). Supplemental DOT T-100 and On-Time Performance data are used to verify airport operations.
new_fields.institutional_context: Southwest Airlines expanded rapidly during 1993-2004, adding service at 22 new airports. A well-documented regularity (and U.S. antitrust enforcement heuristic) is that once Southwest establishes operations at both endpoints of a route, it becomes very likely to begin flying that route: a simple probit shows presence in both endpoints raises the quarterly probability of route entry to roughly 18.5%, about 70 times higher than otherwise. This creates abrupt, observable shifts in the perceived threat of Southwest's entry on specific incumbent-operated routes, distinct from the moment Southwest actually begins flying. Because Southwest's airport-level expansion is driven by broader network considerations rather than conditions on any single not-yet-served route, these discrete changes in entry threat provide plausibly exogenous variation in competitive pressure facing incumbents on affected routes.

title: Adaptation to Climate Change: Evidence from US Agriculture

new_fields.research_question: How much do agricultural producers adapt to longer-run changes in climate, and to what extent does such adaptation mitigate the damaging effects of extreme heat exposure on crop productivity? Relatedly, what are the implications of observed adaptation capacity for projected impacts of future climate change on US corn yields?
new_fields.data_description: The analysis uses county-level data on US agricultural outcomes, principally yields and revenues for corn and soybeans, for counties east of the 100th meridian. The primary sample period spans roughly 1980–2000, with county-level changes over 20-year windows used as the main unit of observation (supplemented by annual panel data for comparison). Climate data include fine-scale temperature and precipitation measures aggregated to the county level over the April–September growing season, including degree-day exposure above threshold temperatures (e.g., days above 29°C). Additional variables cover agricultural inputs, crop choice, farmer education, and county-level voting patterns used to proxy climate-change beliefs. Projections of future impacts draw on output from 18 global climate models to simulate mid-century changes in temperature and precipitation.
new_fields.institutional_context: Identification exploits substantial spatial heterogeneity in recent medium-run climate trends across US counties between 1980 and 2000: temperatures fell by up to 0.5°C in some counties while rising by as much as 1.5°C in others, and precipitation changed by up to ±40 percent. This naturally occurring variation in 20-year climate trends, combined with county fixed effects and state-level time trends to absorb time-invariant and slowly-varying unobservables, approximates an idealized experiment comparing agricultural outcomes under different realized climate trajectories. Crucially, the observed range of historical climate changes largely spans near-term projections from global climate models, enabling out-of-sample extrapolation to be minimized. Comparing long-run responses to these climate trends with short-run responses to annual weather fluctuations allows the authors to isolate the extent of farmer adaptation to gradual climate change in the US agricultural sector.

title: Managing with Style: The Effect of Managers on Firm Policies

new_fields.research_question: Do individual top managers have a causal effect on corporate investment, financial, and organizational policies, beyond what firm- and industry-level characteristics can explain? To what extent do persistent personal 'styles' of managers shape firm outcomes and performance, and are observable managerial traits such as age cohort and MBA training associated with these styles?
new_fields.data_description: The authors construct a manager-firm matched panel data set spanning top executives across multiple firms over time. The primary manager data come from two sources: the Forbes 800 files (1969-1999), which cover CEOs of the 800 largest U.S. firms, and Execucomp (1992-1999), which records the top five highest-paid executives (CEO, CFO, COO, subdivision CEOs) of about 1,500 publicly traded U.S. firms. These are merged with firm-level financial data to measure outcomes including capital expenditures, investment-to-Q and investment-to-cash-flow sensitivities, acquisitions, leverage, interest coverage, cash holdings, dividends, R&D, advertising, diversification, cost-cutting, and performance. The unit of observation is the firm-year, linked to the identity of its top manager(s). Observable managerial characteristics collected include birth cohort and MBA graduation.
new_fields.institutional_context: Identification of manager-specific effects relies on observing the same top executives moving between different firms during the sample period. Because managers switch employers over their careers, one can separate persistent personal contributions to corporate policy from persistent firm-level factors and time-varying firm characteristics. The sample is therefore restricted to the subset of managers (CEOs and other top executives from Forbes 800 and Execucomp firms) who appear in at least two firms, so that their imprint on policies in one firm can be compared to their imprint in another. This mobility of executives across large U.S. publicly traded corporations, combined with rich longitudinal firm-level financial data, provides the variation needed to disentangle managerial 'style' from firm- and industry-specific determinants of corporate behavior.

title: Going to War and Going to College: Did World War II and the G.I. Bill Increase Educational Attainment for Returning Veterans?

new_fields.research_question: Did military service during World War II, combined with the educational subsidies available to returning veterans through the G.I. Bill, causally increase postsecondary educational attainment—particularly college enrollment and completion—for white men who served? The challenge is disentangling the behavioral effect of service and benefits from selection, since physical and mental fitness screening means veterans and nonveterans in the same birth cohort are not directly comparable.
new_fields.data_description: The analysis uses U.S. Census data to construct measures of educational attainment (years of college completed, college completion rates) and veteran status by birth cohort for white men eligible for World War II service. The authors aggregate individual-level observations within birth cohorts to exploit between-cohort variation in the probability of military service generated by wartime manpower requirements. Supplementary information comes from Selective Service administrative records (e.g., Selective Service and Victory, 1948; Annual Reports of the Selective Service), which document registration, classification, deferment categories (II-occupational, IV-F physical/mental unfitness, II-S college), and induction counts by year (e.g., ~1 million drafted in 1941, >3 million in 1942, ~180,000 in 1946). The unit of observation for estimation is the birth cohort of white men spanning those eligible for WWII service through cohorts born too late to serve.
new_fields.institutional_context: The Selective Service Act of 1940 established conscription in the United States, with successive registrations progressively expanding and then contracting the age range of draft-eligible men as wartime manpower needs evolved. By the later years of WWII, voluntary enlistment was largely prohibited and chronological date of birth became the primary determinant of induction probability, generating sharp differences in service likelihood across adjacent birth cohorts. Cohorts born too late to serve in WWII experienced substantially lower military service rates, though some faced subsequent Korean War service risk. Returning WWII veterans qualified for the G.I. Bill, which provided unprecedented federal subsidies for tuition and living expenses for postsecondary education; roughly 1 in 8 returning servicemen (2.2 million) attended college under the program. The Korean-era draft differed by offering college deferments (Class II-S, introduced 1951), altering selection into service relative to WWII.

title: Disease and Development: The Effect of Life Expectancy on Economic Growth

new_fields.research_question: Does a large, exogenous improvement in population health, as measured by life expectancy at birth, causally raise aggregate economic growth and GDP per capita in less developed countries? The paper further asks how such health improvements affect population size, total GDP, and human capital accumulation over horizons of up to 40 years.
new_fields.data_description: The authors assemble a country-level panel covering roughly 47 countries (initially rich, middle-income, and poor, excluding Africa from the base sample due to data quality) from around 1940 through 1980/2000. Pre-1940 disease-specific mortality data (for tuberculosis, malaria, pneumonia, and other major infectious diseases) come from the League of Nations and national public health sources, accessed via the National Library of Medicine and MIT's Retrospective Collection. Life expectancy, population, total births, fertility, GDP, GDP per capita, GDP per working-age population, investment rates, and human capital measures come from standard international sources including Maddison. Key variables include life expectancy at birth, 'predicted mortality' constructed from baseline disease prevalence interacted with global intervention dates, and economic outcomes measured at decadal frequency.
new_fields.institutional_context: Identification exploits the 'international epidemiological transition' beginning in the 1940s — a wave of global health innovations including the discovery and mass production of penicillin and streptomycin, the deployment of DDT against malaria vectors, new vaccines, and international public health campaigns (e.g., WHO programs). These interventions diffused globally at specific, externally-determined dates and dramatically reduced mortality from diseases like tuberculosis, malaria, and pneumonia. Crucially, countries differed in their pre-1940 baseline exposure to each disease, so the same global intervention produced sharply different gains in life expectancy across countries depending on their initial disease burden. This interaction between pre-intervention cross-country disease prevalence and the timing of worldwide medical breakthroughs generates variation in life expectancy plausibly unrelated to countries' other economic conditions, with no predictive power for life expectancy changes before 1940.

title: The Clean Air Act of 1970 and Adult Mortality

new_fields.research_question: Do sustained reductions in ambient particulate air pollution causally reduce adult and elderly mortality rates? Prior associations from daily time-series and cross-sectional cohort studies may reflect harvesting of already-ill individuals or unobserved confounders correlated with long-run pollution exposure, so the question is whether pollution abatement at the county level produces measurable improvements in one-year adult mortality.
new_fields.data_description: The analysis uses county-level annual data for 1969-1974 covering 501 U.S. counties that account for over 60% of the U.S. population aged 50 and older. County population estimates by five-year age block, gender, and race come from the National Cancer Institute SEER database (1969) and the U.S. Census Bureau (1970-1974). Mortality data are from the National Center for Health Statistics Mortality Detail files, a census of U.S. deaths containing age, race, gender, cause, and county of residence, collapsed into county-race-gender-age cells. Annual monitor-level total suspended particulates (TSPs) concentrations were obtained via FOIA from the EPA, including annual geometric means and counts of daily exceedances. County economic controls (per-capita income, earnings, employment shares, transfer payments, medical and family assistance spending) come from the Bureau of Economic Analysis and Regional Economic Information System.
new_fields.institutional_context: The 1970 Clean Air Act Amendments established National Ambient Air Quality Standards for six pollutants, including TSPs. In 1972, the EPA designated each U.S. county as either 'attainment' or 'nonattainment' for TSPs based on 1970 pollution readings: a county was assigned nonattainment status if its annual geometric mean concentration exceeded 75 µg/m³ or its second-highest daily reading exceeded 260 µg/m³. Polluters in nonattainment counties faced substantially stricter abatement requirements than those in attainment counties. Because regulatory assignment was a discrete function of pre-regulation pollution levels rather than expected mortality trends, counties just above and just below the federal thresholds should be similar in other characteristics, providing exogenous variation in subsequent pollution changes that can be linked to changes in mortality between 1971 and 1972.

title: Estimating Teacher Impacts on Student Achievement: An Experimental Evaluation

new_fields.research_question: Do non-experimental value-added estimates of individual teachers' causal impacts on student achievement, derived from observational data, accurately predict the test score gains those teachers produce when classrooms are assigned to them on a level playing field? The paper also asks how teacher impacts on achievement persist or decay in the years after a student leaves the teacher's classroom.
new_fields.data_description: Data come from the Los Angeles Unified School District (LAUSD) covering elementary grades 2-5 over the school years 2003-04 and 2004-05, with follow-up test score observations for two subsequent years. The experimental sample consists of 78 classroom pairs (156 classrooms, 3,194 students) in which rosters were swapped or not between two teachers in the same school, grade, and calendar track. Key variables include student-level math and reading test scores (current and prior year), classroom and peer characteristics, teacher identifiers, teaching experience, and National Board for Professional Teaching Standards (NBPTS) application status. Pre-experimental administrative records from LAUSD are used to compute multiple value-added teacher effect estimates (gain scores, quasi-gains, levels, student fixed effects), with empirical Bayes shrinkage applied.
new_fields.institutional_context: Identification exploits a field experiment conducted jointly with LAUSD's Program Evaluation and Research Branch. Starting from NBPTS applicants in Los Angeles still employed by LAUSD, researchers paired each applicant with a comparison teacher in the same school, grade, and year-round calendar track who had at least three years of experience. Participating principals constructed two class rosters such that they would be equally satisfied with either teacher receiving either roster; on a pre-specified date, LAUSD centrally and randomly determined whether to swap the rosters in the student information system. This random allocation of intact classrooms to teachers within pairs generated exogenous variation in teacher assignment, enabling a direct test of whether pre-experimental teacher effect estimates predict post-assignment student achievement without bias from non-random classroom sorting.

title: Evaluating the Effect of Teachers' Group Performance Incentives on Pupil Achievement

new_fields.research_question: Does offering monetary performance bonuses to teachers, tied to improvements in their students' scholastic outcomes, causally raise pupil achievement (credit units attempted, matriculation rates, dropout reduction)? How do the effects and cost-effectiveness of such group-based teacher incentives compare with an alternative strategy of providing schools with additional resources (teaching time and staff training) aimed at the same objectives?
new_fields.data_description: The study uses administrative panel data from Israel's Ministry of Education covering all Hebrew secondary (high) school graduates for the years 1993-1997. The unit of observation is the school-year, with annual frequency. Key outcome variables include the average number of matriculation credit units per student, the proportion of students in the matriculation track, the proportion of students earning a matriculation certificate, and school dropout rates (tracked across grades using student-level panel data). The data also contain school and student socio-economic background characteristics used as controls and to construct predicted baselines. The sample comprises the 62 schools in the teacher-incentives program, 22 schools in the parallel resources program (drawn from 75 applicants), and other Israeli secondary comprehensive schools serving as comparison groups.
new_fields.institutional_context: In 1995 Israel's Ministry of Education launched an experimental teacher-incentive tournament in secondary comprehensive schools: schools competed for roughly $1.44m in awards, with the top third of performers (ranked by improvement over regression-predicted baselines) receiving bonuses—75% distributed to teachers as salary supplements, the rest for faculty facilities. Crucially, eligibility was restricted to schools that were the only one of their type (religious girls', religious boys', religious coed, or secular coed) within their community. Since the number of same-type schools per community ranged from 1 to over 25, selection was a sharp threshold function of this count, creating quasi-experimental variation around the cutoff between communities with one versus two same-type schools. Simultaneously, a separate 'resources' program endowed 22 high schools (chosen from 75 applicants) with extra teaching hours and staff training, enabling comparison of treated schools to rejected applicants.

title: The Elasticity of Taxable Income: Evidence and Implications

new_fields.research_question: How responsive is reported taxable income to changes in marginal income tax rates, and does this responsiveness vary across the income distribution? Additionally, what are the separate substitution and income effects of tax changes on reported income, and how do responses differ between narrow taxable income and broader income definitions that include tax preferences?
new_fields.data_description: The analysis uses the NBER panel of individual tax returns (the Continuous Work History File) covering 1979–1990. The panel is constructed from IRS Form 1040 filings by selecting specific social security number endings of primary taxpayers, containing line items from Form 1040 and associated schedules. Sample size is roughly 46,000 observations per year in 1979–1981 and smaller in later years, yielding approximately 100,000 stacked observations across pairs of years. The unit of observation is the tax-filing household-year. Key variables include broad income (an extensive gross income measure), taxable income, marginal federal and state tax rates, filing status, and itemization status. Taxpayers whose marital status changes between paired years are excluded. Observations are constructed as 3-year (and alternatively 1- or 2-year) differences in income and marginal tax rates.
new_fields.institutional_context: The 1980s in the United States featured a series of major federal tax reforms that dramatically altered marginal income tax rates, particularly at the top of the distribution. The top federal marginal rate fell from 70% in 1980 to 28% by 1988, with the bracket structure collapsing from 15 brackets to four. Major legislative changes include the Economic Recovery Tax Act of 1981 (ERTA) and the Tax Reform Act of 1986 (TRA86). Parallel reforms occurred at the state level (e.g., New York reducing its top rate from 14% to 7.875% and its brackets from 13 to five). Because these reforms changed marginal tax rates differentially across income groups and across years—and state reforms generated additional cross-sectional variation—different taxpayers experienced distinct tax-rate changes between any two years, providing variation in net-of-tax rates that is plausibly separable from broader trends like rising income inequality.

title: How Large Are Human-Capital Externalities? Evidence from Compulsory-Schooling Laws

new_fields.research_question: How large are the external returns to schooling — that is, does an increase in the average education level of workers in an area raise individual wages over and above the private return to a worker's own schooling? The paper aims to quantify human-capital externalities to assess whether they are large enough to explain cross-country income differences and to justify education subsidies.
new_fields.data_description: The analysis uses U.S. Census microdata, primarily the 1960, 1970, and 1980 Censuses, with supplementary use of the 1950 and 1990 Censuses. The baseline sample consists of white men aged 40–49 (with some specifications using men aged 30–39). Key variables include weekly/annual wages, years of schooling, quarter of birth, state of birth, and state of residence, which are used to construct individual schooling and state-level average schooling. The unit of observation is the individual worker, matched to state-level averages. Historical state-level data on compulsory school attendance ages and child labor laws between 1920 and 1960 are compiled and merged by state and cohort of birth. Blacks are excluded due to large cohort-specific changes in school quality.
new_fields.institutional_context: Identification exploits variation across U.S. states and birth cohorts in compulsory school attendance laws and child labor laws (jointly, compulsory schooling laws, or CSLs) between roughly 1920 and 1960. These laws set minimum ages at which children could leave school or begin work and changed differentially across states over time, generating plausibly exogenous variation in the schooling of cohorts exposed to them during childhood. Because CSLs faced by a person in childhood are set by social and political forces at the time of passage, they cannot be influenced by that person's later adult wages. Moreover, CSLs primarily affected middle- and high-school attendance — not college — which helps rule out confounding from family background or tastes that would also raise college attendance. Quarter-of-birth variation (Angrist–Krueger) is used as an additional source of exogenous variation in individual schooling.

title: Evaluating the Cost of Conscription in the Netherlands

new_fields.research_question: What is the effect of compulsory military service on individuals' subsequent civilian earnings? Specifically, how much do former Dutch conscripts earn approximately a decade after service compared to non-serving men from the same birth cohorts, once selection into service is accounted for?
new_fields.data_description: The authors combine two Dutch sources. From the Central Bureau for Statistics of the Netherlands, they use a large administrative dataset containing the mean and variance of 1989 and 1990 earnings by month-of-birth cohort for Dutch men. From the Dutch Defense Department, they obtain data on the number of potential recruits and the number of enlisted men by birth cohort, along with information on medical/psychological examination categories and their yearly designations. The unit of observation is thus the birth-cohort (month-of-birth) group rather than the individual. Sample cohorts correspond to men aged roughly 22–30 during the early 1980s, for whom about 36% of a given birth cohort actually served 14 months in the armed forces.
new_fields.institutional_context: In the Netherlands, all able-bodied men were legally required to serve 14 months in the military, but numerous exemptions (medical/psychological disqualification, breadwinner status, educational deferments, conscientious objection) meant only about 36% of a cohort actually served, making individual service status endogenous. Identification exploits year-to-year government decisions about aggregate recruit needs: each year, facing relatively constant total demand but fluctuating supply from older cohorts completing obligations, the government designated certain medical/psychological examination categories as 'special exemption' (buitengewoon dienstplichtig), meaning men in those categories would not be drafted except in emergency. This policy-driven variation in which categories were called up across birth cohorts generates exogenous variation in aggregate enrollment rates that is plausibly unrelated to individual earnings potential.

title: Trade Liberalization, Intermediate Inputs, and Productivity: Evidence from Indonesia

new_fields.research_question: How do reductions in tariffs on final goods versus tariffs on intermediate inputs affect firm-level productivity? In particular, do firms that directly import intermediate inputs experience larger productivity gains from input tariff cuts than non-importing firms that merely compete with imported inputs, and how do these effects compare to productivity gains from tougher import competition on final goods?
new_fields.data_description: The primary data source is the Indonesian annual manufacturing census (Statistik Industri) covering all plants with 20 or more employees from 1991 to 2001. Plant-level variables include output, employment, capital, materials, ownership, exports, and crucially the proportion of imported intermediate inputs. Tariff data are at the highly disaggregated five-digit ISIC level (288 industries for outputs) and cover 1991-2001. Input tariffs are constructed as weighted averages of output tariffs across nearly 300 input industries, with weights based on plant-level cost shares of every input used in production in 1998 (assumed constant over the sample). Production functions are estimated at the three-digit ISIC level (29 industries). The unit of observation is the plant-year.
new_fields.institutional_context: Indonesia undertook substantial unilateral and multilateral trade liberalization during the 1990s, with the largest tariff reductions beginning in 1995 following WTO commitments to reduce bound tariffs to 40 percent or less. Average output tariffs fell from 21 percent in 1991 to 8 percent in 2001, and input tariffs fell from about 14 percent to 6 percent, with large heterogeneity across and within industries (some tariffs remained as high as 170 percent). The tariff structure was escalating, with lower tariffs on intermediate inputs than on final goods (e.g., 0 percent on motor vehicle bodies, 11 percent on components, 31.6 percent on finished vehicles). This cross-industry and over-time variation in both output and input tariffs, combined with plant-level information on import status, provides exogenous variation for identifying productivity effects. The Asian financial crisis of 1997-1998 also falls within the sample period and is controlled for.

title: Why is Manhattan So Expensive? Regulation and the Rise in Housing Prices

new_fields.research_question: Why have housing prices in Manhattan and other major U.S. metropolitan areas risen so dramatically, and to what extent can the gap between market prices and construction costs be attributed to constraints on housing supply rather than to demand-side factors like rising incomes or amenities? The paper seeks to quantify how much of observed high prices reflects barriers to new residential construction, particularly land-use and zoning restrictions.
new_fields.data_description: The authors use multiple data sources. For Manhattan, they draw on U.S. Census Bureau residential building permit data, condominium sales prices (exceeding $600/sq ft in recent years), and physical construction cost data from industry sources (e.g., R.S. Means) for high-rise multifamily buildings. They use the New York City Housing and Vacancy Survey (NYCHVS) for building heights and housing stock characteristics. The Freddie Mac Repeat Sales Price Index and NY-NJ-LI metropolitan area CPI for Shelter provide price trends. For the broader analysis, they use the 1998–99 special metropolitan files of the American Housing Survey covering 21 major metropolitan areas. Supplementary data come from the 1997 Economic Census, County Business Patterns, and the 1998 Survey of Consumer Finances. The unit of observation is individual housing units/buildings within metropolitan areas; the sample period spans roughly 1950–2000.
new_fields.institutional_context: The analysis exploits a basic feature of competitive construction markets: in the absence of supply restrictions, free entry of builders should drive housing prices to equal the marginal cost of production. For high-rise apartment buildings, the marginal cost of an additional housing unit is simply the cost of adding another floor to a building, since land and site-preparation costs are fixed and do not scale with vertical expansion. This makes Manhattan an ideal setting because land costs can be abstracted away. Any persistent, large wedge between sale prices and this marginal construction cost—absent monopoly power or technological barriers to tall buildings, both of which the authors rule out—must reflect a 'regulatory tax' stemming from zoning rules, height limits, environmental lawsuits, permitting delays, community opposition, and other land-use restrictions that raise the effective fixed cost of new development.

title: As certain as debt and taxes: Estimating the tax sensitivity of leverage from state tax changes

new_fields.research_question: How sensitive is corporate leverage to changes in corporate income tax rates, and is this sensitivity symmetric between tax increases and tax cuts? The paper also seeks to determine whether the pattern of leverage responses is more consistent with static or dynamic tradeoff theories of capital structure.
new_fields.data_description: The analysis uses U.S. listed (Compustat) firms over 1989–2011, with firm-year as the unit of observation. Key firm-level variables include long-term leverage, total assets, profitability, asset tangibility, credit ratings (investment grade vs. junk), and effective marginal tax rates. These are combined with hand-collected data on 121 staggered changes in top state corporate income tax rates across U.S. states, along with state-level economic controls such as GDP growth, unemployment, and budget deficits. Firm geographic exposure is measured using detailed information on the location of headquarters, subsidiaries, branches, and plants, enabling county-level and cross-border matching. The pre-treatment average firm has roughly $570 million in debt. The sample also spans contiguous-county pairs straddling state borders for geographic comparisons.
new_fields.institutional_context: The identification setting exploits staggered changes in U.S. state-level top corporate income tax rates between 1989 and 2011. Unlike federal tax changes, which are infrequent and affect all firms simultaneously, state tax changes are numerous (121 in the sample), occur at different times in different states, and affect only firms doing business in the changing state. This creates treated firms (headquartered or operating in states that change rates) and untreated firms elsewhere, including in neighboring states and adjacent counties across state borders where local economic conditions are likely similar but tax policy stops at the state line. State tax changes are plausibly exogenous to individual firms—firms rarely lobby for tax increases—and the geographic discontinuity at state borders helps isolate the tax channel from confounding local business cycle variation and unobserved state-level shocks.

title: Economic Impacts of New Unionization on Private Sector Employers: 1984–2001

new_fields.research_question: What are the causal effects of new unionization on private-sector employers in the United States? Specifically, how does a workplace becoming unionized affect business survival, employment, output, productivity, and wages, and are there indirect 'threat effects' on wages even when unions lose organizing drives?
new_fields.data_description: The analysis combines multiple establishment-level data sources covering U.S. private-sector workplaces that faced union organizing drives between 1984 and 1999, with outcomes tracked through 2001. Union certification election data come from the National Labor Relations Board (NLRB), and contract expiration information comes from the Federal Mediation and Conciliation Service (FMCS). Post-election business survival, employment, and output are drawn from InfoUSA, a commercial database built from telephone listings. For manufacturing establishments, employment, production hours, wages, output, and productivity come from the U.S. Census Bureau's Longitudinal Research Database (LRD). The unit of observation is the establishment facing an NLRB representation election, with outcomes measured over horizons ranging from one to fifteen years after the election.
new_fields.institutional_context: Under the National Labor Relations Act, most new unionization in the U.S. private sector occurs via a secret-ballot election administered by the NLRB. After a card drive establishes sufficient worker interest, the NLRB determines the bargaining unit and holds an on-site election. A simple majority—50 percent plus one vote—is legally required for the union to win certification; if achieved, the employer is legally obligated to bargain 'in good faith' with the certified union, while losing unions gain no such rights. This sharp vote-share threshold generates near-identical sets of workplaces on either side of the majority cutoff, where the union barely wins versus barely loses. Because close election outcomes are plausibly unrelated to underlying establishment characteristics, comparisons around the 50 percent threshold isolate the causal effect of union recognition from selection bias driven by firm profitability or management quality.

title: Identification and Estimation of Treatment Effects with a Regression-Discontinuity Design

new_fields.research_question: Under what conditions can the causal effect of a binary treatment on an outcome be nonparametrically identified and consistently estimated when the probability of receiving treatment jumps at a known threshold of an observable assignment variable? The paper asks what minimal continuity and independence restrictions suffice to recover average treatment effects (including local effects under heterogeneity and self-selection) at the threshold, and how best to estimate them in finite samples.
new_fields.data_description: This is a methodological/theoretical paper in econometrics rather than an empirical study, so it does not analyze a specific dataset. The authors work with a generic setup in which one observes, for each unit i, a binary treatment indicator x_i, an outcome y_i, and a continuous assignment (running) variable z_i whose density is positive in a neighborhood of a known cutoff z_0. Key population objects are the conditional expectations E[y_i|z_i], E[x_i|z_i], and their one-sided limits at z_0. The framework accommodates both deterministic (sharp) treatment assignment as a function of z_i and stochastic (fuzzy) assignment in which only the probability of treatment is discontinuous at z_0. Illustrative applications cited from prior literature include scholarships and test-score cutoffs, college financial aid rules, class-size caps, and school attendance boundaries.
new_fields.institutional_context: Identification is enabled by administrative or institutional rules that generate a known discontinuity in the probability of treatment as a function of an underlying continuous variable. Examples motivating the analysis include: scholarship awards granted only to students whose test scores exceed a threshold (Thistlethwaite and Campbell 1960); college financial aid amounts determined in part by discontinuous functions of GPA and SAT scores (Van der Klaauw 1997); maximum class-size rules that force creation of an additional classroom when enrollment crosses a cutoff (Angrist and Lavy 1999); and geographic school attendance boundaries that create sharp changes in school assignment across otherwise similar neighborhoods (Black 1999). Because units just above and just below the cutoff are assumed similar in unobservables (continuity of E[α_i|z_i] at z_0), the induced jump in treatment probability provides exogenous variation that can be exploited to recover average or local average treatment effects at the threshold.

title: Does Medicare Save Lives?

new_fields.research_question: Does gaining near-universal health insurance coverage at age 65 reduce mortality among severely ill patients? Specifically, do the insurance-related changes that occur when individuals cross the eligibility threshold for the U.S. public health insurance program for the elderly translate into more intensive hospital treatment and lower short- and medium-run death rates for emergency patients with serious conditions?
new_fields.data_description: The authors use administrative hospital discharge records from California covering over 400,000 hospital admissions of patients admitted through the emergency room for 'non-deferrable' conditions—diagnoses whose daily admission rates are statistically indistinguishable on weekends versus weekdays. Key variables include patient age (measured finely around 65), demographic characteristics, diagnosis codes, primary insurer (Medicare, private, Medicaid, uninsured), number of in-hospital procedures, total list charges, transfers to other care units (e.g., skilled nursing facilities), 28-day readmission, and mortality at 7, 28, and 90 days and up to two years post-admission (via matched death records). Supplementary insurance-coverage evidence comes from the 1999–2003 National Health Interview Surveys. The unit of observation is the hospital admission.
new_fields.institutional_context: In the United States, individuals become eligible for Medicare—federal hospital (Part A) and physician (Part B) insurance—on the first day of the month they turn 65, provided they have 10+ years of covered employment (or are spouses of such workers). At the 65th birthday, enrollment jumps sharply: Medicare coverage rises roughly 60 percentage points, the uninsured share falls from about 13% to 3%, supplemental multi-policy coverage rises, and managed care penetration falls as most enrollees choose traditional fee-for-service. For patients already admitted to emergency rooms with severe, non-deferrable conditions, the decision to seek care is unlikely to depend on insurance, so the age-65 threshold generates a sharp, arguably exogenous shift in insurance status, treatment intensity, and utilization review rules for an otherwise comparable population of acutely ill patients.

title: Subways, Strikes, and Slowdowns: The Impacts of Public Transit on Traffic Congestion

new_fields.research_question: How much does urban public transit reduce traffic congestion on roadways, and what are the implied congestion-relief benefits of operating a major metropolitan transit system? The paper further asks whether transit riders are disproportionately drawn from the most congested routes, making their marginal impact on congestion larger than average.
new_fields.data_description: The empirical analysis uses hourly freeway traffic speed data for all major Los Angeles freeways, obtained from roadway sensors, covering the period surrounding a 35-day Los Angeles County Metropolitan Transportation Authority (MTA) work stoppage that began in October 2003. The key outcome variable is average highway delay (minutes per mile), computed as the difference between free-flow and observed travel times, measured at the freeway-hour level and aggregated across peak and off-peak periods. Comparison data from freeways in neighboring counties unaffected by the stoppage are used as a falsification check. The theoretical model is calibrated with Los Angeles metro area inputs (rail market shares, wages, access/egress times, free-flow speeds, delay multipliers) drawn from the transportation literature and Parry and Small (2009).
new_fields.institutional_context: In October 2003, unionized workers at the Los Angeles County Metropolitan Transportation Authority began a 35-day strike that abruptly shut down all MTA bus and rail service across Los Angeles County. The strike generated a sharp, plausibly exogenous cessation of public transit provision at a precisely known start date, while transit service in neighboring counties continued to operate normally. Because the timing of the shutdown was determined by labor negotiations rather than by traffic conditions, and because it occurred at a specific calendar moment, the sudden withdrawal of transit creates a clean temporal break that isolates the short-run causal effect of transit service on highway congestion. The neighboring, unaffected counties provide a geographic placebo setting to verify that the observed change in freeway delays is attributable to the loss of transit rather than to coincident regional shocks.

title: Do Students Benefit from Attending Better Schools? Evidence from Rule-based Student Assignments in Trinidad and Tobago

new_fields.research_question: Does attending a higher-quality secondary school—one that enrolls higher-achieving peers and attracts better teachers and resources—causally improve students' academic outcomes, including end-of-secondary examination performance, passing rates, and qualifications for tertiary education? Do these returns to school quality differ by gender and across the school-quality distribution?
new_fields.data_description: The analysis combines administrative records from Trinidad and Tobago's Ministry of Education. The primary source is the 2000 cohort's Secondary Entrance Assessment (SEA) data, covering all 31,593 fifth-grade test-takers, which records incoming test scores, demographic characteristics (gender, religion, primary school district), and each student's ranked list of secondary school preferences. These records are linked to the 2004 and 2005 Caribbean Secondary Education Certification (CSEC) examination data, the end-of-secondary examinations taken after 10th grade (fifth form). Outcomes include CSEC test scores, number of subjects passed, earning prerequisites for tertiary admission, and whether the student remained in school to sit the CSEC. The unit of observation is the individual student; schools are public (Government, Government-assisted, and Comprehensive).
new_fields.institutional_context: Trinidad and Tobago assigns students to secondary schools at the end of fifth grade using a centralized, rule-based mechanism. Students take the SEA examination and submit a ranked list of preferred secondary schools. The Ministry of Education then applies a largely deterministic, non-linear algorithm that combines a student's SEA score with their stated preferences to place them in a school, producing effective test-score cutoffs for each school. Because students typically rank higher-achieving schools first, high-SEA students concentrate in elite schools while low-SEA students cluster in low-performing ones, creating sharp ability-based sorting across schools. All schools follow a national curriculum and have relatively homogeneous student bodies, so across-school differences mainly reflect peer quality and endogenous teacher/input quality. The assignment rule generates two sources of quasi-exogenous variation: placement differences for students with similar scores but different preferences, and placement differences around score cutoffs among students with the same preferences.
