title: Getting Beneath the Veil of Effective Schools: Evidence from New York City

new_fields.research_question: Which school-level inputs and practices explain differences in school effectiveness at raising student achievement? Specifically, do traditional resource-based inputs (class size, per-pupil expenditure, teacher certification, advanced degrees) predict school effectiveness, or do process-oriented practices (frequent teacher feedback, data-driven instruction, high-dosage tutoring, increased instructional time, and high expectations) account for more of the variation in effectiveness among urban charter schools?
new_fields.data_description: The authors compile original, detailed within-school data for 35 charter schools in New York City. Data collection includes structured principal interviews (covering teacher development, instructional time, data-driven instruction, parental outreach, and school culture), teacher interviews (professional development, policies, culture, assessment), and student interviews (environment, discipline, aspirations), plus lesson plans to gauge curricular rigor and videotaped classroom observations to measure student time-on-task. These inner-workings measures are combined with administrative data on class size, per-pupil expenditure, and teacher credentials, and with student-level outcome data used to estimate each school's effectiveness on math and ELA achievement gains. Results are validated on a larger auxiliary sample of NYC charter schools using site visits, state accountability reports, and school websites.
new_fields.institutional_context: New York City charter schools operate with considerable autonomy over inputs (instructional time, tutoring, teacher feedback, discipline, curriculum), producing wide variation across schools—from arts-integrated schools like Bronx Charter School for the Arts to 'No Excuses' schools such as KIPP Infinity, HCZ Promise Academies, and Democracy Prep. Because many of these oversubscribed charters allocate seats via randomized admission lotteries, the authors can obtain credible, quasi-experimental estimates of each school's causal impact on student test scores by comparing lottery winners and losers within each school. These school-specific effectiveness estimates are then linked to the rich measures of school practices collected through interviews and observations, enabling the study to relate heterogeneity in school policies to heterogeneity in causally-identified school effects.

title: Better Schools, Less Crime?

new_fields.research_question: Does attending a higher-quality, first-choice public school reduce adolescents' subsequent criminal activity in young adulthood? To what extent are any reductions in crime driven by improvements in school quality (teachers, resources) versus changes in peer group composition, and do effects vary by ex ante risk of criminal involvement?
new_fields.data_description: The study links longitudinal administrative student records from the Charlotte-Mecklenburg School district (CMS) to adult arrest records from Mecklenburg County and incarceration records from the North Carolina Department of Corrections. Student-level data include demographics, prior test scores, attendance, suspensions, school enrollment histories, detailed neighborhood characteristics, and school choice application submissions. Crime outcomes are tracked through 2009, up to seven years after random assignment occurring in 2002. The unit of observation is the individual student/lottery applicant in CMS middle and high schools. Outcome measures include arrests (by offense type and severity), days incarcerated, enrollment persistence, on-track status, absences, suspensions, and test scores. The sample comprises lottery applicants to oversubscribed schools under the district's open enrollment plan; roughly 95% of students submitted choices and 40% chose a non-guaranteed school.
new_fields.institutional_context: In 2002, Charlotte-Mecklenburg Schools (CMS) implemented a district-wide open enrollment choice plan, ending neighborhood-based assignment. Families ranked schools, and when a school was oversubscribed, seats were allocated via random lottery. Participation was nearly universal (95% submitted at least one choice), and about 40% applied to a non-guaranteed school, including disproportionately high-risk youth. CMS granted a 'priority boost' in the lottery to applicants eligible for free or reduced-price lunch, shaping allocation by income. Because nearly all applicants remained in CMS regardless of lottery outcome, winners and losers attended schools with similar budgets and governance but differed substantially in peer composition and teacher quality—winners experienced a gain roughly equivalent to moving from one of the district's worst schools to an average one. This randomized allocation of scarce seats at preferred schools generates exogenous variation in school quality and peer exposure.

title: Climate Change, Mortality, and Adaptation: Evidence from Annual Fluctuations in Weather in the US

new_fields.research_question: What is the causal impact of temperature exposure on human mortality and on residential energy consumption (as a measure of defensive/adaptive expenditure) in the United States? Building on these dose-response relationships, what are the projected welfare costs of end-of-century climate change operating through mortality and energy use, and to what extent does adaptation via energy-intensive self-protection (e.g., air conditioning) attenuate temperature-related mortality?
new_fields.data_description: The analysis combines several comprehensive US datasets at fine geographic (county) resolution. Mortality data come from the Compressed Mortality Files covering more than 73.2 million death certificates from 1968–2002, allowing construction of annual age-adjusted county mortality rates and separate rates for four age groups (including infants and the elderly). Residential energy consumption data come from the Energy Information Administration at the state-by-year level. Daily weather data (temperature and precipitation) are drawn from thousands of US weather stations and aggregated into counts of days in temperature bins over the year. End-of-century (2070–2099) daily climate predictions under 'business-as-usual' scenarios come from state-of-the-art climate models, including Hadley Centre data. The unit of observation is the county-year for mortality and state-year for energy.
new_fields.institutional_context: Identification exploits plausibly random year-to-year fluctuations in local weather around long-run climate norms. Because the number of extremely hot or cold days in a given county-year deviates unpredictably from local averages, these annual weather realizations are uncorrelated with other determinants of mortality and energy use once county fixed effects (absorbing permanent locational differences, including sorting on health) and state-by-year fixed effects (absorbing regional shocks and differential trends) are included. Daily temperature is modeled semi-parametrically using bins across the temperature distribution, avoiding functional-form assumptions at the extremes. This weather-shock-based setting provides a transparent, data-driven alternative to Integrated Assessment Models for quantifying the dose-response functions that link temperature to mortality and to defensive energy expenditures, which can then be applied to climate-model projections of future temperature distributions.

title: Who Pays a Price on Carbon?

new_fields.research_question: How is the economic burden of placing a price on carbon dioxide emissions distributed across household income groups in the United States? Which industrial sectors experience the largest cost increases, and to what extent is such a price progressive or regressive depending on how income is measured (annual vs. lifetime) and whether household-size adjustments (equivalence scales, per-capita) are applied?
new_fields.data_description: The analysis combines three main data sources. First, household consumption data come from the 2003 Consumer Expenditure Survey (CES) compiled by the Bureau of Labor Statistics, providing annual household-level expenditures across categories such as food, shelter, electricity, natural gas, gasoline, transportation, healthcare, and apparel, reported by income quintile. Households earning under $7,500 annually are excluded. Second, the 1997 US Bureau of Economic Analysis input-output tables, as implemented in the Carnegie Mellon Economic Input-Output Life Cycle Assessment (EIOLCA) model, provide inter-industry transactions across 491 sectors together with greenhouse gas emissions factors (CO2 and CO2-equivalent per dollar of output). Third, BEA Personal Consumption Expenditure categories are used to match IO sectors to NBER CES consumption categories. Prices are deflated using the CPI with category-specific energy deflators. The unit of observation is the household (and per-capita), stratified by income quintile.
new_fields.institutional_context: The study is set against active US congressional debate over national greenhouse gas policy, including proposals for a federal carbon tax and, more prominently, cap-and-trade programs such as the Waxman-Markey bill anticipated under the Obama Administration. Either instrument would, for the first time in the US, impose a price on each ton of CO2 emitted. The authors analyze a representative price of $15 per ton of CO2 (≈$55 per ton of carbon), a figure within the range of EPA allowance price estimates for Waxman-Markey. Because emission costs are passed forward through the supply chain, the price ripples through inter-industry linkages (e.g., fuel used in farming, fertilizer production) to affect final consumer prices. The input-output structure of the US economy, combined with sectoral emissions intensities, determines how the statutory cost on emitters translates into consumer price increases across heterogeneous consumption bundles of different income groups.
